issue.page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, fifth bullet (protocol overhead)
issue.quoted_clause: An NDR 400 Gb/s InfiniBand link delivers a ~380 Gb/s class useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The difference matters when we are computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.
issue.observed: The two figures compare different nominal link speeds (400 vs 200 Gb/s), which makes the 'difference' partly a speed difference and partly an overhead difference. The intended point—that protocol overhead reduces useful payload below the nominal rate, and that the reduction differs between IB and RoCE2—is valid but obscured by the mismatched baselines. A reader may focus on the 380 vs 180 ratio (≈2.1×) and miss that the nominal ratio is 2× (400/200), so the overhead effect is only ~5% additional.
issue.evidence: 400 × 64/66 ≈ 388 Gb/s (IB line-coding); minus IB headers → ~380. 200 × 64/66 ≈ 194 Gb/s (RoCE2 line-coding); minus Ethernet + RoCE headers → ~180. The overhead fractions are ~3% (IB) and ~7% (RoCE2). The 2.1× vs 2× difference is small.
issue.root_cause: The example uses different link speeds, making the overhead comparison less direct than intended.
issue.correction: Either (a) compare at the same nominal speed: 'A 200 Gb/s InfiniBand HDR link delivers ~190 Gb/s useful payload; a 200 Gb/s RoCE2 link delivers ~180 Gb/s. The ~5% gap matters when computing per-second throughput for a fixed data volume.' Or (b) keep the 400/200 comparison but add: 'At the same nominal speed the gap is smaller (~3% for IB vs ~7% for RoCE2), but it compounds over the 2× speed difference, so the 380/180 ≈ 2.1× ratio slightly exceeds the nominal 2×.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can isolate the protocol-overhead effect from the nominal-speed effect and understand the magnitude of each.

issue.quoted_clause: PagedAttention ensures the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV pack fits
issue.observed: PagedAttention does not 'ensure' the KV pack fits. The KV pack fitting is a memory-capacity question (does 24.1 GB × N concurrent requests fit in the available HBM?). PagedAttention is a memory-management strategy that reduces fragmentation so that the available HBM can be efficiently allocated to concurrent requests. Without PagedAttention, the 24.1 GB per request might still fit, but fragmentation would waste a larger fraction of the available memory, reducing the number of concurrent requests that can be served.
issue.evidence: The book's own terminology (Ch 11, §11.6, Fig 11.2) defines state management as 'PagedAttention (fixed-size KV pages)' and describes it as managing 'how KV is allocated/fragmented.' The capacity question (does it fit?) is separate from the allocation question (can the available memory be used without fragmentation waste?).
issue.root_cause: The word 'ensures' conflates the capacity constraint (total HBM ≥ total KV) with the allocation efficiency (fragmentation overhead).
issue.correction: Change to: 'PagedAttention manages the KV allocation so that the ~24.1 GB per request can be packed into the available HBM with minimal fragmentation overhead.' Or: 'PagedAttention ensures that the available HBM is efficiently allocated to the ~24.1 GB-per-request KV packs (minimizing fragmentation waste).'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence distinguishes between the memory-capacity constraint (does the KV fit?) and the allocation-efficiency role of PagedAttention (can the available memory be used without fragmentation waste?).

issue.quoted_clause: At the canonical workload's ~86 average in-flight requests at 10 rps (L_exec = λ × W_exec ≈ 10 × 8.6 per Ch 4; distinct from the ~100 active-user population) with the median single-turn profile (~27.2 GB/request at 10,365 tokens), the aggregate KV alone is ~86 × 27.2 GB ≈ 2.3 TB
issue.observed: The in-flight count (86) is computed from the single-shot service time (8.6 s), but the per-request KV (27.2 GB) is from the T=1 agentic profile. If the agentic service time (W(1) ≈ 11.52 s no-reuse) were used, in-flight would be ~115 and aggregate KV ~3.1 TB. The 2.3 TB figure is therefore a lower bound, but the text does not say so.
issue.evidence: Little's Law: L = λW. With W = 8.6 s (single-shot), L = 86. With W = 11.52 s (T=1 agentic, no-reuse), L = 115.2. The text mixes the two: 86 (from single-shot W) × 27.2 GB (from agentic T=1).
issue.root_cause: The 86 figure is imported from Ch 4's base-system calculation. The text uses it for the agentic KV argument without noting that the agentic service time would increase the in-flight count.
issue.correction: Add a brief qualifier: 'Using the base-system in-flight count (86, from Ch 4's 8.6 s service time) as a lower bound — the agentic T=1 service time of ~11.5 s would raise this to ~115 — the aggregate KV is already ~2.3 TB, far beyond one host's 436 GB budget.' This preserves the argument's force while being honest about the conservative estimate.
issue.acceptance_test: The text explicitly states whether the 86 in-flight figure is a lower bound, exact, or upper bound for the agentic case, and the reader can see that the conclusion (KV >> 436 GB) is robust to the choice.

issue.quoted_clause: in worst cases a fragment of a character
issue.observed: The phrase 'fragment of a character' implies a token can be a proper subset of a single character's visual representation. In practice, byte-level tokenizers split multi-byte character encodings (e.g., a CJK character encoded in 3 UTF-8 bytes becomes 3 byte-tokens), but each byte-token is a complete byte, not a 'fragment' of a character in the usual sense.
issue.evidence: BPE tokenizers operate on bytes or byte-pairs. A 'fragment of a character' would require sub-byte tokenization, which is not standard. The accurate description is 'a byte that is part of a multi-byte character encoding.'
issue.root_cause: Loose informal phrasing.
issue.correction: Replace 'in worst cases a fragment of a character' with 'in worst cases a single byte of a multi-byte character encoding' or 'a byte-level piece of a character that the encoding spans multiple bytes.'
issue.acceptance_test: The phrase accurately describes byte-level tokenization without implying sub-byte splitting.

issue.quoted_clause: The prefill phase (9.2K tokens) dominates TTFT: at ~1.08 s (Ch 5) vs prefills throughput per host (8×H100) ~19,800 tokens/s (Ch 8)
issue.observed: The canonical scenario states prefill takes ~1.08 s (implying ~8,519 tokens/s per host, ~15% MFU on 8×H100), while Chapter 8's 35% MFU calculation gives ~19,800 tokens/s per host (~0.465 s prefill). This is a 2.32× discrepancy.
issue.evidence: 9,200 tokens / 19,800 tokens/s = 0.465 s (Ch 8 at 35% MFU). 1.29 PFLOP / 1.08 s = 1.19 PFLOPS → 1.19 / 7.912 = 15.1% MFU (Ch 5/6 canonical scenario).
issue.root_cause: The canonical scenario's prefill time (1.08 s) implies ~15% MFU, while Chapter 8 uses 35% MFU for throughput calculations. The text doesn't explain the discrepancy (e.g., TP overhead, kernel inefficiency, or a different MFU assumption).
issue.correction: Either (a) explain why the canonical scenario's prefill time implies lower MFU than Chapter 8's 35% assumption, (b) use consistent MFU assumptions across chapters, or (c) explicitly state that 1.08 s is a budget allocation, not a measurement, and distinguish it from the MFU-derived estimate.
issue.acceptance_test: After correction, the prefill time implied by the canonical scenario should be consistent with Chapter 8's MFU-based calculation, or the discrepancy should be explicitly explained.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6 §3, Reading Telemetry Into a Decision
issue.quoted_clause: aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s vs the 8×H100 aggregate ~7.9 PFLOPS, ~6.5× oversubscribed
issue.observed: The oversubscription calculation uses peak FLOPS (7.9 PFLOPS = 8 × 989 TFLOPS) instead of sustained capacity (2.77 PFLOPS at 35% MFU). The actual oversubscription against sustained capacity is ~18.8×, not 6.5×.
issue.evidence: 8 × 989 TFLOPS = 7,912 TFLOPS ≈ 7.9 PFLOPS (peak). At 35% MFU: 7.9 × 0.35 = 2.765 PFLOPS ≈ 2.77 PFLOPS (sustained). 52 / 2.77 = 18.8×.
issue.root_cause: The text uses peak FLOPS for the comparison without specifying that it's peak. This understates the oversubscription and is inconsistent with Chapter 8's use of sustained (35% MFU) for fleet sizing.
issue.correction: Either (a) use sustained capacity (2.77 PFLOPS) and state ~18.8× oversubscribed, or (b) explicitly state that 7.9 PFLOPS is the peak and note that the actual oversubscription against sustained capacity is ~18.8×.
issue.acceptance_test: After correction, the oversubscription figure should be consistent with Chapter 8's fleet sizing (which uses sustained capacity), or the use of peak should be explicitly justified.

issue.quoted_clause: Deploying a higher-throughput configuration can *reduce* goodput
issue.observed: The text claims goodput 'can reduce' but the example shows goodput is unchanged ('effectively unchanged in this case') and the counterexample shows it rises (50×0.96=48 vs 70×0.94=65.8). The claim 'can reduce' is not directly supported by any example.

issue.root_cause: The claim 'can reduce' is stronger than what the examples demonstrate. The examples show goodput can be unchanged or rise despite a p95 breach, but not that it can reduce.
issue.correction: Either (a) provide an example where goodput actually reduces (compliant fraction drops below 68.6%), or (b) change the claim to 'can fail to improve' or 'can be unchanged despite higher raw throughput'.
issue.acceptance_test: After correction, the claim should be directly supported by the examples provided, or the examples should be extended to support the claim.

issue.quoted_clause: reports up to 525% throughput lift
issue.observed: '525% throughput lift' is ambiguous: it could mean 525% of baseline (5.25×) or 525% improvement (6.25×). The Mooncake paper reports 5.25×, which equals 525% of baseline or 425% improvement. The word 'lift' conventionally means improvement over baseline, which would imply 6.25× and overstate the paper.
issue.evidence: Mooncake (arXiv:2407.00079) reports 'up to 5.25× higher throughput.' 5.25× = 525% of baseline = 425% improvement. '525% lift' read as 'improvement' would mean 6.25×, overstating the paper's result by 1×.
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous use of 'lift' with a percentage that matches the paper's multiplier (5.25× = 525%) but not the standard meaning of 'lift' (improvement over baseline).
issue.correction: Reword to 'up to 5.25× throughput' or 'up to 425% throughput improvement' to match the Mooncake paper's reported figure unambiguously.

issue.quoted_clause: about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case
issue.observed: '11× below' and '180× below' are ambiguous phrasings. 'X× below' is not standard mathematical English and could be misread.
issue.evidence: The intended meaning is that the NVLink ring time is ~1/11th of the InfiniBand time and ~1/180th of the RoCE time (0.54 s vs 6.1 s vs 98 s). 6.1/0.54 ≈ 11.3, 98/0.54 ≈ 181.5.
issue.root_cause: Use of 'X× below' instead of clearer comparative phrasing.
issue.correction: Reword to 'about 1/11th the time of the assumed InfiniBand case and about 1/180th the time of the assumed RoCE case' or 'about 11× faster than... and about 180× faster than...'
issue.acceptance_test: The comparative phrasing unambiguously indicates that the NVLink time is smaller by the stated factor.

issue.quoted_clause: 75% more requests on a real Kimi workload

issue.evidence: The Mooncake paper compares against specific baseline configurations; the text does not identify which baseline. Without the baseline, the reader cannot assess what the 75% represents.

issue.quoted_clause: the cloud legs are $87,600 ≈ $14.04/1K at the default paid-occupancy input
issue.observed: 'Default paid-occupancy input' is unclear. $87,600 = 6 hosts × $20/hr × 730 hr, suggesting 6 hosts (the average-load fleet) running 24/7, but the phrase 'paid-occupancy' implies something different from 'always-on' (used for the $306,600 figure). The reader cannot determine what distinguishes the two cloud legs.
issue.evidence: 6 × $20 × 730 = $87,600. 21 × $20 × 730 = $306,600. The contrast between 'default paid-occupancy' and '21 hosts always-on' is not explained in the text.
issue.root_cause: The phrase references a Ch 16 cost-model parameter without explaining what it means in this context.
issue.correction: Clarify: 'the cloud legs are $87,600 (6 hosts × $20/hr × 730 hr, the average-load fleet) ≈ $14.04/1K and $306,600 (21 hosts always-on) ≈ $49.13/1K.'
issue.acceptance_test: The $87,600 figure's derivation (host count × rate × time) is explicit.

issue.quoted_clause: the ~2% gap is the fractional-slot rounding

issue.quoted_clause: the input tokens billed across the task's calls are amplified by the agentic factor *α* from Section 4 (cumulative-context total vs the single-shot equivalent)
issue.observed: §6 states that billed input tokens are amplified by α, but §4 explicitly states α is NOT the billed token multiplier: "It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier." Under the no-prefix-cache policy, billed input amplification at T=3 is 41,990/9,200 ≈ 4.56×, not α ≈ 1.27×. Under perfect prefix cache it is 11,795/9,200 ≈ 1.28× ≈ α. The §6 claim is only true under perfect prefix caching, and the cache policy is not specified.
issue.evidence: §4: "α measures retained/accumulated task context... It is not the total model-processed or API-billed token multiplier." §4 event ledger: task_input = 41,990 at T=3 (no-reuse), billed no-cache = 42,485 total. 42,485/9,500 ≈ 4.47× vs α(3) = 1.27×. Under perfect cache: 12,290/9,500 ≈ 1.29× ≈ α. The §6 comment tells the reader to use α as the billed amplifier without stating the cache policy.
issue.root_cause: §6 cost formula comment conflates retained-context amplification (α) with billed-token amplification, contradicting §4's explicit warning.
issue.correction: Either (a) specify "under perfect prefix caching, billed input is approximately α × single-shot input" and note that under no caching the amplification is ~4.5×, or (b) replace α with the correct billed-token multiplier for the stated policy, or (c) remove the claim that α amplifies billed tokens and instead say the cost formula's tokens/call term must be computed from the execution-trace totals under the stated cache policy.
issue.acceptance_test: After correction, §6's cost formula comment must not state or imply that α is the billed-token multiplier without specifying a cache policy under which that is true, and must not contradict §4's explicit statement that α is not the billed multiplier.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19 §4, Tool-call latency budget and W(T) scope note
issue.quoted_clause: λ_tool ≈ 100 ms (median, tool backend) ... The tool/retrieval leg here uses Chapter 17's ~133 ms/turn rate
issue.observed: Two different tool-backend rates are used for the same conceptual quantity: λ_tool ≈ 100 ms in L_agent (the orchestration overhead) and λ_tool/retr ≈ 133 ms in W (the full service time). The text acknowledges the inconsistency ("Chapter 17 §8 itself notes that a single model should use one rate consistently") but does not resolve it. A reader trying to apply the book's framework must choose between 100 ms and 133 ms for tool latency without guidance on which is correct.
issue.evidence: L_agent = 120 + 100 = 220 ms/turn. W uses 133 ms/turn for the tool leg. At T=3: 3×100 = 300 ms vs 3×133 = 399 ms, a 99 ms difference. The text explicitly notes the inconsistency but leaves it unresolved.
issue.root_cause: Chapter 17 and Chapter 19 independently chose different tool-latency rates without a unifying decision.
issue.correction: Either unify to one rate (state which and why), or explicitly explain why the two rates measure different things (e.g., L_agent's 100 ms is search+SQL median while Ch 17's 133 ms includes retrieval+rereanking) and give the reader a rule for choosing.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can determine which tool-latency rate to use in a given calculation without guessing, and the text explains any remaining difference.

issue.quoted_clause: A vendor pitches the architect a newer, cheaper model: "just swap it in — it scores better on the bench."
issue.observed: The mini-case is purely narrative. It describes what happens when the factory works (the gate catches a regression) but requires no calculation, no decision under uncertainty, no application of the chapter's promotion-gating economics, and no reasoning the reader could not do without the chapter. Compare Ch 19 §8 or Ch 20 §8, which require the reader to compute expected values, percentiles, or host counts.
issue.evidence: The mini-case contains no numbers to compute, no competing interpretations to resolve, and no architecture consequence that follows from a calculation. It is a story about a successful gate, not a test of the reader's ability to use the chapter's tools.
issue.root_cause: Mini-case written as illustration rather than as an exercise requiring the chapter's reasoning.
issue.correction: Add a quantitative decision: e.g., given a candidate that improves quality by X% but increases p95 TTFT by Y ms, and a canary budget of Z requests, should the architect promote, reject, or extend the canary? Require the reader to compute the blast radius, the expected cost of a bad release, or the canary duration needed to detect a regression of a given size.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case requires at least one calculation or decision that uses the chapter's promotion-gating economics or measurement framework, and the answer is not stated in the preceding text.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19 §4, Tool-call latency budget and W(T) scope note
issue.quoted_clause: the LLM's short decision step to formulate the tool call ... averages ~120 ms for a 10,000-token context
issue.observed: The 120 ms "model's tool-call decision step" in L_agent is not clearly related to the γ decode in W. In the per-turn convention, each turn is one model invocation producing γ = 65 tokens, which at 25 ms/token takes 1,625 ms. The 120 ms corresponds to ~4.8 tokens at 25 ms/token. The text does not explain whether the 120 ms is (a) a subset of the 65-token output (the tool-call portion) or (b) a separate short generation. If (a), the remaining ~60 tokens (1,500 ms) of reasoning are not counted in L_agent; if (b), the per-turn convention (one invocation) is inconsistent.
issue.evidence: 120 ms / 25 ms per token = 4.8 tokens. γ = 65 tokens × 25 ms = 1,625 ms. The text says L_agent includes "the LLM's short decision step" (120 ms) but W includes the full γ decode (1,625 ms). The relationship between these two quantities is not stated.
issue.root_cause: L_agent and W decompose the model's per-turn work differently without an explicit mapping.
issue.correction: State explicitly: "The 120 ms is the decode time for the ~5 tool-call tokens within the 65-token γ output; the remaining ~60 reasoning tokens (~1,500 ms) are counted in W's γ decode, not in L_agent." Or, if the 120 ms is a separate generation, reconcile it with the one-invocation-per-turn convention.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can determine which portion of the model's per-turn time is counted in L_agent and which is counted in W, and the two decompositions are consistent with the one-invocation-per-turn convention.

issue.quoted_clause: model calls/task × tokens/call × $/token
issue.observed: The cost formula uses "tokens/call" as if it were a single value, but tokens per call varies across calls in the event-level ledger (9,200 for call 1, 10,065 for call 2, 10,930 for call 3, 11,795 for call 4 at T=3). The ≈ sign indicates approximation, but the simplification is not acknowledged.
issue.evidence: Event ledger: call inputs are 9,200 / 10,065 / 10,930 / 11,795. A single "tokens/call" cannot represent these.
issue.root_cause: Conceptual formula written with a scalar where a vector is needed.
issue.correction: Either note that "tokens/call" is an average across calls and varies with T, or rewrite as Σ over calls of input(call_i) × $/input-token + Σ over calls of output(call_i) × $/output-token.
issue.acceptance_test: The formula or its surrounding text acknowledges that per-call token counts vary and states how the single-term form is an approximation.

issue.page_hint: Ch 21 §3, Cost of a bad ungated release
issue.observed: The input rate is given to 16 significant digits (24.97066185897436) in an illustrative worked example. The output is rounded to 4 significant digits ($5,394). The excessive input precision is inconsistent with the [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] label and with the book's general practice of using ~3 significant figures for illustrative values.
issue.evidence: 24.97066185897436 has 16 significant digits. The same rate appears elsewhere as ~$24.97/1K (3 significant digits).
issue.root_cause: Full-precision division result pasted into prose without rounding to the context's precision.
issue.correction: Round the input rate to ~$24.97/1K (matching the rest of the book) and recompute: 216,000 × 24.97 / 1,000 = $5,393.52 ≈ $5,394. Same for the cloud rate: ~$14.04/1K → 216,000 × 14.04 / 1,000 = $3,032.64 ≈ $3,033 (or keep $3,032 if using 14.038).
issue.acceptance_test: Input rates in illustrative examples use the same precision (~3 significant figures) as elsewhere in the book, and the output is consistent with that precision.

issue.quoted_clause: (The earlier example crossed the boundary by summing two *incl.-300-output* totals as if they were call inputs.)

The §3 hand-worked trace reports retained-context totals (10,000, 10,350) but does not sum them as call inputs. This may refer to content in a previous chapter or a removed passage.

issue.root_cause: Stale cross-reference to a removed or relocated example, or reference to content outside this chunk.
issue.correction: Identify the specific earlier example and cite it precisely (chapter/section), or remove the parenthetical if the example no longer exists.

issue.quoted_clause: the same table is carried in the archetypes are reference points, not measured clusters
issue.observed: Grammatically broken sentence — two clauses merged without conjunction or punctuation. Reads as if 'the same table is carried in the archetypes' and 'are reference points, not measured clusters' were accidentally fused.

issue.acceptance_test: The sentence parses as a single grammatical clause with a clear subject and predicate.

issue.quoted_clause: [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]])
issue.observed: Double closing parenthesis — an extra ')' after the evidence labels.
issue.evidence: Direct text inspection. The string ends with ']])' where only one ']' and one ')' (or neither, depending on intent) is expected.
issue.root_cause: Typographical error during editing.

issue.quoted_clause: the baseline's 320 ms compute is a worst-case figure carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1 … The 450 ms is a service-time sum with no queueing term
issue.observed: Internal ambiguity: 'prefill-queue inflation' naturally reads as queue-wait time included in the 320 ms, but the text simultaneously asserts 'no queueing term' and 'a real queueing delay sits on top.' The two statements appear contradictory unless 'inflation' means resource-contention slowdown rather than queue-wait time — a distinction the text never makes explicit.
issue.evidence: Three clauses in the same paragraph: (a) 'carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1', (b) 'service-time sum with no queueing term', (c) 'a real queueing delay sits on top.' Reading (a) as queue-wait time contradicts (b) and (c).
issue.root_cause: The term 'prefill-queue inflation' is used without defining whether it denotes queue-wait time or compute-time inflation from resource contention at high load.
issue.correction: Replace 'prefill-queue inflation' with an unambiguous phrase, e.g. 'compute-time inflation from resource contention at ρ near 1 (not queue-wait time)' or 'prefill compute slowdown under heavy GPU contention.' Add one sentence explaining the physical mechanism (e.g., time-slicing between concurrent prefill work inflates each request's wall-clock prefill time).
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can determine from the text alone whether the 320 ms includes queue-wait time or only compute-time inflation, and the answer is consistent with 'no queueing term' and 'queueing sits on top.'

issue.quoted_clause: compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50
issue.observed: The mechanism by which per-request compute drops from 320 ms to 120 ms when offered load falls from ~2.0 rps to ~1.3 rps is asserted but not explained. The reader is not told whether the drop comes from reduced resource contention, reduced queue-wait time, smaller effective batch size, or some combination.
issue.evidence: The text states the drop (320→120 ms) and attributes it to 'the queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps' but never specifies the physical mechanism. At ρ = 0.65 (1.3/2.0), queuing theory predicts shorter queues, but the text has already stated the 450 ms baseline has 'no queueing term,' so the reader cannot reconcile the two.
issue.root_cause: The causal link between load reduction and compute-time reduction is left implicit.
issue.correction: Add one sentence explaining the mechanism, e.g. 'At ρ near 1 the GPU time-slices prefill work across many concurrent requests, inflating each request's wall-clock prefill time; at 1.3 rps the contention eases and prefill returns to its uncontended ~120 ms.' Ensure this is consistent with the 'no queueing term' framing from CH26-03.
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can explain why compute time decreases when load decreases, and the explanation is consistent with the 'no queueing term' statement.

issue.quoted_clause: through attention re-architecture alone — the parameter count is unchanged, so the saving is architectural, not a smaller model
issue.observed: The phrase 'the parameter count is unchanged' is ambiguous. V4-Pro is 1.6 T parameters; V3.2's parameter count is not stated in this chunk. If V4 and V3.2 have different total parameter counts, the claim is wrong as written. The claim is likely intended to mean 'the attention-related parameters that determine KV size are unchanged,' but the text says 'parameter count' without qualification.
issue.evidence: The sentence appears in the context of KV-cache reduction (~10–14×). KV size depends on attention dimensions (layers × heads × head_dim), not total parameter count (dominated by MoE experts). V3.2's parameter count is not provided, so the reader cannot verify 'unchanged.'
issue.root_cause: Ambiguous referent for 'parameter count' — total parameters vs. attention parameters.
issue.correction: Specify which parameter count is unchanged, e.g. 'the attention dimensions (layers, heads, head_dim) that determine KV size are unchanged' or provide V3.2's parameter count for comparison.
issue.acceptance_test: The reader can determine which parameter count is claimed to be unchanged and verify it against stated figures.

issue.quoted_clause: | Fine-tuning | N/A | N/A | Memory + interconnect | … | | Training | N/A | N/A | Compute + interconnect | … |

issue.acceptance_test: Every matrix row either connects to a pattern in this chapter or is explicitly marked as a cross-chapter pointer outside this chapter's pattern scope.

issue.quoted_clause: **Quantization decision record.** The architecture decision record names the active constraint, affected tensors, and proposed deployment configuration.
issue.observed: The Quantization decision record paragraph is placed between the workload-to-strategy matrix and Fig 26.1 (workload fingerprints). For quantization specifically: …'

issue.quoted_clause: DeepSeek-V4 (A.3) … Kimi K3 (A.4) … Qwen3.8-Flash-Next (A.5) … GLM-5.3-Flash (A.6) … A.8 … A.10
issue.observed: The A.N cross-references (A.3, A.4, A.5, A.6, A.8, A.10) are offset by +2 from the explicit section numbers shown in the markdown (sections 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8). The offset is consistent, suggesting the two unnumbered sections ('The Signal in One Paragraph' and 'How to read this appendix') are counted as A.1 and A.2. If the rendered book displays sections with their explicit markdown numbers (1–8), readers looking for 'A.3' will not find it.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'The Signal in One Paragraph', efficiency lever 3

issue.figure: Figure 15.1 — FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic
issue.issue: In the BEFORE panel, the red annotation reads "O(L²) HBM traffic: every query re-reads the K/V row-block". The colon attributes the O(L²) traffic to K/V row-block re-reads — but K/V row-block reads from HBM are O(L²) in BOTH the naive and FlashAttention implementations (each query tile still needs all K/V). The quantity that actually drops is the materialized L×L intermediate, which the AFTER panel mentions only as "no L×L intermediate at HBM" with no complexity label. Juxtaposing an "O(L²)" label on the left against no complexity label on the right invites the reader to infer that FlashAttention changes the asymptotic HBM-traffic class — precisely the "quadratic-to-linear swap" misconception that the book's own prose on PDF 247 explicitly warns against ("the precise I/O complexity is more nuanced than a clean quadratic-to-linear swap").
issue.evidence: Fig 15.1 BEFORE panel: "O(L²) HBM traffic: every query re-reads the K/V row-block". AFTER panel: "K/V reused per tile — no single global K/V pass; no L×L intermediate at HBM" (no big-O label). Prose on PDF 247 / printed 227: "the precise I/O complexity is more nuanced than a clean quadratic-to-linear swap, but the materialized-intermediate traffic is what drops". The caption scopes the "read once" claim but does not scope the O(L²) label.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the BEFORE annotation so the O(L²) attaches to the intermediate (e.g., "O(L²) intermediate traffic: the L×L scores matrix is written to HBM and re-read"), and/or add a matching qualifier to the AFTER panel (e.g., "K/V reads still O(L²) — fewer round-trips, not sub-quadratic"). Rebuild and confirm a reader cannot infer an asymptotic-class change from the figure alone, consistent with the PDF 247 prose.

issue.figure: none (prose, §16.8 mini-case; no figure on this page)

issue.issue: The caption links the figure's 4-host fleet to 'the same rule' that yields '~21 hosts' for the canonical peak, but the two numbers are on different bases: the rule alone gives 3 hosts for the 5.5 req/s burst, and the drawn N = 4 includes the +1 N-1 failover reserve, which applied to the canonical peak would give 22 (the book's case (ii)), not 21.

issue.issue: Row C's derivation uses 24.9037 GB per whole context without stating the context length it represents, so the number cannot be independently checked from the table; the implied length must be confirmed against the canonical whole-context used elsewhere because C = 17 (not 18) is what produces the canonical 21 hosts.
issue.evidence: Table 17-1 row C, quoted: 'per-host whole-context KV slots: 436 GB / 24.9037 GB = 17.51 -> floor 17' | '17 slots'. Arithmetic checks: 436 / 24.9037 = 17.5074 -> 17.51 -> floor 17 (correct), and 40 x 8.6 / 17 = 20.24 -> 21 hosts (correct). But 24,903.7 MB / 2.62144 MB per token (the book's canonical FP16 full-MHA 70B KV per token) = 9,500.0 tokens exactly, i.e. the table silently assumes a 9,500-token whole context. The book elsewhere derives 1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200 as an in-book token sum; if 9,200 were the KV whole-context, per-context KV = 24.117 GB, C = floor(436 / 24.117) = 18, and the canonical host count becomes ceil(40 x 8.6 / 18) = 20, not 21. The exact 9,500 match makes the benign reading (8,000 in + 1,500 out = 9,500) likely, but the table never says so. NOT VERIFIED against Chs. 4/17/20 in this pass.
issue.root_cause: The derivation shows the division but omits the quantity being divided into (context tokens), so the one input a reader needs in order to re-derive C is missing.
issue.correction: Add the context length to the Meaning cell, e.g. '436 GB / 24.9037 GB (9,500-token whole context at 2.62 MB/token FP16 full-MHA) = 17.51 -> floor 17', and confirm that 9,500 is the same whole-context used in the Ch. 4 workload table and the Ch. 17/20 host counts.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 17-1 states the token count behind 24.9037 GB; that token count matches the canonical whole-context stated in Ch. 4 / Table 4-2; and re-deriving C and N_min from the stated context reproduces 17 slots and 21 hosts.

issue.quoted_clause: Continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is nearly mandatory to achieve the 1.2 s TTFT budget under 10 rps input-heavy traffic; without it, prefill of 9.2 K tokens per request would serialize and push TTFT well above 2 s.

issue.evidence: Ch 4 canonical box gives 10 rps and 9.2K input tokens; Ch 4 derivation notes and Ch 8 planning rate give ~19,800 tok/s per host. Ch 4 later says the canonical workload needs ~6 hosts at average and ~21 at peak.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §6 (Architecture Consequence), decode levers and P/D paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: higher-bandwidth memory topologies (NVSwitch, HBM3e) ... a decode cluster optimized for bandwidth (faster HBM, larger NVLink domains)
issue.observed: NVSwitch and NVLink are inter-GPU interconnect technologies, not HBM memory bandwidth. HBM3e is per-GPU memory. The text conflates memory bandwidth with interconnect bandwidth.

issue.root_cause: Terminology and resource-model conflation.
issue.correction: Separate HBM3e (per-GPU memory bandwidth) from NVLink/NVSwitch (inter-GPU communication). Explain that NVSwitch helps tensor-parallel sharding, not single-GPU weight-read bandwidth.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace the phrase with correct categories and add one sentence on when each helps; no clause may call NVSwitch a memory topology.

issue.quoted_clause: The model is large enough to answer factual enterprise questions without fine-tuning
issue.observed: No evidence or benchmark is given that a 70B dense model meets the >85% factual-accuracy target. The quality target is an assumption, not a demonstrated model property.
issue.evidence: Table 4-1 labels the quality target [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; no model evaluation is cited.
issue.root_cause: Capability claim presented as fact.
issue.correction: Say that the canonical assumes a 70B dense model meets the quality target and that this must be validated against the quality dimension.
issue.acceptance_test: The claim is tied to a quality evaluation or explicitly labeled as an assumption.

issue.quoted_clause: Multi-region deployment (active-active) provides availability but doubles the infrastructure cost.
issue.observed: Active-active multi-region can require more than 2× cost because of capacity duplication, replication, cross-region traffic, and failover policy. 'Doubles' is a lower-bound or illustrative estimate, not a general law.
issue.evidence: The same bullet later says the topology is UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED and must be costed separately.
issue.root_cause: False precision in an operational-cost claim.
issue.correction: Replace 'doubles' with 'can roughly double or more, depending on failover and replication policy; must be costed separately.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer asserts a universal 2× multiplier and cross-references the unpriced-topology caveat.

issue.quoted_clause: Input-to-output ratio: 9,200 ÷ 300 ≈ 30× more input tokens than output tokens. This ratio is [canonical scenario][DERIVED] from the canonical numbers and is the single biggest factor in why this workload is KV-capacity- and prefill-dominated rather than decode-throughput-limited.
issue.observed: The input/output ratio is a signal, not the single determinant. KV capacity depends on context length and concurrency; decode can dominate wall-clock latency even in input-heavy workloads. The chapter itself later says decode is ~87% of per-request wall-clock.
issue.evidence: Ch 2 and Ch 4 both distinguish resource regime from wall-clock latency; measured per-phase utilization and goodput are required to confirm dominance.
issue.root_cause: Claim strength exceeds the evidence.
issue.correction: Soften to 'a first signal' and point to measured per-phase utilization and goodput before concluding dominance.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer claims a single biggest factor; it cross-references Ch 2/Ch 8 and the need for measurement.

issue.quoted_clause: a 70B FP16 model on one host meets the per-request latency SLO (TTFT/TPOT)
issue.observed: Ch 2's arithmetic is a first-order analytical lower bound that excludes attention overhead, MFU, communication, and scheduling. 'Meets' overstates what has been shown.
issue.evidence: Ch 2 repeatedly labels the arithmetic 'Analytical bound — not a benchmark'; Ch 4 later says both bounds must be confirmed by benchmark goodput.
issue.root_cause: Claim strength exceeds the analytical evidence.
issue.correction: Say 'is analytically feasible under the first-order model; benchmark confirmation is required.'
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence carries the analytical/benchmark qualifier.

issue.quoted_clause: From the token-level work alone (which we worked through in this chapter), the architect can already establish: ... the workload is input-heavy
issue.observed: Token-level work defines the unit and the request shape, but it cannot establish that the workload is input-heavy. That requires the workload characterization in Ch 4 (prompt, retrieved context, output mix).
issue.evidence: Ch 4 is where the token profile is quantified; Ch 1 only introduces the token as a unit.
issue.root_cause: Premature conclusion in the mini-case.
issue.correction: Say 'assuming the request shape includes retrieved context, the working hypothesis is input-heavy; Ch 4 quantifies it.'
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case distinguishes assumption from derivation and does not claim token-level work alone establishes input-heaviness.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2 §1 'The work unit changes with the generator'; Ch 3 §1 'Alternative inference: the token is not the execution step'
issue.quoted_clause: The prefill/decode split describes the autoregressive text path developed here. It does not describe every generative workload. ... Dense versus MoE describes parameter allocation. Autoregressive versus diffusion generation describes a different axis...
issue.observed: The diffusion/video material is a multi-page digression that interrupts the core prefill/decode and dense-vs-MoE/KV threads before those mental models are consolidated. It introduces many new concepts (DDPM, SDE, flow matching, LLaDA, block diffusion, Wan2.2) at a point where the chapter promises a narrower architectural question.
issue.evidence: Ch 2's Architect's Question is about prefill/decode and system constraints; Ch 3's is about dense vs MoE, total vs active parameters, and KV cache. The diffusion sections are not required for those core arguments.
issue.root_cause: Scope creep and misplaced depth.
issue.correction: Move the diffusion/alternative-inference material to an appendix or a later chapter, or reduce it to a short scope note with a cross-reference.
issue.acceptance_test: The main chapter threads flow from prefill/decode and dense/MoE to KV without a multi-page diffusion detour; the diffusion material has a clear home.

issue.quoted_clause: At 10 concurrent full-context requests the MHA figure is ~241 GB of KV on top of the 140 GB weights — pressing against the 640 GB pool well before concurrency reaches 100.
issue.observed: At 10 concurrent requests, 241 GB KV + 140 GB weights = 381 GB, leaving ~259 GB free. The pool is not 'pressing' at 10; it becomes tight around ~20 full-context requests.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise wording.
issue.correction: State the actual total at 10 requests and the approximate concurrency at which the pool tightens.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence gives 381 GB at 10 requests and says the pool tightens around ~20, not at 10.

issue.quoted_clause: long enough for Little's Law and service-time occupancy to reach the modeled steady state (seconds of sustained 40 rps)
issue.observed: Little's Law steady state requires at least the service-time scale W ≈ 8.6 s, not merely 'seconds.' A 2-second burst would not populate the queue to λ·W.
issue.evidence: The chapter's own W_exec ≈ 8.6 s.
issue.root_cause: Imprecise duration.
issue.correction: Say 'for at least the service-time scale (~8.6 s), not a one-second spike.'
issue.acceptance_test: The burst duration is tied to W_exec ≈ 8.6 s.

issue.quoted_clause: Self-host — 21-host peak KV-screen fleet | $155,816.93 | ≈ $24.97
issue.observed: The figure $155,816.93 carries cent-level precision for an illustrative included-cost input. The surrounding numbers are rounded estimates; the precision implies a derivation that is not shown.
issue.evidence: The sidebar labels all four rows as illustrative included-cost inputs, not measured duty cycles.
issue.root_cause: False precision.
issue.correction: Round to a defensible precision (e.g. ~$156K/mo) or show the exact derivation if the cents are meaningful.
issue.acceptance_test: The self-host figure is rounded consistently with its illustrative status, or its derivation is shown.

issue.quoted_clause: the auto-regressive pass reuses the same parameters every step
issue.observed: The hyphenated form 'auto-regressive' appears here, while the same chapter and the rest of the manuscript use 'autoregressive' (no hyphen) consistently (e.g., 'autoregressive model', 'autoregressive decode', 'autoregressive text path').
issue.evidence: Search of the chunk: 'autoregressive' appears ~15 times without hyphen; 'auto-regressive' appears once (this instance). The standard spelling in ML literature and in the rest of this book is 'autoregressive'.
issue.root_cause: Typographical inconsistency; the hyphenated form slipped in during drafting.
issue.correction: Change 'auto-regressive' to 'autoregressive' at this one location.
issue.acceptance_test: A global search for 'auto-regressive' (with hyphen) in the built PDF returns zero hits.

issue.page_hint: Ch 2, §6 Architecture Consequence, decode levers bullet
issue.quoted_clause: continuous batching (vLLM, PagedAttention) to amortize weight reads across many tokens in flight
issue.observed: PagedAttention is listed in the same parenthetical as vLLM as if it were a form of continuous batching. The book's own vocabulary table (same chapter, §1) explicitly distinguishes them: PagedAttention is a memory-allocation scheme for the KV cache, not a batching technique. vLLM is a serving engine that implements both continuous batching and PagedAttention.
issue.evidence: Vocabulary table in Ch 2 §1: 'PagedAttention — a memory-allocation scheme for the KV cache (splits it into fixed-size pages, cuts fragmentation/waste) — not a way to reduce the amount of KV state.' The architecture-consequence bullet conflates the two by listing them as co-referents of 'continuous batching'.
issue.root_cause: The parenthetical was intended to name the system (vLLM) and its key technique (PagedAttention) that together enable efficient continuous batching, but the syntax reads as if PagedAttention is a type of continuous batching.
issue.correction: Reword to separate the mechanism from the implementation, e.g.: 'continuous batching (as implemented in vLLM, which pairs it with PagedAttention for KV memory management) to amortize weight reads across many tokens in flight.' This preserves the information while respecting the book's own terminological distinction.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer syntactically equates PagedAttention with continuous batching; a reader who has just read the vocabulary table sees no contradiction.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3, §3 Worked Example, Table 3-2 caption and 'Why MoE saves compute' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: the active fraction for top-2-of-8 routing is ~24–27% of total, not single-digit
issue.observed: The stated range '24–27%' does not follow cleanly from the numbers in the table. The table gives: 2 × 5.7B / (8 × 5.7B) = 25% of expert mass, and 12.8B / 47B = 27.2% of total. The lower bound of 24% has no derivation shown. A reader checking the arithmetic finds 25% and 27%, not 24% and 27%.
issue.evidence: Table 3-2: '2 × 5.7B routed experts + ~1.4B always-on = 12.8B (~27% of the ~47B total; ~24% counting expert-FFN mass alone).' The 24% figure for 'expert-FFN mass alone' would require 11.4B / 47B = 24.3%, but that mixes the numerator (expert-only active) with the denominator (total including always-on). The consistent expert-only fraction is 11.4/45.6 = 25%. The total fraction is 12.8/47 = 27.2%.
issue.root_cause: The 24% appears to be 11.4/47 (active expert params / total params), which is a mixed-basis ratio. The text labels it 'counting expert-FFN mass alone' but the denominator is still the full 47B, not the 45.6B expert mass.
issue.correction: Either (a) change the range to '~25–27%' (25% = expert-mass fraction 2/8; 27% = total fraction 12.8/47), or (b) if the 24% is intended, show the derivation explicitly: '11.4B active expert / 47B total ≈ 24%'. Option (a) is cleaner and avoids the mixed-basis confusion.
issue.acceptance_test: Every percentage in the 24–27% (or corrected) range has a visible numerator/denominator in the adjacent text or table, and no mixed-basis ratio appears without explicit labeling.

issue.quoted_clause: a 100k × 4096 table holds 100,000 × 4,096 ≈ 409.6M ≈ 0.4B params — a rounding error next to a 70B model, but not zero
issue.observed: 0.4B / 70B ≈ 0.57%. Calling 0.57% 'a rounding error' slightly overstates the negligibility. In a 70B model, 0.4B parameters is small but not at the level of a rounding error (which would imply <0.1%). The 'but not zero' qualifier partially rescues the sentence, but the phrase 'rounding error' could mislead a reader into thinking the embedding table is architecturally irrelevant.
issue.evidence: 409.6M / 70,000M = 0.00585 = 0.585%. In a 70B model, this is a small but non-trivial fraction. For a 7B model (409.6M / 7,000M = 5.8%), it would be far from a rounding error.
issue.root_cause: Rhetorical shorthand ('rounding error') used for a 0.6% figure. The intent is 'negligible for sizing purposes,' which is true, but the phrase is imprecise.
issue.correction: Replace 'a rounding error next to a 70B model, but not zero' with 'a small fraction (~0.6%) of a 70B model — negligible for capacity planning, but not zero.' This preserves the point (it's small) without the imprecise 'rounding error' label.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence no longer uses 'rounding error' for a 0.6% figure; the quantitative relationship is stated explicitly.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3, §1, 'Alternative inference: the token is not the execution step' (entire subsection, ~2 pages)
issue.quoted_clause: A diffusion language model can itself be dense or MoE. The active-parameter count still matters, but final output tokens no longer count the model's work on their own.
issue.observed: The subsection is technically correct and well-sourced, but its density and length are disproportionate to the architectural leverage it provides in a 458-page AI Solution Architecture handbook. It covers 8+ specific papers (DDPM, score-based SDEs, discrete diffusion, MDLM, LLaDA, flow matching, rectified flow, DFlash, Fast-dLLM, dKV-Cache, Block Diffusion, LLaDA2.2, DiffusionGemma) with mathematical formulations (SDEs, ODEs, vector-field regression) that an AI Solution Architect does not need to make deployment decisions. The key architectural consequences (different execution schedule, different state-reuse boundaries, 'decode' ambiguity, parallel-position trade-offs) are stated but buried under ~1.5 pages of mechanism detail.
issue.evidence: The subsection's own summary: 'The architectural consequence is conditional, and it is the reason this section sits in the model-understanding chapter rather than in a serving chapter. Parallel positions can improve matrix utilization at low request concurrency, but repeated evaluation can increase total compute and communications. Block size changes both parallel work and the delay before commitment. A useful deployment comparison therefore fixes the task-quality requirement first, then measures the inference schedule, peak state and committed-output latency together.' This 4-sentence paragraph captures the architectural content. The preceding ~1.5 pages establish the mechanism but do not each add a distinct architectural decision lever.
issue.root_cause: The section was written to be comprehensive about diffusion language models (a research topic) rather than to serve the book's stated purpose (teaching an architect to reason about deployment). The 'why is this here' test is partially met: the reader learns that the execution model changes, but the depth of the change is more than the book's other sections provide for their topics.
issue.correction: Restructure the subsection to lead with the 3–4 architectural consequences (execution schedule, state-reuse boundary, 'decode' disambiguation, parallel-position trade-off) as a compact summary, then provide the mechanism detail in a more condensed form. The specific paper references can be retained as footnotes or a compact 'Further reading' list rather than inline citations that interrupt the architectural argument. Target: reduce the subsection by ~40% while preserving all architectural consequences and the key distinctions (bidirectional vs block-causal state reuse, parallel predictions ≠ joint reasoning, VAE decode ≠ autoregressive decode). The Ch 2 video-generation paragraph already handles the 'decode' disambiguation; the Ch 3 section can cross-reference it rather than re-derive it.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who skips the mechanism detail (e.g., the SDE/ODE discussion, the flow-matching paragraph) and reads only the architectural-consequence sentences can still answer: (1) how does the execution schedule differ from autoregressive? (2) what changes about KV/state reuse? (3) what does 'decode' mean in a VAE context? (4) what is the parallel-position trade-off? If the answer requires the full mechanism text, the restructuring is insufficient.

issue.quoted_clause: in-flight concurrency λ·W ≈ 344 at the ~8.6 s service time
issue.observed: The component arithmetic gives 8.7 s, not 8.6 s: TTFT 1.2 s + decode 300 × 25 ms = 1.2 + 7.5 = 8.7 s. The text then uses 8.6 s to compute 40 × 8.6 = 344. The 0.1 s discrepancy is within the '~' tolerance on '25 ms' (at 24.5 ms, total = 8.55 s ≈ 8.6 s), but the worked example in the same section explicitly states '300 output tokens take ~7.5 s of decode' (using 25 ms exactly), which gives 8.7 s total. The two statements in the same chapter are 0.1 s apart.
issue.evidence: §3: 'at the canonical ~25 ms/token, 300 output tokens take ~7.5 s of decode vs a ~1.08 s prefill budget' → 7.5 + 1.2 = 8.7 s. §3 scope paragraph: 'λ·W ≈ 344 at the ~8.6 s service time' → 40 × 8.6 = 344. The 8.7 s figure would give 40 × 8.7 = 348.
issue.root_cause: The 8.6 s was likely computed with a slightly different TPOT (e.g., 24.5 ms) or rounded from 8.55 s, while the 7.5 s decode figure uses 25 ms exactly. Both are within '~' tolerance, but the 0.1 s gap between two numbers in the same section is visible to a careful reader.
issue.correction: Either (a) change '~8.6 s' to '~8.7 s' and '344' to '≈ 348' (or '≈ 350'), or (b) add a brief note: '(using 24.5 ms TPOT: 300 × 0.0245 = 7.35 s; total 8.55 s ≈ 8.6 s; 40 × 8.6 = 344).' Option (a) is simpler and consistent with the 25 ms figure used elsewhere. The 4-unit difference (344 vs 348) is architecturally immaterial, but internal consistency in a worked example matters for reader trust.
issue.acceptance_test: The service-time figure and the concurrency figure in the scope paragraph are arithmetically consistent with the TTFT and TPOT values stated in the same section, using the same rounding convention.

issue.quoted_clause: or in worst cases a fragment of a character
issue.observed: The phrase 'a fragment of a character' is technically correct (a single byte of a 3-byte UTF-8 CJK character is a fragment of that character), but it may lead a reader to believe that sub-byte tokens exist or that the tokenizer can split a byte. In BPE-over-bytes, the minimum token is one byte; a 'fragment of a character' is a byte that does not constitute a complete character. The phrasing is accurate but potentially confusing for readers unfamiliar with UTF-8 encoding.
issue.evidence: The sentence lists: 'a whole word, a common subword, a single character, a short punctuation+space pair, or in worst cases a fragment of a character.' The progression implies decreasing granularity, ending below the character level. For a reader who thinks of 'character' as the atomic unit, 'fragment of a character' is surprising and may prompt the question 'can a token be half a byte?'
issue.root_cause: The author is being precise (byte-level BPE can produce tokens that are sub-character for multi-byte encodings) but the phrasing doesn't signal that the 'fragment' is still a whole byte.
issue.correction: Optional: 'or, in worst cases for multi-byte scripts, a single byte that is only part of a character (e.g., one byte of a 3-byte CJK glyph).' This preserves the precision while preventing the sub-byte misreading. If the author prefers brevity, the current phrasing is defensible and this is a very minor point.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who is not a UTF-8 expert does not conclude from this sentence that tokens can be smaller than one byte.

issue.quoted_clause: MoE (8×7B class)
issue.observed: The table header labels the MoE challenger as '8×7B class', implying 8 experts of 7B parameters each (56B expert mass). However, every other figure in the table and the surrounding text uses a 47B total, which implies 45.6B expert mass (47B − 1.4B always-on) and 5.7B per expert (45.6B ÷ 8). The active-params derivation in the same table confirms this: 'top-2 from 8 = 2/8 = 25% of expert mass ≈ 11.4B' → expert mass = 11.4B / 0.25 = 45.6B, not 56B.
issue.evidence: 8 × 7B = 56B expert mass + 1.4B always-on = 57.4B total ≠ 47B. Conversely, 47B − 1.4B = 45.6B expert mass; 45.6B / 8 = 5.7B per expert. The 94 GB residency (47B × 2), the 46 GB saving (140 − 94), and the 32.9% figure all trace to 47B, not 57.4B.
issue.root_cause: The '8×7B' label was likely a rough class descriptor written before the 47B total was locked, or a conflation with a different model (e.g., Mixtral 8×7B = 47B total if the 7B includes the shared parameters: 8×5.7B experts + 1.4B shared ≈ 47B). As printed, it contradicts the table's own arithmetic.
issue.correction: Change the column header to 'MoE (8-expert, ~47B total)' or 'MoE (8×~5.7B class)'. If the intent was to evoke a familiar model family, add a footnote: 'per-expert size is ~5.7B (45.6B expert mass ÷ 8); the 1.4B always-on attention/shared parameters bring the total to ~47B.'
issue.acceptance_test: The column header's implied per-expert size, multiplied by 8 and added to the always-on parameters, equals the 47B total stated in the 'total parameters' row. No reader can derive 56B or 57B from the header.

issue.quoted_clause: Tools such as `torch.profiler` can count active parameters, but this is an empirical measurement, not a first-party spec.
issue.observed: `torch.profiler` is a general-purpose execution profiler (CPU/GPU time, memory allocation, operator counts). It does not have a built-in 'count active parameters' feature for MoE models. Determining active parameters requires custom instrumentation (e.g., hooking the routing function, tracing which expert weights are accessed per token, or using model-specific tools from the framework that implements the MoE). As written, a reader may look for a `torch.profiler.count_active_params()` API that does not exist.
issue.evidence: PyTorch documentation for torch.profiler lists capabilities: CPU/GPU operator timing, memory profiling, key-value tracing, export to Chrome/PyTorch format. No 'active parameter count' feature. MoE-aware parameter counting requires either (a) reading the routing config (top-k, expert sizes) from the model definition, or (b) instrumenting the forward pass to log which expert tensors are accessed.
issue.root_cause: The sentence conflates 'profiling the execution to observe which parameters are touched' (possible with custom hooks) with a built-in tool capability.
issue.correction: Rewrite to: 'For a given input, one can instrument the forward pass (e.g., via PyTorch hooks on the routing module or the expert layers) to log which parameter tensors are actually read per token; this yields an empirical active-parameter count. Framework-specific tools (e.g., the model's own config parser reading top-k and expert dimensions) are more direct. Neither is a first-party spec.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader following the instruction can identify a concrete method (hook, config parse, or framework tool) without assuming a non-existent torch.profiler API.

issue.quoted_clause: KV cache for 9.2 K context adds ~20–30 GB of GPU memory per request at peak, leaving headroom but not abundance.
issue.observed: The same section, three bullets later ('Memory planning'), gives the exact figure: 2.62 MB/token × 9,200 = 24.1 GB (FP16, full-MHA) or 12.05 GB (FP8). The '20–30 GB' range is neither the FP16 figure (24.1) nor the FP8 figure (12.05), and no intermediate precision or context-length variation is invoked to justify the range. A reader encountering '20–30' before the precise '24.1' may form a vague mental model that the later exact figure then contradicts.
issue.evidence: 2.62 MB × 9,200 = 24,104 MB ≈ 24.1 GB. 1.31 MB × 9,200 = 12,052 MB ≈ 12.05 GB. Neither endpoint of '20–30' matches a standard precision at the canonical 9.2K context.
issue.root_cause: The '20–30' was likely written as a rough order-of-magnitude before the exact 24.1 GB figure was finalized, and not updated when the precise number was added later in the same section.
issue.correction: Replace '~20–30 GB' with '~24 GB (FP16 full-MHA; ~12 GB at FP8)' to match the precise figure given in the 'Memory planning' bullet three lines below. Alternatively, if the range is meant to span precisions, write '~12–24 GB depending on KV precision (FP8 to FP16) at the canonical 9.2K context.'
issue.acceptance_test: The KV-per-request figure in the 'Model selection' bullet is either identical to or a clearly scoped range that encompasses the exact figure in the 'Memory planning' bullet, with no unexplained gap.

issue.page_hint: Ch 3, §6, 'Why the trend signal should not be read as dense is dead' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: the ~100B-and-up tier that anchor ~2.8T-parameter fleets
issue.observed: The verb 'anchor' is used intransitively with a plural subject ('tier that anchor'), which is grammatically acceptable but semantically unclear. The intended meaning is that the 100B+ models are the foundational/anchor components of the 2.8T-parameter fleet (Kimi K3). As written, a reader may parse 'anchor' as 'are anchored by' (passive) or 'serve as the anchor of' (active), and the object '~2.8T-parameter fleets' is ambiguous (is it one fleet or a class of fleets?).
issue.evidence: The 2.8T figure refers specifically to Kimi K3 (stated two sentences earlier: 'Kimi K3 104B of 2.8T'). The sentence is trying to say: the 100B+ tier is where the 2.8T-class models live; it is not a claim about all fleets.
issue.root_cause: Compressed phrasing in a parenthetical clause.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'the ~100B-and-up tier that includes the ~2.8T-parameter frontier models (e.g., Kimi K3)'. This removes the ambiguous verb and makes the 2.8T a specific example rather than a general 'fleet' class.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can identify exactly which models the '2.8T' refers to without re-reading the preceding sentence.

issue.quoted_clause: C ≈ 17.5 is the analytical quotient, floored to 17 deployable whole-context slots per the book's whole-slot convention, Chapters 14/16/17
issue.observed: The available KV memory on the canonical host is 640 − 140 (weights) − 64 (runtime) = 436 GB. At 24.1 GB per request (2.62 MB × 9,200), the quotient is 436 / 24.1 = 18.09, not 17.5. The text uses ≈ and defers the exact derivation to Ch 14/16/17, so this may account for additional overhead (PagedAttention page-table metadata, KV alignment, or a slightly different runtime budget) not shown in this chunk. However, a reader doing the arithmetic from the numbers visible in this chapter will get 18, not 17.5, and may be confused by the 0.5-slot gap.
issue.evidence: 436 GB / 24.1 GB = 18.09. 436 / 24.9 = 17.51 (would require 24.9 GB/request, not the 24.1 stated elsewhere). 428 / 24.1 = 17.76 (would require 72 GB runtime, not 64).
issue.root_cause: The 17.5 likely comes from a more detailed memory budget in Ch 14/16/17 (e.g., including PagedAttention block overhead, CUDA context, or a slightly larger runtime allocation). The cross-reference is present but the visible arithmetic in this chapter does not reproduce 17.5.
issue.correction: Add a brief parenthetical: 'C ≈ 17.5 (the 0.5-slot gap vs. the naive 436/24.1 = 18.1 accounts for PagedAttention block metadata and CUDA context overhead; full derivation in Ch 14 §4.2)'. This prevents the reader from flagging a 0.5-slot discrepancy as an error.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who computes 436/24.1 = 18.1 from the visible numbers can find an in-text explanation for why the book uses 17.5, without needing to open Ch 14.

issue.page_hint: Ch 6, §3, 'Reading Telemetry Into a Decision' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: each ~1.29 PFLOP — aggregate prefill demand at the 40 rps peak is 40 × 1.29 ≈ 52 PFLOP/s vs the 8×H100 aggregate ~7.9 PFLOPS, ~6.5× oversubscribed
issue.observed: The 40 rps oversubscription calculation uses 1.29 PFLOP (linear 2PL FLOPs only). The same paragraph's earlier sentence states the full prefill is '≈ 1.5 PFLOP full-square total' (1.29 linear + 0.22 attention). Using the full figure gives 40 × 1.5 / 7.9 ≈ 7.6×, not 6.5×.
issue.evidence: 1.29 PFLOP is the linear-only term (2 × 70e9 × 9.2e3). The attention term adds ≈ 0.22 PFLOP (4 × 8192 × 9200² × 80 ≈ 222 TFLOP). Full prefill ≈ 1.51 PFLOP. 40 × 1.51 / 7.912 ≈ 7.65×. The text explicitly acknowledges the full number two sentences earlier.
issue.root_cause: The linear-only figure was carried into the aggregate calculation for brevity, but the text already stated the full number in the same paragraph, making the 6.5× slightly inconsistent with the 1.5 PFLOP figure the reader just saw.
issue.correction: Either use the full figure ('40 × 1.5 ≈ 60 PFLOP/s … ~7.6× oversubscribed') or add a brief parenthetical: 'using the linear-only 1.29 PFLOP; the full ~1.5 PFLOP gives ~7.6×'. The conclusion (severely oversubscribed) is unchanged either way.
issue.acceptance_test: The oversubscription multiplier in the 40 rps sentence is consistent with the full prefill FLOP figure stated in the same paragraph, or the linear-only scope is explicitly noted at the point of use.

issue.quoted_clause: the ~30× input-to-output ratio is the single biggest driver of this system's cost structure (Ch 4)
issue.observed: 'The single biggest driver' is a superlative claim. The 70B model size (140 GB weights, 2×70B FLOPs/token) and the 8×H100 hardware choice are equally major cost determinants. The 30× ratio is the primary *workload-shape* differentiator, but not unambiguously 'the single biggest driver' of total cost.
issue.evidence: If the model were 13B instead of 70B, the cost would drop ~5× regardless of the 30× ratio. If the hardware were A100 instead of H100, the cost would change. The 30× ratio determines the *shape* of the cost (prefill-dominated, KV-heavy) but the *magnitude* is set by model size and hardware.
issue.root_cause: The sentence is in the context of model selection (choosing among models for a fixed workload), where the token profile is indeed the primary input. But 'cost structure' without scoping to 'among candidate models for this workload' reads as a universal claim.
issue.correction: Scope the claim: 'the ~30× input-to-output ratio is the dominant workload-shape driver of this system's cost structure — it determines that prefill FLOPs and KV residency, not decode bandwidth, set the binding constraints (Ch 4).' Or: '…is the single biggest *workload-derived* driver…'
issue.acceptance_test: The superlative 'single biggest' is either scoped to workload-shape/model-selection context or replaced with a less absolute formulation that a reader cannot misread as 'the 30× ratio matters more than the 70B model size.'

issue.quoted_clause: the value scales linearly with query length, so the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet)
issue.observed: The 2 × params × L formula captures only the linear (projection/MLP) FLOPs. The attention FLOPs scale as 4 × d_model × L² per layer, which is quadratic in L. At L = 64 the attention term is ~2–3% of total (MiniLM) to ~1% (bge-large), so the linear approximation is excellent. But the statement 'scales linearly' is technically imprecise, and 'the model-to-model ratio equals the parameter ratio' is only approximately true (the attention term depends on d_model, not just total params).
issue.evidence: MiniLM (d=384, 12 layers): attention = 4×384×64²×12 ≈ 0.075 GFLOP vs linear 2.94 GFLOP → 2.5%. bge-large (d=1024, 24 layers): attention = 4×1024×64²×24 ≈ 0.40 GFLOP vs linear 42.88 GFLOP → 0.9%. The ratio bge/mpnet is 43.28/14.16 ≈ 3.06 (with attention) vs 42.88/14.08 ≈ 3.05 (linear only). The difference is negligible at L=64.
issue.root_cause: The formula is a standard first-order approximation for short sequences. The text is making a practical point (the 3× ratio), not a mathematical one. But 'scales linearly' without a scope qualifier could mislead a reader who applies it at L=4096 where the attention term becomes significant.
issue.correction: Add a brief scope: 'the value scales approximately linearly with query length at short L (the quadratic attention term is <3% at 64 tokens), so the model-to-model ratio closely tracks the parameter ratio (bge-large ≈ 3× mpnet).'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who applies the 'linear scaling' claim at L=4096 is warned that the approximation degrades, or the text explicitly scopes the claim to short queries.

issue.quoted_clause: 8×H100 GPUs provide 8 ×80 GB = 640 GB aggregate HBM memory
issue.observed: Missing space between '×' and '80': '8 ×80 GB' should be '8 × 80 GB'.
issue.evidence: Typographic inconsistency. Elsewhere in the same chapter and in Ch 7, the pattern is '8 × 80 GB' or '8 ×80 GB' (Ch 7 Table 7-1 uses '8 ×80 GB'). The spacing is inconsistent within the manuscript.
issue.root_cause: Typo / inconsistent spacing around the multiplication sign.
issue.correction: Standardize to '8 × 80 GB' (space on both sides of ×) throughout, or '8×80 GB' (no spaces) throughout. Pick one convention and apply it.
issue.acceptance_test: All instances of '8 × 80 GB' / '8×80 GB' / '8 ×80 GB' use the same spacing convention.

issue.page_hint: Ch 5, §3(a), 'Takeaway for the canonical RAG workload' paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: It places the workload in the quality-positive regime without introducing per-request latency that threatens the TTFT SLO
issue.observed: 'Quality-positive regime' is not defined anywhere in the chapter or the book (as far as this chunk shows). The reader is expected to understand that this means 'sufficient retrieval quality for the workload's answer-quality requirements,' but the phrase is jargon-like and could be misread as a formal classification.
issue.evidence: The preceding paragraph discusses retrieval quality depending on 'model architecture, training objective/data, corpus/query distribution, normalization, and retrieval strategy' and notes that 'any observed quality-vs-dimension relationship … is domain- and corpus-specific and must be validated on the target corpus.' The 'quality-positive regime' is not a term established by this discussion.
issue.root_cause: The author used a shorthand that reads like a formal category but is actually an informal judgment ('good enough quality for this workload').
issue.correction: Replace with: 'It provides adequate retrieval quality for this workload's answer requirements (to be validated on the target corpus) without introducing per-request latency that threatens the TTFT SLO.' Or: 'It sits in the quality-sufficient range for this workload…'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who has not seen 'quality-positive regime' defined elsewhere can understand the sentence without inferring a formal classification system.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7, §4 Measurement, point 1 (KV per-token formula introduction)
issue.quoted_clause: The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached (MHA) attention head is
issue.observed: The word 'head' is incorrect. The formula that follows (2 × n_layers × d_hidden × bytes-per-value) computes the total per-token KV for the entire model across all layers, not for a single attention head. The parenthetical '(one key and one value per layer, each d_hidden wide)' confirms the formula spans all layers. A single head's per-token KV would be 2 × d_head × bytes (no layer count).
issue.evidence: Formula: 2 × 80 × 8192 × 2 = 2,621,440 B. This is the whole-model value (all 80 layers). Per-head would be 2 × 8192/64 × 2 = 512 B (for 64 heads of 128 dim each). The text's own worked example confirms the 2.62 MB/token figure is the model total.
issue.root_cause: Typo or editing artifact: 'head' should be 'model' (or 'transformer').
issue.correction: Change to: 'The per-token KV footprint of a fully-cached (MHA) model is' or 'The per-token KV footprint for a fully-cached (MHA) transformer is'.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence introduces a formula whose result (2.62 MB/token) matches the whole-model KV, not a per-head value. A reader should not be able to interpret the formula as per-head.

issue.page_hint: Ch 7, §5 Common Mistakes, bullet 4 (KV quantization per bit width)
issue.quoted_clause: FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving) is what serving stacks realize today
issue.observed: The phrase 'is what serving stacks realize today' is a universal present-tense claim about all current serving stacks. The text itself immediately qualifies this in §4 point 4: 'Do not generalize a fixed ratio to all FP8-KV deployments: the realized per-token footprint depends on the engine version, cache-block layout, scale/offset metadata, allocator rounding, and the accounting boundary.' The Common Mistakes bullet slightly overstates relative to the text's own qualification.
issue.evidence: §4 point 4 explicitly warns against generalizing the 50% ratio. The Common Mistakes bullet uses 'is what serving stacks realize today' without the same hedging.
issue.root_cause: The Common Mistakes section compresses the qualified statement into a shorter form, losing the 'raw byte-halving, before metadata' scope.
issue.correction: Change to: 'FP8 KV ≈50% of FP16 (raw byte-halving, before block/scale metadata) is the first-order figure serving stacks use today' or add '(raw payload; see §4.4 for the full accounting caveat).'
issue.acceptance_test: The bullet no longer implies that every serving stack's observed resident memory is exactly 50% of FP16; it identifies the raw byte-halving as the first-order planning figure.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8, 'The chapter unfolds by section' paragraph (after the backend-portability section)
issue.quoted_clause: §4 turns to measurement, §5 to common mistakes, §6 to architecture consequences, and §8 closes with a mini-case that threads the prefill/decode divide.
issue.observed: The chapter outline jumps from §6 to §8, omitting §7 ('What We Still Don't Know'). The actual chapter has sections 1–8, with §7 being the Unknowns section. The reader following this roadmap will be confused about where §7 fits.
issue.evidence: The chapter's actual structure: §1 Concept, §2 Mental Model, §3 Worked Example, §4 Measurement, §5 Common Mistakes, §6 Architecture Consequence, §7 What We Still Don't Know, §8 Mini-Case. The outline paragraph lists 1–6 and 8 but not 7.
issue.root_cause: Editing oversight when the chapter outline was written or updated.
issue.correction: Add '§7 to open questions,' before 'and §8 closes with a mini-case.' Full: '§4 turns to measurement, §5 to common mistakes, §6 to architecture consequences, §7 to open questions, and §8 closes with a mini-case that threads the prefill/decode divide.'
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter outline paragraph names every section 1 through 8 in order with no gap.

issue.page_hint: Ch 8, §3 'Decode: bandwidth-bound at low batch', scope note paragraph (after the KV-read caveat)
issue.quoted_clause: each GPU streams only its own shard (~0.70 TB/s against its own ~3.35 TB/s, Ch 6)
issue.observed: The 0.70 TB/s figure is correct (17.5 GB per-GPU weight shard ÷ 25 ms TPOT budget = 700 GB/s) but its derivation is not shown. A reader encountering this parenthetical for the first time cannot verify the number without reconstructing: (140 GB / 8 GPUs) / 25 ms. The 'Ch 6' cross-reference may help but the arithmetic is not self-evident in context.
issue.evidence: 140 GB / 8 = 17.5 GB per GPU. 17.5 GB / 0.025 s = 700 GB/s = 0.70 TB/s. The 25 ms is the TPOT design budget stated earlier in the chapter.
issue.root_cause: The figure is presented as a parenthetical fact without its two-step derivation, making it appear arbitrary.
issue.correction: Expand to: 'each GPU streams only its own 17.5 GB shard, requiring ~0.70 TB/s (17.5 GB ÷ 25 ms TPOT) against its ~3.35 TB/s HBM bandwidth (Ch 6)'. Alternatively, add a brief footnote showing the division.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can verify the 0.70 TB/s figure from the stated inputs (140 GB, 8 GPUs, 25 ms) without consulting another chapter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, parenthetical
issue.quoted_clause: by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor
issue.observed: The cross-reference uses '§3' (within-chapter shorthand) while every other reference to the same section in this chapter uses '§9.3' (e.g., 'the §9.3 worked example', 'The eight-rank ring in §9.3', '§9.4 measurements').
issue.evidence: Search of Chapter 9 text: '§9.3' appears 4 times; '§3' appears 1 time (this instance). The chapter's own convention is the fully-qualified form.
issue.root_cause: Inconsistent cross-reference style within a single chapter.
issue.correction: Change '§3' to '§9.3' to match the chapter's established convention.
issue.acceptance_test: All intra-chapter section references in Chapter 9 use the '§9.N' form; no bare '§N' remains.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, §3 Worked Example, Pipeline Parallelism subsection, paragraph after the speedup formula
issue.quoted_clause: the P−1 term in the denominator is the bubble: the pipeline fills and drains exactly once per m-batch pass, so P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots each stage would otherwise work
issue.observed: The phrase 'P−1 stage-slots are wasted out of the m·P slots' is slightly imprecise. The m·P quantity is the total useful work (m micro-batches × P stages), but the pipeline's total time is (m+P−1) stage-time units, not m·P. The P−1 extra time units are the bubble, but they are not 'wasted out of m·P slots'—they are added to the m useful time units to make m+P−1 total. A reader doing the arithmetic may be confused by the denominator framing.
issue.evidence: For P=4, m=8: total time = 11 stage-units; useful work = 32 stage-units (8×4); bubble = 3 stage-units (P−1). The speedup is 32/11, not 32/(32−3). The 'P−1 out of m·P' framing conflates the time-domain bubble with the work-domain total.
issue.root_cause: The explanation tries to give intuition for the denominator (m+P−1) by referencing the numerator (mP), but the 'wasted out of' phrasing implies a subtraction from mP rather than an addition to m.
issue.correction: Rephrase to: 'the pipeline takes m+P−1 stage-time units to complete m·P units of useful work; the P−1 extra units are the fill-and-drain bubble. The ideal speedup over a single serial pass (m·P units) is therefore mP/(m+P−1).'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can verify the P=4, m=8 case: 11 time units for 32 useful units → speedup 32/11 ≈ 2.9, without needing to reconcile 'P−1 out of m·P' with the actual denominator.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10, §7 What We Still Don't Know, second bullet (MoE scaling)
issue.quoted_clause: Kimi K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE
issue.observed: A reader doing the arithmetic gets 16/896 × 2.8T ≈ 50B, not 104B. The discrepancy is because 'active parameters' in MoE literature includes non-expert components (attention, shared layers, embeddings), but the text does not state this. The subsequent sentence '16/896 ≈ 1.8% expert activation' correctly refers to the expert routing fraction, but the juxtaposition with '104B active' without explanation invites confusion.
issue.evidence: 16 × (2.8T / 896) = 16 × 3.125B = 50B (expert-only active). 104B − 50B = 54B (non-expert active: attention, shared FFN, embeddings, etc.). The text does not decompose this.
issue.root_cause: The parenthetical '(2.8T total / 104B active)' uses the standard MoE 'active parameters' convention without flagging that it includes non-expert components, creating an apparent arithmetic inconsistency with the 16/896 routing ratio.
issue.correction: Add a brief clause: '(2.8T total; 104B active, of which ~50B is the 16 routed experts and the remainder is attention and shared layers)'. Alternatively, rephrase to: 'activates 16 of 896 routed experts per token (≈1.8% expert activation; 2.8T total parameters, 104B active including non-expert components)'.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who computes 16/896 × 2.8T does not encounter an unexplained gap between the result (~50B) and the stated 'active' figure (104B).

issue.page_hint: Ch 9, §5 Common Mistakes, first bullet, final sentence
issue.quoted_clause: Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; design against the measured number, not the spec sheet peak.
issue.observed: The 40–60% range is reasonable for the specific context described (multi-GPU, multi-link, moderate-to-large messages), but as stated it reads as a universal planning constant. For small messages (latency-dominated), effective bandwidth can be well below 40% of peak; for very large messages on a well-tuned single-rail path, it can approach 80–90%. The [ILLUSTRATIVE] tag helps, but the sentence structure ('typically 40–60%') presents it as a general rule.
issue.evidence: The preceding sentence scopes the context: 'in multi-GPU topologies the traffic is split across multiple GPUs and multiple links, so one link rarely carries the whole transfer.' The 40–60% is appropriate for that context but the sentence does not explicitly bind the range to it.
issue.root_cause: The planning heuristic is stated as a general 'typically' rather than as a context-specific range.
issue.correction: Tighten the scope: 'For the multi-link, multi-GPU case described above, measured effective bandwidth is often in the 40–60% range of the per-link peak [ILLUSTRATIVE]; for small messages the ratio is lower (latency-dominated), and for a single large transfer on one well-configured link it can be higher. Design against the measured number for your specific message size and topology, not the spec sheet peak.'
issue.acceptance_test: A reader does not apply '40–60%' to a 64-byte all-reduce or to a single 140 GB transfer on one NVLink without questioning whether the range applies.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11, §3 Worked Example, 'When to Disaggregate' subsection, first sentence of the P/D paragraph
