A cross-read of Ch 11 §6, Ch 12 §3 (19.8K vs 92K) and Ch 13 §3 (1.98 rps/host) yields no apparent contradiction; the phrase 'per-request latency' and 'aggregate capacity' are used distinctly wherever the 10 rps figure appears.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Options B and C; Ch 9 §5 bullet 1; Ch 9 §6 (11× / 180× ratios)
issue.quoted_clause: A realistic *effective* throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node) ... With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s. ... Measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak [ILLUSTRATIVE] ... keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 11× below the assumed InfiniBand case and about 180× below the assumed RoCE case (§9.3)
issue.observed: Two related inconsistencies. (1) The worked example assumes 80% effective bandwidth in both fabric cases — 40 GB/s of a 50 GB/s two-rail HDR nominal (2 × 25 GB/s per Table 9-1), and 2.5 GB/s of a 3.125 GB/s 25 GbE nominal — while §5 states measured effective bandwidth is typically 40–60% of peak. The chapter's own numbers contradict its own rule. (2) The headline 11× and 180× ratios in §6 compare the NVLink *peak* (450 GB/s directional) against *effective* fabric numbers (40 and 2.5 GB/s), so the ratios overstate the on-node advantage by roughly the peak-to-effective factor.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 40/50 = 0.80; 2.5/3.125 = 0.80; both exceed the chapter's stated 0.40–0.60 band. Ratio check: 6.125/0.5444 = 11.25× and 98/0.5444 = 180.0×, where the denominator is a peak and the numerators are effective. Under the chapter's own 40–60% band, the two-rail HDR ring would be 245/30 ≈ 8.2 s to 245/20 ≈ 12.3 s and the 25 GbE ring 245/1.875 ≈ 131 s to 245/1.25 ≈ 196 s, i.e. ratios of roughly 15–23× and 240–360×.
issue.root_cause: No single convention is declared for the peak-vs-effective denominator, so the worked example, the Common Mistakes heuristic and the architecture-consequence ratios each use a different one.
issue.correction: Declare the convention once (e.g. 'all fabric comparisons use an effective, contention-inclusive bandwidth; the NVLink figure is a peak and is labelled as such') and then either (a) lower the assumed effective values into the 40–60% band and restate the 98 s / 6.1 s / 11× / 180× figures accordingly, or (b) keep the optimistic values but label them explicitly as an upper bound and add a sensitivity band (e.g. 'at 40–60% effective the Ethernet ring is 131–196 s'). Restate the §6 ratios so that peak and effective are never compared in one quotient.
issue.acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure used in a time or ratio computation in Ch 9 carries an explicit peak/effective label; the effective values used in §3 fall inside the band stated in §5, or §5's band is revised to match; the §6 ratios are either peak-vs-peak or effective-vs-effective, and the text says which.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §2 (Mental Model), paragraph containing 'For a flat one-way 140 GB transfer'
issue.quoted_clause: For a flat one-way 140 GB transfer, the nominal 25 GB/s of one HDR port gives a best-case 5.6 s; an assumed practical-effective 2.5 GB/s Ethernet path gives 56 s. The eight-rank ring in §9.3 instead sends 245 GB per rank: about 0.54 s at the H100 directional peak, 6.1 s at an assumed effective two-rail 40 GB/s, and 98 s at 2.5 GB/s.
issue.observed: The paragraph places a flat single-port transfer (5.6 s) next to a ring over two rails (6.1 s) without noting that the two are not comparable. A reader sees 'more bandwidth, more time' and must reconstruct that the ring moves 1.75× the logical bytes and that the 5.6 s figure uses one port while the 6.1 s figure uses two. The chapter never states the like-for-like number (ring over one HDR port = 245/25 = 9.8 s).
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 140/25 = 5.6 s (flat, one port, logical bytes); 245/40 = 6.125 s (ring, two rails, 1.75× bytes); ring over one port would be 245/25 = 9.8 s. The apparent 'slower with more bandwidth' is entirely an artifact of comparing different algorithms and different port counts.
issue.root_cause: The mental-model section interleaves two independent variables (traffic multiplier and link count) without labelling which comparison is being made.
issue.correction: Split the sentence into two labelled comparisons: (i) flat transfer of the logical tensor at one port = 5.6 s; (ii) ring traffic (1.75×) at two rails = 6.1 s, with the note 'the ring at one port would be 9.8 s — the ring's 1.75× traffic, not the port count, dominates'. Add the one-port ring figure so the reader can see the traffic multiplier's effect.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can state, from Ch 9 §2 alone, why 6.1 s exceeds 5.6 s despite double the bandwidth; the 9.8 s one-port ring figure appears in §2 or §3.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case; Ch 11 Fig 11.3 caption; Ch 11 Note 11.3-1; contradicted by Ch 11 §3 and Ch 12 §3
issue.quoted_clause: e.g. ~35 GB of KV moved over NVLink (~0.08 s at 450 GB/s per direction, §9.2) when a P/D sequence transfers a ~13K-token context (35 GB ÷ 2.62 MB/token ≈ 13.3K) between prefill and decode pools. ... it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB, §9.8) across the joining link ... Transfer times: 24.1/450 = 0.054 s (NVLink) and 24.1/40 = 0.60 s (fabric) for the canonical context, versus the printed 0.08 s and 0.9 s.
issue.root_cause: A worked-example context length (13.3K) was promoted into a caption that describes the canonical workload's per-request state, without a scope marker.
issue.correction: In Fig 11.3's caption and Note 11.3-1, state the scope explicitly: '~35 GB corresponds to a 13.3K-token context (§9.8); the canonical 9.2K-token request carries ~24.1 GB, for which the same transfers are ~0.05 s on NVLink and ~0.6 s on the fabric'. Either add the canonical-context figures alongside the 13.3K ones or relabel the caption as a 13.3K-context example.
issue.acceptance_test: Every KV-transfer number in Ch 9 §8, Ch 11 Fig 11.3 and Note 11.3-1 states its context length; the canonical 24.1 GB figure and the 13.3K/35 GB figure are never conflated; the 1.4 TB/s aggregate is labelled with the context it assumes.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §8 mini-case; Ch 10 §3 (Tensor Parallelism worked example)
issue.quoted_clause: for the canonical 8×H100 host the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations (tens of MBs, not GBs)
issue.observed: Ch 9 characterises the per-layer TP activation exchange as 'tens of MBs'. Ch 10's worked example, for the same canonical host, computes 256 KiB logical per collective and 448 KiB of ring traffic per rank per collective — i.e. hundreds of KiB per layer, with 'tens of MBs' (70 MiB) being the whole-step total across 160 calls. Read literally, Ch 9 overstates the per-layer quantity by roughly two orders of magnitude; read as a per-step total, the phrase contradicts its own 'per-layer' qualifier.
issue.evidence: Recomputation from Ch 10's stated inputs: M = 16 × 8,192 × 2 = 262,144 B = 256 KiB; ring traffic 1.75M = 448 KiB per rank per collective; 160 calls → 70 MiB per rank per decode step. Per-layer (two collectives) ≈ 0.875 MiB.
issue.root_cause: The Ch 9 mini-case was written before or independently of the Ch 10 arithmetic and was not reconciled with it; 'per-layer' and 'per-step' are used for the same quantity.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'the meaningful per-step data movement is a TP all-reduce of the per-layer activations — ~448 KiB of ring traffic per rank per collective, ~70 MiB per rank per decode step for the 160-collective case of Ch 10 (not GBs)'. Cross-reference Ch 10 §3 explicitly.
issue.acceptance_test: The Ch 9 mini-case's activation-exchange magnitude matches the Ch 10 worked example at the stated granularity (per collective, per layer, per step), and the two chapters use the same units.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10 §3, Tensor Parallelism subsection (formula and the 160-call example)
issue.quoted_clause: the bandwidth term is $T_\text{tp} \approx n_\text{layers} \times 2(N-1)/N \times M_\text{act}/B_\text{dir}$ ... (The bandwidth term above counts one collective per layer; this budget's two-per-block assumption is why the call count below is 160 rather than 80.)
issue.observed: The general formula is written in terms of n_layers, but the common transformer block issues two collectives (attention output and MLP). The example then silently corrects the formula by using 160 calls, and the correction is relegated to a parenthetical. A reader who applies the formula as written underestimates TP byte traffic by 2× for the canonical 80-layer model — a factor-of-two error in the chapter's central TP budget.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: formula as written gives 80 × 1.75 × 256 KiB = 35 MiB per rank per step → 0.0816 ms at 450 GB/s; the example's 160 calls give 70 MiB → 0.163 ms. The printed 0.163 ms is correct for the example; the printed formula is not the formula that produced it.
issue.root_cause: The formula was written for a one-collective-per-layer abstraction and the example was later specified with two collectives per block; the mismatch was patched in prose rather than in the formula.
issue.correction: Replace n_layers with n_collectives (or n_layers × c where c is the collectives per block, c ≈ 2 for attention+MLP), define c explicitly, and state the assumption inline: 'T_tp ≈ n_collectives × 2(N−1)/N × M_act/B_dir, with n_collectives = c × n_layers and c ≈ 2 for a standard attention+MLP block'. Then the example's 160 follows directly and the parenthetical can be deleted.
issue.acceptance_test: Substituting the example's own inputs into the printed formula reproduces the printed 70 MiB / 0.163 ms; the symbol n_layers no longer appears in a byte-budget formula without a collectives-per-layer multiplier.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §3 (Worked Example) vs Ch 9 §8 (mini-case) and Ch 10 §3
issue.quoted_clause: For a communication-only illustration, a 70B model has 140 GB of FP16 weights. We separately assume an FP16 gradient tensor of logical size $M=140$ GB at each rank. ... Chapter 10 instead assumes FP32 gradients, so its logical tensor is 280 GB.
issue.observed: The chapter's central worked example is a training gradient all-reduce — a training object in a book whose spine is inference serving — and the inference-relevant communication objects (TP activation reductions, KV transfer) appear only in the closing mini-case, after the reader has already absorbed the training arithmetic and the 11×/180× ratios. The chapter's own framing ('moving the same data over a slower layer adds minutes to training time or inference latency') shows the inference case is in scope but is not the worked example. The result is that the chapter's headline numbers are about a workload the book's canonical scenario never runs.
issue.evidence: Structural: the book's canonical workload (Ch 4 Table 4-2) is inference-only; Ch 10 §3 supplies the inference object (TP activations, 70 MiB/step) and Ch 9 §8 supplies the KV-transfer object (35 GB, 0.08 s), but neither is developed as the chapter's worked example.
issue.root_cause: The chapter inherited a training-flavoured worked example and the inference framing was added later as an appendix-like mini-case rather than as the primary worked object.
issue.correction: Either (a) promote the inference object to the worked example — a TP activation all-reduce at the canonical 8×H100 shape, with the gradient all-reduce retained as the explicitly labelled training counterpart — or (b) keep the gradient example but add a short, parallel inference worked example (TP activation exchange + one KV transfer) before §4, so the chapter's headline ratios are anchored to the workload the book actually serves.
issue.acceptance_test: Ch 9 contains a worked example whose object is the canonical inference workload, and the training gradient example is explicitly labelled as the training counterpart; the §6 architecture-consequence ratios reference the inference-relevant object as well as the training one.

issue.page_hint: Ch 10 §1 item 6; Ch 11 §1 item 4; Ch 11 §4 item 3; Ch 12 §2
issue.quoted_clause: separates the compute-bound prefill stage from the bandwidth-bound decode stage onto different GPU pools ... splitting the compute-bound *prefill* stage from the bandwidth-bound *decode* stage onto separate pools, because they bottleneck on different resources ... a FLOP-bound prefill core and a bandwidth-bound decode core running on one pool tells us when to disaggregate ... compute (prefill throughput — prefill is compute-bound, Ch 11), memory bandwidth (decode throughput — decode is bandwidth-bound)
issue.observed: In four places the prefill/decode regime split is stated as an unqualified property of the phases rather than as a first-order regime whose validity depends on sequence length, batch size, precision, kernels and hardware. The book's own numbers show the regime is workload-dependent (a 9.2K-token prefill on the canonical 8-GPU host is compute-heavy, but a short-prompt, large-batch decode step can be compute-heavy too, and a large-batch prefill can become memory-bound on activations). A reader can carry away 'prefill is always compute-bound, decode is always bandwidth-bound' as a law, which is exactly the inference the book elsewhere warns against.
issue.evidence: Internal: Ch 11 §3's own figures are regime-specific (1.19 PFLOPS required vs 0.989 peak for a single device; 5.6 TB/s vs 0.70 TB/s per GPU for decode) and are stated without the conditions that make them true; Ch 12 §3's 19.8K tok/s prefill ceiling is an MFU-based aggregate that already embeds a batch-size assumption.
issue.root_cause: A useful first-order heuristic has been promoted to a definitional statement at each point of use, without a single place where the regime conditions are stated once and referenced thereafter.
issue.correction: State the regime once with its conditions (e.g. 'at long prompt lengths and modest batch, prefill is compute-bound; at small batch and short prompts, decode is bandwidth-bound; both regimes move with batch size, precision and kernel efficiency — see Ch 6 for the crossover arithmetic') and reference it at each of the four sites. Where a specific canonical number is quoted, keep the number and add the condition that produced it.
issue.acceptance_test: Each of the four sites either carries an explicit regime qualifier or points to a single place where the qualifier is stated; no sentence in Chs 10–12 asserts the compute-bound/bandwidth-bound split without a scope.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11 §3 ('When to Disaggregate' paragraph) and Fig 11.3 caption; reconciled by Ch 12 §3
issue.quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak), decode is **bandwidth-bound** (the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU; under the canonical 8×H100 host it is sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU)
issue.observed: The prefill feasibility comparison is a single-device comparison (1.19 PFLOPS required vs one H100's 0.989 PFLOPS peak) presented in a chapter whose canonical deployment is an 8×H100 host with TP=8. Under that deployment the same 1.29 PFLOP prefill is 0.161 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at the book's own 35% MFU — comfortably inside the ~1.08 s budget. The prose does not say 'single device', so a reader can conclude the canonical host cannot meet the prefill budget, which contradicts Ch 12's per-host prefill rate of ~19,800 tok/s (9,200 tokens in ~0.47 s). The Fig 11.3 caption does say 'single-H100'; the prose does not.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 1.288e15 FLOP ÷ 8 GPUs = 1.61e14 FLOP/GPU; at 989 TFLOP/s × 35% = 346.15 TFLOP/s → 0.465 s. Ch 12's 19,776 tok/s ÷ 9,200 tok = 0.465 s — the same number, confirming the canonical host meets the prefill budget. The printed 1.19 PFLOPS figure is correct only for a single device.
issue.root_cause: A single-device feasibility check was carried over from the single-host framing of earlier chapters into a multi-GPU canonical context without re-scoping the denominator.
issue.correction: Add 'on a single device' to the prose and add the canonical reconciliation in the same sentence: '…vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak on one H100; under the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 host the same prefill is ~0.16 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (Ch 12), so the single-device figure describes a one-GPU deployment, not the canonical host.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every prefill-feasibility statement in Ch 11 names the device count it assumes; the 1.19 PFLOPS figure is never presented as a property of the canonical 8-GPU host.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11 §4 (block headed 'Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability'); Ch 11 §6 (block headed 'The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically')
issue.quoted_clause: ### Serving qualification: model support is not serving capability ... ### The serving concerns transfer; the text mechanisms do not transfer automatically
issue.observed: Two substantial digressions are placed under headings whose intellectual job they do not perform. The §4 block (hybrid models, looped-depth models, adaptive depth, depth-aware latency, economic denominator) sits inside 'Measurement' but is a capability-qualification argument, not a measurement protocol. The §6 block (Wan2.2, VAE reconstruction, CFG, Ulysses, FSDP, video admission records) sits inside 'Architecture Consequence' but is a transfer note about a different media domain; it introduces a large new vocabulary (VAE, CFG, Ulysses, timestep schedules) in a chapter about LLM serving, and it is the last thing a reader meets before the mini-case. Together these blocks are roughly a third of the chapter's prose, and neither is signposted in the chapter's opening promise ('how requests are batched, how KV cache memory is managed, how repeated prefixes are reused, and when to split prefill from decode').
issue.evidence: Structural: the chapter's stated scope in 'The Architect's Question' lists four mechanisms; the qualification and video blocks address none of them. The video block's own content is explicitly about a different workload class ('A text prefill/decode split does not prove that the same split is useful here').
issue.root_cause: Two later additions (model-capability qualification and non-text transfer) were inserted into whichever section was open rather than being given their own signposted place in the chapter's argument.
issue.correction: Give each block its own numbered subsection with a title that states its job — e.g. §4.x 'Capability qualification is not serving capability' (moved out of Measurement) and §6.x 'Transfer: the serving concerns transfer, the mechanisms do not' — and add one sentence to the chapter's opening promise acknowledging them. Consider moving the video material to an appendix if the chapter is to stay within its stated scope, keeping only the two-paragraph principle in the body.
issue.acceptance_test: Every subsection in Ch 11 has a heading whose claim matches the subsection's content; the chapter's opening promise enumerates the subsections it contains; a reader who reads only the chapter's own promise can predict its subsections.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11 Table 11-2 and its surrounding text; Ch 11 §6 footnotes oct-ix-openvino-paged-attention and oct-ix-sglang-xpu-graph
issue.quoted_clause: #### Table 11-2 — Serving engines by architectural capability (time-sensitive) ... | supported hardware | NVIDIA / AMD / CPU | NVIDIA / AMD | NVIDIA-only | CPU + consumer GPUs | deployment niche |
issue.observed: Two defects in the book's most explicitly time-sensitive table. (1) It carries no observation date, although the book dates every other implementation snapshot (Table 9-3 '(2026-10-28 snapshot)', the 'Dated implementation note', the OpenVINO and SGLang XPU footnotes all dated 2026-10-28) and the text itself says the rows 'must be re-verified against each engine's current first-party documentation'. An undated capability table cannot be re-verified against anything. (2) The 'supported hardware' row omits Intel XPU for both vLLM and SGLang, even though this same chapter's footnotes document a vLLM XPU platform source and SGLang XPU documentation — the table contradicts the chapter's own evidence.
issue.evidence: Internal: Ch 11 §6 cites 'vLLM XPU platform source, pinned to revision 5df63a7' and 'SGLang XPU documentation at pinned revision a1966e1', and §4 discusses the vLLM XPU configuration selecting the XCCL backend. Table 11-2's supported-hardware row lists no Intel entry for either engine.
issue.root_cause: The table was authored as a vendor-neutral capability map and then the dated implementation material was added separately, without reconciling the two or propagating the date.
issue.correction: Retitle as 'Table 11-2 — Serving engines by architectural capability (observed 2026-10-28; time-sensitive)' and add a per-row or per-table source note. Add Intel XPU to the supported-hardware cells for vLLM and SGLang (or replace the cell with 'NVIDIA / AMD / Intel XPU / CPU' as observed), and add a 'not observed' marker convention so that absence of evidence is distinguishable from absence of support.
issue.acceptance_test: Table 11-2 carries an observation date; every cell is either sourced or marked 'not observed'; no engine's supported-hardware cell contradicts a dated footnote elsewhere in the same chapter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11 §3 (Prefix Caching paragraph) vs Ch 12 §3 (Candidate (a)) and Ch 12 §7
issue.quoted_clause: Without caching, every request re-runs the ~1.12 PFLOP prefill for those 8K tokens ... a new request reuses the shared-document KV and prefills only the unique query tail — cutting the dominant prefill FLOPs and TTFT for repeated-context traffic ... Prefix caching from Ch. 11 amortizes the prefill attention over repeated requests with the same prompt prefix, reducing effective prefill FLOPs by ~30% at 10 rps average and ~50% at peak 40 rps
issue.observed: Ch 11 describes the saving as 'the dominant prefill FLOPs' — the 8K shared prefix is 8,000/9,200 = 87% of the canonical prefill FLOPs, so a prefix hit removes ~87% of prefill work. Ch 12 then assumes only 30–50% amortization, with no bridge between the two. The book never states the prefix-hit rate that reconciles them, so the reader cannot tell whether 30–50% is a hit-rate-weighted average (implying h ≈ 34% and h ≈ 57% respectively) or a different mechanism. The number is then used to raise the effective prefill ceiling (19.8K → ~28K tok/s) and to rank prefix caching as 'the highest-leverage optimization'.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 8,000/9,200 = 0.870; saving = 0.870 × h. For a 30% saving, h = 0.345; for 50%, h = 0.575. Ch 12's derived ceiling 19,800/0.70 = 28,286 ≈ 28K tok/s is arithmetically correct given the 30% assumption, but the assumption's provenance is unstated.
issue.root_cause: Two chapters model the same mechanism at different levels of abstraction (per-hit saving vs traffic-weighted average) without an explicit hit-rate parameter linking them.
issue.correction: Introduce the hit rate explicitly in Ch 11 §3 or Ch 12 §3: 'the shared 8K prefix is ~87% of canonical prefill FLOPs; a traffic-weighted saving of 30% therefore implies a prefix-hit rate of ~35% (and 50% implies ~57%)'. Then state the assumed hit rate as the [ASSUMPTION] and the resulting amortization as the [HYPOTHESIS] it already is.
issue.acceptance_test: The 30–50% amortization figure is accompanied by the prefix-hit rate that produces it from the 87% upper bound; Ch 11 and Ch 12 use the same parameterisation of prefix reuse.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 Table 12-2 ('Monthly fully loaded cost' row) and Ch 12 §8 mini-case; Ch 13 §3 (fleet sizing)
issue.quoted_clause: ~21 hosts, ~$155.8K/mo total ($155,816.93 ≈ $24.97/1K; self-host, Ch 16); cloud-equivalent ≈$306.6K ($306,600 ≈ $49.13/1K, §12.8) ... Ch16/17 size the fleet to ~21 hosts at the 40 rps peak on the full-utilization screen — ⌈344/17⌉ = 21; under the 70% × 95% policy — applied to the unrounded 344/17 ≈ 20.2, not the rounded 21 — that becomes 31 working + 1 spare = 32 total, Table 17-1
issue.observed: Ch 12's cost figures are computed on a 21-host fleet, which Ch 13 identifies as the full-utilization *screen*, while Ch 16/17's actual provisioning policy yields 32 hosts at the same 40 rps peak. Ch 12 attributes the 21-host cost to Ch 16 and calls it 'the fleet the canonical workload requires', so the cost basis and the sizing basis disagree by ~50%. The mini-case's conclusion (the $15K ceiling fails at fleet scale) survives either basis, but the printed dollar figures understate the policy fleet: 32 hosts × $14,600 ≈ $467K cloud-equivalent, not $306.6K.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 344/17 = 20.235 → 21 (full utilization); 20.235/0.665 = 30.43 → 31 working + 1 spare = 32 (Ch 13's policy). 21 × $14,600 = $306,600 ✓ (matches Ch 12); 32 × $14,600 = $467,200. $155,816.93/6,240 = $24.97/1K ✓; $306,600/6,240 = $49.13/1K ✓. The arithmetic is internally consistent; the host-count basis is the problem.
issue.root_cause: Ch 12 adopted the un-headed screen number for a cost figure that Ch 13/17 then supersede with a policy-adjusted fleet, and the two were never reconciled.
issue.correction: State the basis explicitly in Table 12-2 and §12.8: '21 hosts = full-utilization screen; the 70% × 95% provisioning policy of Ch 17 yields 32 hosts (Ch 13), i.e. ~$237K self-host / ~$467K cloud-equivalent at the same per-host rate'. If Ch 16's $155,816.93 is in fact computed on the policy fleet, correct the host count shown in Ch 12 instead.
issue.acceptance_test: Every host count used in a cost computation in Ch 12 is labelled as screen or policy fleet, and matches the corresponding figure in Ch 13/17; the $155.8K / $306.6K figures can be reproduced from a stated host count and a stated per-host rate.

issue.quoted_clause: (A two‑rank collective over one path is the exception — it can saturate the link; and by the ring model of §3 each link still carries (N−1)/N of the tensor.)
issue.observed: For N = 2 the parenthetical is misleading: each link carries (N−1)/N = 1/2 of the tensor per phase, but the two phases together put the entire tensor on the link — so the link does carry 'the whole transfer', which is exactly what the bullet says never happens. The per-phase figure is stated without the phase qualifier.
issue.evidence: Ring accounting: per-phase per-link traffic = (N−1)/N × M; total across both phases = 2(N−1)/N × M. At N = 2: 0.5M per phase, 1.0M total.
issue.root_cause: A per-phase quantity is quoted where the surrounding sentence is about total link traffic.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: '…and by the ring model of §3 each link carries (N−1)/N of the tensor per phase — 2(N−1)/N in total, which for N = 2 is the whole tensor on the link.'
issue.acceptance_test: The parenthetical states the phase scope of the (N−1)/N figure and does not imply that a two-rank link carries less than the full tensor.

issue.quoted_clause: With protocol overhead and multi-node tree contention, a practical effective bandwidth might be 2.5 GB/s.
issue.observed: Option C computes a ring model but justifies the effective bandwidth with 'multi-node tree contention'. The algorithm named in the justification is not the algorithm used in the computation, in a chapter that elsewhere insists that algorithm, transport and topology be labelled separately.
issue.evidence: The same subsection's formula is T_ring ≈ 2(N−1)/N × M/B_eff, a ring; the justification invokes a tree.
issue.root_cause: Copy-paste of a generic contention phrase from a tree-based discussion into a ring-based one.
issue.correction: Replace 'multi-node tree contention' with 'multi-node contention (ring forwarding and shared-fabric contention)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every effective-bandwidth justification in Ch 9 §3 names the same collective algorithm used in the accompanying formula.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet
issue.quoted_clause: NVLink‑Switch and the next‑generation switch fabrics are pushing intra‑node bandwidth higher (NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU)
issue.observed: The figure is stated without the bidirectional/directional qualifier that the chapter itself insists on twice ('Directionality comes before division'; Table 9-1's 'bidirectional aggregate'). A reader who has internalised the chapter's own convention will read '1.8 TB/s per GPU' as a directional rate and over-estimate transfer times by 2×.
issue.evidence: Internal convention: Ch 9 §2 states '900 GB/s bidirectional per GPU, or 450 GB/s per direction'; Table 9-1 labels the NVLink row 'bidirectional aggregate'. The NVLink 5 figure carries no such label.
issue.root_cause: A forward-looking hardware figure was added without the direction convention the chapter establishes.
issue.correction: Write 'NVLink 5 provides 1.8 TB/s per GPU bidirectional aggregate (900 GB/s per direction)', matching the chapter's convention.
issue.acceptance_test: Every bandwidth figure in Ch 9 carries a direction qualifier; the NVLink 5 figure is stated on the same convention as the H100 figure.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §7, 'Optical interconnects and the next generation' bullet
issue.quoted_clause: optical intra‑rack fabrics (400 Gb/s–800 Gb/s per lane) are entering data centers
issue.observed: 'per lane' is the wrong unit for the quantities named. 400 Gb/s and 800 Gb/s are per-port link rates (400G/800G Ethernet, NDR/XDR); a lane in these fabrics is a fraction of a port (e.g. 100 Gb/s per electrical lane in some designs). The phrase will mislead an architect sizing ports or optics.
issue.evidence: Terminology: the chapter's own Table 9-1 uses 'per port' for the same class of figure.
issue.root_cause: Loose unit vocabulary in a chapter whose value proposition is precise unit discipline.
issue.correction: Change 'per lane' to 'per port'.
issue.acceptance_test: All link-rate figures in Ch 9 use 'per port' or 'per GPU' consistently; no figure uses 'per lane'.

issue.quoted_clause: | Chip-to-memory | HBM3 (H100) | 3.35 TB/s | ~ns | — | [1P][FACT] | ... | Rack/cluster | InfiniBand HDR/NDR | 200/400 Gb/s ≈ 25/50 GB/s per port | ~us | high capex | [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] | ... *(Hierarchy: bandwidth drops ~2 orders of magnitude from HBM to the cluster fabric ... Figures are established hardware specs [1P][FACT], except where a row is tagged otherwise.)*
issue.observed: Three small defects in the book's foundational hierarchy table. (1) The 'Cost' column ('high capex', 'low', 'medium', 'high capex') is an unsourced qualitative judgement, yet the footnote asserts that 'Figures are established hardware specs [1P][FACT]' — the cost column is neither a spec nor tagged. (2) The HBM latency entry '~ns' is uninformative next to '~us' rows and is not a device access latency figure in the same sense as a link latency; HBM access latency is on the order of 100 ns. (3) The table is titled 'The interconnect hierarchy' but its first row is chip-to-memory, which is not an interconnect between devices.
issue.evidence: Table-internal: the footnote's blanket claim does not cover the Cost column; the row labels mix device-local bandwidth with link bandwidth.
issue.root_cause: The table grew columns and rows faster than its footnote's scope statement.
issue.correction: Either tag the Cost column explicitly (e.g. [ILLUSTRATIVE] relative capital-intensity ordering) and narrow the footnote to the Bandwidth and Latency columns, or drop the Cost column and move the qualitative ordering into prose. Replace '~ns' with '~100 ns (device access)' or state the metric the column holds; retitle the table 'The memory-and-interconnect hierarchy'.
issue.acceptance_test: The footnote's scope statement matches the columns it covers; the Cost column is either sourced or labelled; the Latency column states what latency it measures.

issue.quoted_clause: When a GPU is *idle* waiting, we reach for DP/CP (more work per GPU).
issue.observed: The parenthetical mischaracterises sequence/context parallelism. CP does not give a GPU more work per token; it partitions the sequence so that a context too large for one GPU can be processed at all, at the cost of per-layer attention exchanges. Grouping CP with DP under 'more work per GPU' gives the reader the wrong reason to choose it, and the chapter's own Table 10-1 row for CP ('long contexts, KV too big') says otherwise.
issue.evidence: Internal: Table 10-1 lists CP as splitting 'the token sequence' and fitting when 'long contexts, KV too big'; §1 item 5 says CP is 'useful for very long contexts where the KV cache or attention activations exceed one GPU'.
issue.root_cause: The triangle's three corners (weights / activations / data) were mapped onto strategies, and CP was assigned to the 'data' corner because it also splits a dimension.
issue.correction: Separate the two: 'When a GPU is idle waiting for work, we reach for DP (more requests per GPU). When a single sequence no longer fits one GPU, we reach for CP (split the sequence, pay per-layer attention exchanges).'
issue.acceptance_test: The resource-triangle paragraph's parentheticals match the 'Fits when' column of Table 10-1 for every strategy it names.

issue.quoted_clause: For DP, time the gradient all-reduce as a fraction of step time — if it exceeds ~20%, it caps scaling.
issue.observed: The same ~20% threshold appears in Ch 13 §4 with an evidence label ('>~20% [ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic] of step time on collectives') and in Ch 10 without one. The book's evidence taxonomy requires the label, and the inconsistency means a reader cannot tell whether Ch 10's threshold is a measured rule or a heuristic.
issue.evidence: Cross-chapter: Ch 13 §4 item 3 labels the identical threshold; Ch 10 §4 item 3 and Ch 10 §8 mini-case ('stays under ~20% of step time') do not.
issue.root_cause: The threshold was introduced in Ch 10 and later restated in Ch 13 with a label; the label was not back-ported.
issue.correction: Add '[ILLUSTRATIVE heuristic]' to the Ch 10 §4 threshold and to the Ch 10 §8 mini-case restatement, matching Ch 13.
issue.acceptance_test: The ~20% threshold carries the same evidence label in every chapter where it appears.

issue.page_hint: Ch 9 §3 Option A; Ch 10 §3 (Data Parallelism paragraph)
issue.quoted_clause: Equivalently, 490 GB of sent-plus-received traffic divided by 900 GB/s gives the same time. ... for $N=8$ the per-rank traffic is $1.75 \times 280 \approx 490$ GB and the sync time is $T_\text{ring} = 2\frac{N-1}{N}\,\text{bytes} / B_\text{eff}$
issue.observed: The numeral '490 GB' denotes two different quantities in adjacent chapters: in Ch 9 it is the total sent-plus-received traffic (245 sent + 245 received) divided by the bidirectional 900 GB/s; in Ch 10 it is the per-rank *send* volume (1.75 × 280) divided by the directional 450 GB/s. Both are correct in their own context, but a reader moving between chapters will reasonably assume the same object and can mis-scale a time by 2×.
issue.evidence: Ch 9: 245 + 245 = 490 GB total, ÷ 900 GB/s bidirectional = 0.544 s. Ch 10: 1.75 × 280 = 490 GB sent (and 490 GB received), ÷ 450 GB/s directional = 1.089 s.
issue.root_cause: The two chapters use the same ring normalisation but different byte-counting conventions, and the coincidence of the numeral hides the difference.
issue.correction: Name the quantity in words at each site: Ch 9 '490 GB of total (sent + received) traffic'; Ch 10 '490 GB sent per rank (and 490 GB received)'. Consider stating the convention once in Ch 9 §2: 'this chapter counts send volume; total link traffic is twice that.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of '490 GB' in the book names whether it is send volume or total traffic; a reader can reproduce both 0.54 s and 1.09 s from the stated convention.

issue.page_hint: Ch 11 Fig 11.2 caption; Ch 11 §3 subsection headings
issue.quoted_clause: resource specialization joins when the workload outgrows a node (§11.3.6)
issue.observed: The reference '§11.3.6' points to a numbered subsection, but the six subsections of §11.3 carry unnumbered headings in the manuscript ('### The Canonical Workload in a Serving System', '### Discrete Batching Wastes the GPU', '### Continuous Batching Fills the Bubbles', '### PagedAttention: Killing the Fragmentation Tax', '### Prefix Caching: Don't Re-Prefill the Same Documents', '### When to Disaggregate: Prefill and Decode Want Different Pools'). A reader cannot resolve '§11.3.6' from the rendered headings.
issue.evidence: Six unnumbered '###' headings exist under §11.3, so the ordinal happens to match the intended target, but the numbering is not visible to the reader.
issue.root_cause: A numeric subsection reference was written against a numbering scheme the headings do not expose.
issue.correction: Either number the §11.3 subsections in the rendered book (e.g. 11.3.1 … 11.3.6) or change the reference to the subsection title: '…joins when the workload outgrows a node (see "When to Disaggregate", §11.3)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every subsection-level cross-reference in Ch 11 resolves to a heading the reader can see; no reference uses a number the rendered headings do not display.

issue.observed: The symbol K is invoked without definition at the point of use, and the arithmetic that follows ('1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200') does not involve K at all. A reader who has not met K in the FLOP model cannot tell what it scales, and the parenthetical as written does not explain the 1.12 PFLOP figure it sits inside.
issue.evidence: The sentence's own arithmetic (1,200 + 8,000 = 9,200) is a token-count decomposition, unrelated to a scaling constant K; the FLOP figure 2 × 70e9 × 8,000 = 1.12e15 is derived from the 8,000-token prefix alone.
issue.root_cause: A cross-reference to a symbol defined in another chapter was inserted mid-sentence without the definition or a pointer.
issue.correction: Either define K inline ('K = 1,000 is the book's token-scaling constant for the FLOP model, Ch 6') or remove the reference and state the derivation directly: '2 × 70 × 10⁹ FLOP/token × 8,000 tokens ≈ 1.12 PFLOP for the shared prefix; the full 9,200-token input is ~1.29 PFLOP'.
issue.acceptance_test: Every symbol used in a derivation in Ch 11 is defined at or before first use, or carries an explicit chapter pointer.

issue.quoted_clause: and it faces the same throughput demand at peak, making it provisionally non-viable.
issue.observed: The stated reason for candidate (c)'s non-viability contradicts the chapter's own table: Table 12-2 shows candidate (c) needs ~4 hosts at average and ~15 at peak, fewer than candidate (a)'s ~5 and ~19, so the throughput demand does not make it non-viable. The chapter's actual reason, stated two sentences later, is the quality gate. The stray clause invites the reader to reject (c) for the wrong reason — the exact parameter-counting error the chapter spends a paragraph warning against.
issue.evidence: Table 12-2: '(c) … ~4 (92,000 ÷ 24,725 ≈ 3.72)' and '~15 (368,000 ÷ 24,725 ≈ 14.88)'; candidate (a): '~5' and '~19'. Ch 12 §8 later: 'Because candidate (c) is strongly suspected to fail the quality gate [HYPOTHESIS], it is not a finalist'.
issue.root_cause: An earlier draft's rejection reason survived alongside the corrected one.
issue.correction: Delete the clause, or replace it with the correct statement: 'and it faces the same peak demand at a per-host rate that requires ~15 single-H100 hosts (Table 12-2) — a capacity question, not the reason it is gated; the quality gate is.'
issue.acceptance_test: Every stated reason for a candidate's verdict in Ch 12 is consistent with Table 12-2; candidate (c)'s non-viability is attributed only to the quality gate.

issue.page_hint: Ch 12 §5, second Common Mistake bullet; compare Ch 12 §3
issue.quoted_clause: the KV cache is ≈15% of total residency at the canonical 9.2K context (24.1/164.1; rising past 20% beyond ~13.4K) and is often the binding constraint.
issue.observed: The arithmetic is correct (24.1/164.1 = 14.7%; the 20% crossover solves KV/(140+KV) = 0.20 → KV = 35 GB → 13.4K tokens), but the trailing clause 'is often the binding constraint' sits in tension with the chapter's own analysis, which concludes that for the canonical workload the binding constraint is prefill compute (a single host is 4.65× short on prefill while KV residency has ample headroom). The reader is left with two different 'binding constraints' for the same workload.
issue.evidence: Ch 12 §3: 'the memory gate passes with one host; the throughput gate does not' and 'prefill is compute-bound at this operating point'. Ch 12 §5: KV 'is often the binding constraint'.
issue.root_cause: A general statement about input-heavy workloads was placed in a list whose other bullets are about the canonical workload, without the scope marker.
issue.correction: Scope the clause: '…and becomes the binding constraint as context grows (past ~13.4K at this model size); for the canonical 9.2K workload the binding constraint is prefill compute (§12.3).'
issue.acceptance_test: The binding constraint named in Ch 12 §5 for the canonical workload matches the one named in Ch 12 §3.

issue.quoted_clause: the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21)
issue.observed: Two different host counts (5 and 6) are given for the same average load, from two different screens, without saying which governs. The larger (6, the KV/service-time screen) is the one Ch 12's own candidate (a) paragraph uses ('~6 hosts are needed for the canonical average'), so the reader must infer that the prefill screen is not binding — but the chapter never says so. The peak figure (21) is likewise the un-headed screen, while Ch 13 applies the 70% × 95% policy to reach 32.
issue.evidence: Recomputation: 92,000/19,800 = 4.65 → 5; 86/17 = 5.06 → 6; 344/17 = 20.24 → 21. Ch 13 §3: 'under the 70% × 95% policy … that becomes 31 working + 1 spare = 32 total'.
issue.root_cause: Two independent screens are reported side by side without a governing rule, and the headroom policy is applied in Ch 13 but not in Ch 12.
issue.correction: State the governing rule explicitly ('the binding screen is the larger of the two; at the canonical average the KV/service-time screen governs at 6 hosts') and mark the peak figure as 'before headroom (Ch 13 applies the 70% × 95% policy → 32)'.
issue.acceptance_test: Wherever two or more host-count screens appear together, the text names the governing one and states whether headroom has been applied.

issue.quoted_clause: 70B FP16 weights = 140 GB; KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference residency ≈ 165 GB
issue.observed: The canonical residency is stated as 164 GB in Ch 12 (140 + 24.1 GB at the 9.2K input context) and as 165 GB here (140 + 24.9 GB at a 9.5K context). Both are defensible — 9.5K is input + generated output, so the KV grows during decode — but the book never says which context length each figure assumes, so the two read as an inconsistency in the canonical residency number.
issue.root_cause: Two chapters size the canonical KV at different context lengths without labelling the assumption.
issue.correction: Label both: Ch 12 '164 GB at the 9.2K input context (input-only KV)'; Ch 13 '165 GB at the 9.5K max context (input + 300 generated tokens)'. Add one sentence in Ch 7 or Ch 12 noting that KV residency grows with generated tokens, so the two figures are the same quantity at two context lengths.
issue.acceptance_test: Every canonical residency figure in the book states its context length; the 164 GB and 165 GB figures are not presented as competing values for the same quantity.

issue.page_hint: Ch 13 §1 item 1; Ch 13 Table 13-1, rows 'Local / edge' and 'Server'
issue.quoted_clause: Serves small models (up to ~7-13B at tight context) ... | Local / edge | 1 | — | ≤7-13B dense | low (on-device) | privacy, offline, connectivity | ... | Server | 1-8 | NVLink | ≤~70-180B dense |
issue.observed: Three small defects. (1) '≤7-13B' and '≤~70-180B' apply a less-than sign to a range, which is not a well-formed bound; the reader cannot tell whether 13B or 7B is the ceiling. (2) The Server tier's Interconnect cell names 'NVLink' specifically, while the chapter's own §1 says the tier is 'joined by NVLink/NVSwitch' and Ch 9 insists that scale-up fabrics are vendor examples, not a universal component — the table's other rows are generic ('InfiniBand/Eth'). (3) The 'Local / edge' row's Interconnect cell is '—' although the chapter's own §1 says 'Interconnect is not the question; memory capacity is', which would be a better cell value than an em dash.
issue.evidence: Internal: Ch 9 §2 'NVLink and NVSwitch are examples for the NVIDIA configuration in Table 9-1, not universal server components'; Ch 13 §1 item 2 'typically H100/H200, joined by NVLink/NVSwitch'.
issue.root_cause: The table was compressed from the prose without preserving the prose's vendor-neutral framing or its range semantics.
issue.correction: Write the model ranges as '7–13B dense' and '70–180B dense' (drop the ≤), change the Server interconnect cell to 'scale-up fabric (NVLink/NVSwitch)', and set the Local/edge interconnect cell to 'n/a (memory-bound)'.
issue.acceptance_test: No table cell applies an inequality to a range; the Server tier's interconnect cell uses the same vendor-neutral phrasing as Ch 9 and Ch 13 §1.

issue.page_hint: Ch 14 §3 'Result worksheet' table (Status column) and Ch 14 §8 mini-case
issue.quoted_clause: | Load trace | ... | to be captured | [UNMEASURED] | ... [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION][UNMEASURED]
issue.observed: The status label [UNMEASURED] is used in the worksheet table and in the mini-case but is not one of the book's defined evidence labels (provenance: [1P] [2°] [LAB] [ILLUSTRATIVE]; status: [FACT] [DERIVED] [ASSUMPTION] [HYPOTHESIS] [UNRESOLVED]; plus [ANALYTICAL] and [CANONICAL]). The book's own rule is that a label binds its clause or split caption span, and that only labels in the defined sets may be used. [UNMEASURED] is a new, unregistered label — semantically close to [UNRESOLVED] but not identical (it describes the absence of a measurement rather than an open question).
issue.evidence: The label appears in the Status column of eight worksheet rows and once in the §8 mini-case; the taxonomy is defined in Ch 4 and the Appendix A axis table.
issue.root_cause: A useful third status (measured / unmeasured / unresolved) was introduced locally without being registered in the taxonomy.
issue.correction: Either register [UNMEASURED] in the Ch 4 taxonomy and the Appendix A axis table (as a status value distinct from [UNRESOLVED]), or replace it with the existing [UNRESOLVED] status and add a one-line note that the row denotes a measurement not yet taken.
issue.acceptance_test: Every evidence label used in Ch 14 appears in the Ch 4 / Appendix A taxonomy; the taxonomy lists [UNMEASURED] if it is retained.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3 'Simultaneous feasibility check (prefill + decode coexistence)'; canonical prefill latency also used in Ch 19 §4 and Ch 22 §3/Note 22.1-1
issue.quoted_clause: The idealized prefill ceiling is 8 × 0.989 PF/s × 35% / (2 × 70e9) ≈ 19,780 tokens/s (Chapter 8, 35% MFU, prefill-only — case (i), linear-only FLOP convention). The ratio is 18,400 ÷ 19,780 ≈ 93% under case (i)
issue.observed: The book's two canonical prefill numbers are mutually inconsistent by ~2.2x, and Ch 20's prefill feasibility screen uses one of them while the latency budget (8.6 s service time) uses the other, without any reconciliation.
issue.evidence: Canonical prefill latency: 1.08 s for 9,200 tokens = 8,519 tok/s = 1.193 PFLOPS = 15.1% of the 8x989 TFLOPS host peak (case i). Canonical prefill ceiling: 19,780 tok/s at 35% MFU = 9,200 tokens in 0.465 s. Consequence at the chapter's own 2.0 rps/host: the 1.08 s basis implies a prefill duty cycle of 2.0 x 1.08 = 2.16 s of prefill per second of wall clock (216%), i.e. the host can sustain at most ~0.93 rps of prefill, not 2.0. The 93% figure is computed from the throughput ceiling and never mentions the 1.08 s. If the 1.08 s basis is the deployed one, the 40-rps prefill screen becomes 368,000 / 8,519 ≈ 43 hosts, not 19 — a material change to the fleet sizing.
issue.root_cause: The canonical prefill latency and the canonical prefill throughput ceiling were derived on different efficiency bases (single-request latency vs sustained 35%-MFU ceiling) and are then used interchangeably inside one screen.
issue.correction: State the reconciliation explicitly (e.g. '1.08 s is a single-request prefill latency at ~15% effective MFU; 19,780 tok/s is the sustained 35%-MFU ceiling') and restate the feasibility check against the basis actually used for sizing. If the two are meant to be the same basis, one of them must change.
issue.acceptance_test: A single stated effective-MFU figure reconciles 1.08 s / 9,200 tokens with the 19,780 tok/s ceiling, and the Ch 20 prefill screen and the Ch 19 / Ch 22 latency budget cite the same basis. The 93% figure must be reproducible from whichever basis is declared.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19 §8 'Unconditional fallback-inclusive ledger' paragraph; contradicted by Ch 19 §7
issue.quoted_clause: Under the fallback-inclusive ledger the unconditional p95 equals the conditional p95 — the fallback occupies only the top 2% — mass entirely above p95 — so it cannot move the 95th percentile (under the zero-turn convention it lands exactly on the boundary, CDF(*T* ≤ 2) = 95.0%, and reads *T* = 2 → 440 ms — which is exactly why the convention must travel with the number)
issue.observed: One sentence asserts two different values for the same percentile, and the CDF quoted inside the parenthetical is false under the convention the sentence is about.
issue.evidence: Ledger distribution (added orchestration): 68% @ 220 ms, 25% @ 440 ms, 5% @ 660 ms, 2% @ 860 ms. CDF(440) = 93.0%, CDF(660) = 98.0% → unconditional p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms (which is what §7 states). Under the zero-turn convention (fallback at 0 ms) CDF(440) = 2+68+25 = 95.0% → p95 = 440 ms, p99 = 660 ms. The parenthetical's '95.0%' belongs to the zero-turn convention, not to the fallback-inclusive ledger the sentence is describing; and under the zero-turn convention the fallback sits at the bottom of the distribution, not 'on the boundary' of the top.
issue.root_cause: Two percentile conventions are interleaved in one sentence without labels, and the parenthetical's arithmetic was computed under the other convention.
issue.correction: Split into two labelled statements: (a) fallback-inclusive ledger: CDF(T<=2) = 93.0%, CDF(T<=3) = 98.0% → p95 = 660 ms, p99 = 860 ms; (b) zero-turn convention: CDF(T<=2) = 95.0% → p95 = 440 ms, p99 = 660 ms. Keep §7's cross-reference consistent with (a).
issue.acceptance_test: Each percentile is stated once per convention together with its CDF; no sentence contains two values for the same percentile; §7's 'same p95 but p99 = 860 ms' matches the labelled ledger statement.

issue.quoted_clause: plus ~30 GB activations at the peak for this worked example (K+V alone: 2 × 80 layers × 9.2K × 8,192 × 2 B ≈ 24 GB, plus hidden/MLP working tensors ≈ 30 GB total) [DERIVED], giving ≈ 170 GB total derived footprint. ... the ~30 GB is a transient single-request prefill peak, reused across the batch rather than held per request in flight (17 concurrent × 30 GB is not implied) — so the envelope closes as 140 + 436 + 64 = 640, not 670.
issue.observed: The 30 GB figure is 24 GB of per-request KV plus ~6 GB of transient activation, but the parenthetical characterises the whole 30 GB as transient and batch-reused. That is false for the 24 GB KV component, which is precisely what the 436 GB KV budget already holds per request.
issue.evidence: 17 concurrent requests x 24.9 GB = 423 GB ≈ the 436 GB KV budget — so the KV is per-request resident and multiplied by concurrency, exactly as the parenthetical denies. The envelope 140 + 436 + 64 = 640 closes only if the transient part is ~6 GB drawn from the 64 GB reserve; adding a 30 GB 'activations' line that contains 24 GB of KV double-counts the KV against the 436 GB line.
issue.root_cause: A per-request persistent quantity (KV) and a transient quantity (activation/workspace) were summed into one 'activations' figure and then characterised as wholly transient, so the reader cannot tell which envelope line each component belongs to.
issue.correction: Split the derivation into two lines: 'per-request KV at 9.2K = 24.1 GB (already inside the 436 GB KV line)' and 'transient activation/workspace ≈ 6 GB (inside the 64 GB runtime/workspace reserve)'. State that the ADR's single-request arithmetic is not an envelope term.
issue.acceptance_test: The ADR's memory table lists KV and transient workspace on separate lines, each mapped to exactly one envelope line; 140 + 436 + 64 = 640 closes with no quantity appearing twice; and the phrase 'transient ... reused across the batch' is applied only to the ~6 GB component.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §3 'Fleet aggregate throughput' vs Ch 20 §8 mini-case, Fig 20.1 caption, and Ch 25 §6 ADR 0015 requirement-coverage matrix row R1
issue.quoted_clause: case (ii) rises to ⌈21.81 / 0.95⌉ = **23 hosts** — the largest requirement before the full policy ... The correct statement is: the fleet must satisfy every named screen, and the *larger* requirement wins
issue.observed: The largest named screen (23 hosts) is derived in §3 and then dropped everywhere the sizing headline is stated, so the book's stated fleet requirement (21/22 hosts) is smaller than its own max-over-screens rule.
issue.evidence: Screens under the ρ = 0.95 derate: KV screen 344/(0.95x17) = 21.3 → 22; prefill case (i) ⌈18.60/0.95⌉ = 20; case (iii) ⌈20.21/0.95⌉ = 22; case (ii) ⌈21.81/0.95⌉ = 23. Max = 23. But the §8 mini-case states 22 hosts ('the ρ-derate of the KV screen; the independent full-square case (ii) prefill compute screen also gives 22, ⌈21.81⌉'), Fig 20.1's caption says the curve 'flattens ... once 22 hosts are provisioned — 21 ideal / 22 at 95% efficiency', and ADR 0015 R1 lists '21 hosts (KV, case-independent); prefill screen 19 case (i) / 22 case (ii)' with no 23 anywhere.
issue.root_cause: The ρ derate was applied to the KV screen in the mini-case but not to the prefill screen, so the mini-case's '22' is not the max over all screens as §3's own rule requires; the figure and the ADR inherited the mini-case's number.
issue.correction: Either state 23 hosts as the ρ-derated requirement (and propagate it to the mini-case, Fig 20.1 and ADR 0015 R1), or state explicitly that the prefill screen is excluded from the ρ policy and justify that exclusion. Do not leave the two readings in the book.
issue.acceptance_test: Every host-count statement lists the max over all named screens under one named policy; the number 23 appears wherever the ρ-derated requirement is quoted; Fig 20.1's caption and ADR 0015 R1 agree with §3.

issue.quoted_clause: **Boundary rule.** A call's *input* never contains output tokens, so `task_input` must sum per-call inputs only — never the “Total tokens (incl. 300 output)” column
issue.observed: The rule as written is false against the chapter's own ledger: a later call's input does contain earlier calls' output tokens.
issue.evidence: Ledger row 2 has input 10,065 = 9,200 + call 1's 65 output tokens + call 1's 800 tool-output tokens. Row 3's input 10,930 likewise contains calls 1-2's outputs. The rule is only true of a call's *own* output.
issue.root_cause: The rule was written to stop the reader adding the 300 final-output tokens to an input sum, but was phrased as a universal property of inputs, which contradicts the ledger printed immediately above it.
issue.correction: Rewrite as: 'A call's own output is never part of its own input; a later call's input does contain earlier calls' outputs and tool results — which is exactly why Σ per-call inputs double-counts carried context and why Σ per-call inputs (41,990) exceeds the retained context (12,095).'
issue.acceptance_test: The boundary rule is true of every row of the ledger printed above it; a reader can apply it without contradiction.

issue.page_hint: Ch 19 §4 'Multi-step reasoning cost' (W(T) definition and the no-reuse / reuse lead calculations); Table 19-1 W rows
issue.quoted_clause: yields a prefill sum of (41,990 / 9,200) × 1.08 ≈ 4.93 s
issue.observed: The W evaluator scales prefill time linearly in token count, contradicting the book's own attention accounting (Ch 22 Table 22-1), so W understates the prefill leg and the error grows with turn count.
issue.evidence: Case-(ii) prefill FLOPs at the four call lengths 9,200 / 10,065 / 10,930 / 11,795 are 1.5099 / 1.6747 / 1.8434 / 2.0160 PFLOP (sum 7.044) versus the linear-only sum 1.288 + 1.4091 + 1.5302 + 1.6513 = 5.879 — a ratio of 1.198. Case (iii) gives ≈1.10. So W_no-reuse(3) ≈ 18.2-18.7 s rather than 17.70 s, and the gap widens with T (the T=4 case is worse still). The chapter elsewhere insists the quadratic term is ~17% of prefill FLOPs at 9.2K and grows with context.
issue.root_cause: The evaluator inherits a linear prefill model from the single-request case and does not carry the quadratic attention term the book derives two chapters later; the W numbers are then used for fleet sizing in Ch 17.
issue.correction: State the prefill-scaling assumption inside the W definition ('prefill time proportional to tokens, case (i) linear-only') and add a sensitivity line giving W(3) under case (ii) and case (iii); or compute the prefill sum from the case-(ii) FLOPs.
issue.acceptance_test: The W definition names its prefill-scaling assumption; the chapter states W(3) under at least one attention-aware case; and Ch 17's fleet sizing cites which W variant it used.

issue.page_hint: Ch 21 §3 'Cost of a bad ungated release'; Ch 22 §6 ADR 0015 'Context'
issue.quoted_clause: The canonical service does ~288,000 requests/workday (10 rps × 8 h × 3,600 s; ~6.24M/month — Ch 4's 8-h × 260-workday calendar basis, computed in Ch 16).
issue.observed: The headline monthly volume 6.24M is correct, but neither of the two derivations given for it is reproducible as written: Ch 21 omits the annual-to-monthly step and Ch 22 omits the seconds factor.
issue.evidence: 10 rps x 8 h x 3,600 s = 288,000 requests/workday. 260 workdays is an annual figure, so 288,000 x 260 = 74.88M requests/year and 74.88M / 12 = 6.24M/month. Ch 21's parenthetical ('8-h x 260-workday calendar basis') yields 74.88M, not 6.24M. Ch 22 §6's parenthetical is dimensionally wrong as written: '10 rps x 8 h x 260 workdays ÷ 12' = 1,733 requests, because the x 3,600 s is missing. Every $/1K figure in the book ($155.8K/mo, $87.6K/mo, $129.8K/mo) divides by 6.24M, so this is the denominator of the entire cost chapter.
issue.root_cause: The annual-to-monthly conversion was folded into an unstated '÷ 12' in one place and dropped in another, so the canonical volume cannot be re-derived from the printed formula.
issue.correction: Print the full derivation once, in Ch 4 or Ch 16, and reference it: '10 rps x 8 h x 3,600 s x 260 workdays/yr ÷ 12 = 6.24M requests/month (business-hours basis)'. Correct Ch 22's parenthetical to include the x 3,600 s and label 260 as workdays per year.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can reproduce 6.24M/month from the printed formula alone; the same formula string appears wherever the monthly volume is stated; the $/1K divisions in Ch 16, Ch 21 and Ch 22 all use 6.24M.

issue.quoted_clause: §1: 'the Red Team probes the system across three domains: 1. Prompt injection ... 2. RAG corruption ... 3. System-level exploits'; §2 table layers: 'Prompt / Retrieval / Tool use / Model behavior / Fleet orchestration'; Fig 24.1 caption: 'Probes sweep three domains (model behavior, tool use, retrieval/RAG)'
issue.observed: The chapter uses three mutually inconsistent taxonomies of the same thing — the Red Team's probe domains — in §1, §2 and the figure caption.
issue.evidence: §1's three domains are prompt injection / RAG corruption / system-level exploits. §2's table has five layers. The figure caption's three domains are model behavior / tool use / retrieval-RAG, which map to none of §1's three groupings one-to-one (model behavior is not one of §1's domains; system-level exploits is not in the caption's list).
issue.root_cause: The chapter's probe taxonomy was restated locally in each section instead of being defined once and referenced.
issue.correction: Define one taxonomy (the §2 five-layer table is the most complete) and have §1 and the Fig 24.1 caption reference it, or state the mapping between the three groupings explicitly in one place.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can map every domain named in §1, §2 and the Fig 24.1 caption onto a single list without inference; the figure caption's domain names appear in §1 or §2.

issue.page_hint: Ch 23 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Next Month Customer Portal'
issue.quoted_clause: quality means "resolve the ticket, not just answer" (a capability that rules out the cheaper model) ... The mirrored restatement turns "let's ship AI next month" into "a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU, resolving baseline tickets under 3 s ..."
issue.observed: The mini-case's stated reasoning excludes the cheaper model and then selects a 7B-class model, which is the book's own cheap tier (Ch 20 §7: '70B for complex queries, 7B for quick ones').
issue.evidence: The mini-case's own premise is that the quality bar 'rules out the cheaper model'; the resulting scope is 'a 7B-class model on one on-prem GPU'. Either the premise or the conclusion must change, and as written the mini-case does not require the reader to use the chapter's reasoning — it contradicts it.
issue.root_cause: The scenario was written with a generic 'smaller model is insufficient' premise and then given a concrete 7B conclusion without reconciling the two.
issue.correction: Make the premise specific and consistent: either state that the capability bar rules out a sub-7B model (and why 7B suffices), or change the conclusion to a larger model and re-derive the one-GPU feasibility (7B at 500 tokens: 5 rps x 7 TFLOP = 35 TFLOP/s; a 70B at 500 tokens: 5 x 70 TFLOP = 350 TFLOP/s, still inside one H100's 989 TFLOPS peak, so the burst arithmetic must be redone).
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case's quality premise and its selected model size are consistent, and the burst arithmetic in the conclusion is recomputed for the model actually named.

issue.page_hint: Ch 24 §3.3 'The benchmark trap' and its [DERIVED] note
issue.quoted_clause: its per-token cost is ~45% lower (fewer host-hours) ... [DERIVED] — the ~45% per-token cost delta follows from the candidate host-hour difference
issue.observed: A [DERIVED] numeric claim has no derivation, and the naive derivation from the stated inputs gives a different number.
issue.evidence: Candidate A = 4 hosts, Candidate B = 8 hosts. Host-hour ratio 4/8 = 50%, i.e. ~50% lower cost per token at equal served volume — not 45%. A 45% figure would require an unstated intermediate host count (e.g. 4.5 hosts, which is between the 4.07-host prefill floor at 40% MFU and the 5.43-host floor at 30% MFU), which the text does not state.
issue.root_cause: The cost delta was asserted rather than computed, and the label [DERIVED] was applied to a number whose derivation is absent.
issue.correction: Show the derivation (host-hours x $/hr / tokens served for each candidate) and print the resulting percentage, or restate as '~50% fewer host-hours at equal served volume' and label it [ILLUSTRATIVE].
issue.acceptance_test: The percentage is reproducible from the two candidates' host counts and the $/hr figure; the label matches the derivation actually shown.

issue.page_hint: Ch 20 §6, final subsection 'The useful completion is an accepted clip'
issue.quoted_clause: The same accepted-completion goodput accounting applies to any fixed-output-contract workload; a video-generation fleet is the clearest parallel beyond RAG. ... The rejection/OOM/cancellation counters, the cost-per-accepted-clip basis, and the zero-pass edge case follow the same rules as the accepted-completion definition above; placement follows the measured-service-time rule, with warm replicas trading idle cost for avoiding checkpoint downloads, initialization, compilation, and encoder loading on the request path.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §8 (Mini-Case), Step 1 and Step 2; also §3 'Capstone Execution'
issue.quoted_clause: The 450 ms is a *service-time sum with no queueing term*; at the offered ~2 rps against the ~2.0 req/s analytical ceiling (ρ near 1), a real queueing delay sits on top ... the baseline's 320 ms compute is a worst-case figure carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1, and the miss value assumes that queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps (compute falls from the inflated 320 ms to ~120 ms, so 250 ≈ 120 + 80 + 50) ... (both sides are service-time sums with no queueing term — at ρ near 1 a real queue would sit on top of the baseline too)
issue.observed: The baseline's 450 ms is asserted to contain no queueing term, while its 320 ms compute component is asserted to carry prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1. Both statements cannot hold. The cached/miss side (250 ms) is explicitly queue-drained, so the headline comparison is a queue-inflated baseline against a queue-drained treatment — and the chapter twice claims both sides are queue-free.
issue.evidence: Step 1: 320 + 80 + 50 = 450 ms, declared 'a service-time sum with no queueing term'. Step 2: the 320 ms term is 'a worst-case figure carrying prefill-queue inflation at ρ near 1', and the miss value 'assumes that queue has drained at the cached ~1.3 rps'. Step 2 then asserts 'both sides are service-time sums with no queueing term'. §3 repeats the same claim. The offered load in Step 1 is ~2 rps against a ~2.0 req/s ceiling (ρ ≈ 1), the regime the chapter itself says produces unbounded queueing delay.
issue.root_cause: The baseline was authored as a queue-free service-time sum, then re-described as queue-inflated when the miss path needed a smaller compute term. The two framings were never reconciled, and the reconciliation was then asserted away in prose.
issue.correction: Choose one baseline definition and state it once. Either (a) baseline = queue-free service-time sum of 450 ms (320 ms compute with no queue inflation), in which case the miss path must be re-derived on the same queue-free basis and the 120 ms compute figure justified independently; or (b) baseline = queue-inflated, in which case the cached side must also be evaluated at ρ ≈ 1, or the comparison must be explicitly labelled 'queue-drained treatment vs queue-inflated baseline'. Then restate the −44% on the reconciled basis.
issue.acceptance_test: One sentence in Step 1 defines the baseline's queue treatment; Step 2's 250 ms and the −44% use the same treatment; a reader can recompute both sides from the printed components and reproduce the same percentage.

issue.quoted_clause: *Deeper continuous batching on the single host instead of sharding* raises throughput by lengthening the in-flight queue, adding queueing delay exactly where the p99 TTFT SLO binds
issue.observed: Two errors. (i) Continuous batching raises throughput by keeping the decode batch occupied (admitting a new request as another completes), not by 'lengthening the in-flight queue'; a longer queue is a symptom of saturation, not the mechanism of higher throughput. (ii) On this host the resident-request ceiling is set by KV residency (C ≈ 17.5 within the ~436 GB KV budget of the ~500 GB non-weight pool), so 'deeper' batching cannot add resident requests at all — it can only add queueing delay and prefill interference. The alternative is infeasible on this host, not merely harmful.
issue.evidence: §3 Pattern A: 'can hold ~17.5 concurrent 9,500-token requests within the canonical ~436 GB KV budget from Chapter 15'; 640 GB pool − 140 GB weights = 500 GB, of which ~436 GB is KV. §3 Alternatives: the deeper-batching rejection as quoted.
issue.root_cause: The rejection reason was written as a generic queueing argument without checking the host's binding constraint, which the same chapter establishes two paragraphs earlier.
issue.correction: Rewrite the rejection around the binding constraint: 'the host's resident-request capacity is already KV-bound at C ≈ 17.5 (Ch 15); deeper batching cannot raise concurrency, only queueing delay and prefill interference, so it cannot raise throughput on this host.' If the intent is to compare against a host with more KV headroom, say so and quantify the headroom required.
issue.acceptance_test: The rejection names the binding constraint (KV residency) and does not attribute throughput gain to queue length; a reader can confirm from C ≈ 17.5 that concurrency is capped.

issue.quoted_clause: Three obvious alternatives were weighed against the canonical constraints, and each is rejected for a stated, testable reason — not merely because it "changes the wrong term."
issue.observed: The second alternative is explicitly not rejected: 'A second serving host with load balancing is not rejected ... the capstone treats it as an open sizing question to be tested over an actual offered-load interval, not as a rejected alternative'. The lead sentence's 'each is rejected' is therefore false, and its promise of a 'testable reason' is not met for that alternative.
issue.evidence: §3 Alternatives, second bullet: 'the capstone treats it as an **open sizing question to be tested over an actual offered-load interval**, not as a rejected alternative'.
issue.root_cause: The lead sentence was written when all three alternatives were rejections and was not updated when the second was converted into a deferred sizing question.
issue.correction: Rewrite the lead: 'Three obvious alternatives were weighed. Two are rejected for stated, testable reasons; the third — a second serving host — is not rejected but deferred to a load-curve / goodput test over an actual offered-load interval.'
issue.acceptance_test: The lead sentence's claim matches the three treatments that follow; no alternative is described as rejected in the lead and then treated as open.

issue.quoted_clause: | Inference Sharding | SM utilization % | per-GPU token latency p99 | All-Reduce time | | Semantic Response Cache | hit ratio @ TTL=T | stale read rate | cache memory pressure | | Circuit Breaker | timeout count / 30s | fallback activation rate | recovery grace-period latency |
issue.observed: (a) The semantic cache's FACT set contains no isolation-violation counter, although Pattern B makes authorization / corpus-version isolation the precondition for calling the component a semantic cache at all ('a cross-user hit could leak another user's authorized response'). (c) The 'Inference Sharding' row asks for FACTs to validate a pattern the capstone declares to be baseline configuration with no parallelism change, and omits the quantities that actually determine a sharding decision (weights per rank, KV slots per host, TP degree).
issue.evidence: §3 Pattern B: 'the cache key must carry **authorization and corpus-version isolation** ... a cross-user hit could leak another user's authorized response'. §3 Pattern C: 'the ~7% fallback share is labeled a separately-tracked degraded outcome'. §3 Pattern A: '**Sharding here is *baseline configuration*, not an incremental optimization (R-04)**'.
issue.root_cause: Table 26-1 was drafted from a generic pattern-monitoring template rather than from the quantities the chapter's own patterns actually depend on.
issue.correction: Add 'isolation-violation count (target 0)' to the cache row; add 'degraded-outcome (shed) rate' and 'SLO-compliance rate over completed useful requests' to the breaker row; either drop the sharding row or restate it as 'sharding configuration — FACTs to monitor, not to validate' and add weights-per-rank, KV-slots-per-host and TP degree.
issue.acceptance_test: Every quantity the chapter says is tracked (the ~7% degraded share, the authorization-isolation requirement) appears in Table 26-1; the sharding row states its purpose.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §2.1, Fig 26.1 provenance note; quantization decision record paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: batch 0.55 / 0.60 / 0.30 / 0.85 / 0.35 / 0.90 — the same table is carried in the archetypes are reference points, not measured clusters. **Because each bar is an author-chosen input, the bar values are [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]; only a value computed *from* them (e.g. a ratio of two bars) would be [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED].** [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]]). ... [ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual
issue.observed: (a) 'the same table is carried in the archetypes are reference points, not measured clusters' is not a sentence — it is a botched merge of two clauses. (b) The note ends with a stray ']' after '[ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION]' and an unbalanced closing parenthesis, which will print as a visible typographic defect. (c) The quantization decision record paragraph ends with a bare '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' label with no figure, table or claim in scope.
issue.evidence: Quoted text as printed in the chunk; the orphan label follows 'A recommendation becomes defensible when those records describe the same configuration and agree, not when a format name appears in a support matrix.'
issue.root_cause: Editing residue from a caption/label refactor: a sentence was truncated during a merge and a label was left behind when its target was moved.
issue.correction: Repair the sentence (e.g. 'the same table is carried in the archetypes; the archetypes are reference points, not measured clusters.'), delete the stray bracket, and either attach the orphan '[ILLUSTRATIVE] conceptual' to a specific claim or remove it.
