issue.quoted_clause: ~2,000 registered users with ~5% concurrently active at peak (~100 concurrent *users*, a population measure) ... as the canonical ~40 rps peak (Ch 4) would if concentrated on one host
issue.observed: If ~100 users each hold one outstanding request of ~8.6 s, the implied offered rate is 100 / 8.6 ≈ 11.6 rps, not ~40 rps. Reaching ~40 rps at an 8.6 s service time requires ~344 concurrent requests. The chapter uses both numbers in the same reasoning — Pattern C argues that the canonical peak would saturate a single host — without stating the relationship between 'concurrently active users' and 'in-flight requests'.
issue.evidence: §3: '~100 concurrent *users*, a population measure'; 'the canonical request's total end-to-end time is ~8.6 s'; 'the canonical ~40 rps peak (Ch 4)'. 100 / 8.6 s = 11.6 rps; 40 rps × 8.6 s = 344 in-flight requests.
issue.root_cause: Two different canonical quantities — a user-population measure and a request-rate measure — are used side by side without the conversion the reader needs, and the parenthetical '(a population measure)' flags the issue without resolving it.
issue.correction: State the relationship explicitly: either define the peak rps as a burst measure distinct from the sustained rate implied by 100 concurrent users, or state the outstanding-requests-per-active-user figure (≈3.4) that reconciles ~40 rps with ~100 active users. Add the one-line conversion so the reader can check it.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader can compute the canonical peak rps from the stated user population and service time using only numbers printed in the chapter, and obtain ~40 rps — or the chapter states explicitly that the peak is a different measure and gives that measure's definition.

issue.quoted_clause: the canonical request's total end-to-end time is ~8.6 s (1.08 s prefill + ~7.5 s decode of 300 output tokens) ... the per-host ceiling is ~2.0 req/s (Ch 17/20)
issue.observed: 300 output tokens in ~7.5 s is 40 tok/s per request; at the host's operating concurrency C ≈ 17.5 that is ~700 tok/s aggregate. For a 140 GB FP16 weight set on 8×H100 (3.35 TB/s each, ~26.8 TB/s aggregate), the weight-read-bound decode rate is ~191 tok/s at batch 1 and scales roughly with batch, i.e. ~3.3k tok/s at batch 17.5. The canonical decode therefore sits at roughly 20% of the batch-scaled bandwidth roofline, yet the chapter asserts the decode regime ('decode latency is bandwidth-bound in the low-batch decode regime of Ch. 8') without showing the check. The ~2.0 req/s ceiling derived from this service time is the load-bearing number for the capstone, the mini-case, and (by the chapter's own references) Ch 17/20 fleet sizing.
issue.evidence: 7.5 s / 300 tokens = 40 tok/s per request; 40 × 17.5 = 700 tok/s aggregate; 140 GB / 26.8 TB/s = 191 tok/s at batch 1; 191 × 17.5 ≈ 3,350 tok/s at batch 17.5; 700 / 3,350 ≈ 21%. (Roofline constants from the H100 datasheet; Ch 8's own numbers were not available in this chunk and must be used to confirm.)
issue.root_cause: The canonical service time is carried into Ch 26 as a recalled constant; the chapter invokes Ch 8's roofline rhetorically but never reconciles the recalled constant against it, so the reader cannot tell whether the gap is queueing, kernel inefficiency, or deliberate planning conservatism.
issue.correction: Add a short reconciliation: state the assumed decode efficiency (or the queueing / overhead share) that turns the 8×H100 bandwidth roofline into the canonical 40 tok/s per request, and state that the ~2.0 req/s ceiling is therefore a planning cap rather than a hardware limit — which is exactly how the mini-case then uses it ('conservative planning caps').
issue.acceptance_test: The chapter states the efficiency factor (or overhead share) between the 8×H100 bandwidth roofline and the canonical 40 tok/s per request, and the reader can reproduce the ~2.0 req/s ceiling from it.

issue.quoted_clause: the capstone declares as the baseline **p99** scenario value (a scenario input, not a derived quantile of a distributed sample; a real baseline p99 must come from a measured latency distribution) ... **p99 TTFT ≈ 250 ms** (the miss value, not a blend). **−44% TTFT** against the ~450 ms uncached p99 baseline
issue.observed: The cached side's p99 is derived from an explicit two-point distribution (F(50) = 0.35, F(250) = 1.0). The baseline's 450 ms is a sum of 'representative worst-case estimates' for a single request, declared as a p99 input but with no distribution behind it. The headline −44% therefore compares a distribution quantile against a single-request worst-case sum, and the chapter's own note that the baseline is 'not a derived quantile of a distributed sample' is precisely the reason the two sides are not the same kind of object.
issue.evidence: Step 2: 'the pooled latency has the CDF F(50)=0.35, F(250)=1.0 ... its **p99 is 250 ms**'. Step 1: 'the component values are *representative worst-case* estimates for a baseline request, and the ~450 ms is therefore the baseline TTFT figure used throughout; the per-query values are not a p99 of a separate measured distribution.'
issue.root_cause: The baseline was specified as a point estimate and then promoted to a quantile label so that the comparison would read cleanly; the two sides were never given the same modelling treatment.
issue.correction: Give the baseline the same treatment: state that the baseline is modelled as a point mass at 450 ms (hence p99 = 450 ms) and that the cached side is modelled as the two-point distribution, so both sides are quantiles of stated models; or relabel the headline as a service-time reduction and remove 'p99' from the baseline side.
issue.acceptance_test: The −44% figure is reproducible from two explicitly stated latency models, and the metric name used for each side matches the model used for that side.

issue.quoted_clause: The architect never promotes a pattern from HYPOTHESIS to ACCEPTED unless all FACTs stabilize within expected ranges across at least two load cycles
issue.observed: ACCEPTED is a new lifecycle state introduced here. The book's Axis-2 status set is [FACT]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION]/[HYPOTHESIS]/[UNRESOLVED] (Ch 4 and the Appendix A axis table). A reader who has internalized the taxonomy will look for ACCEPTED in the axis table and not find it, and will not know whether it is a status, a workflow state, or an informal word.
issue.evidence: Appendix A: 'Axis 2 status [FACT]/[DERIVED]/[ASSUMPTION]/[HYPOTHESIS]/[UNRESOLVED]'. Ch 26 §2 lists only FACT / DERIVED / HYPOTHESIS as the loop's three labels.
issue.root_cause: A workflow state was written in the same typographic form as the book's epistemic statuses without being registered in the taxonomy.
issue.correction: Either add ACCEPTED to the Axis-2 status set in Ch 4 and the Appendix A axis table, explicitly marked as a validation state distinct from an epistemic status, or reword to 'promotes a HYPOTHESIS to an accepted design decision' so that no new bracketed status token is introduced.
issue.acceptance_test: Every bracketed status token used in Ch 26 appears in the book's axis table; a reader can classify 'ACCEPTED' without ambiguity.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'Mapping onto the book's evidence taxonomy' and 'One fact, three registers'
issue.quoted_clause: **Interpretation** ↔ **[INTERPRETATION]** — an explicit analysis/interpretation marker for the book's own read of the evidence. It is **not** a sixth arithmetic status and adds nothing to Axis 2 (where a three-axis status is required, an interpretation is recorded as [ASSUMPTION] — a stated reading, not a measurement — with [INTERPRETATION] marking it inline) ... (b) descriptive interpretation — "sparsity this extreme makes long-context serving a memory problem before a compute problem" is [INTERPRETATION]: our read of what the number means, analysis that could be wrong and earns no arithmetic status
issue.observed: The same paragraph says [INTERPRETATION] 'is not a sixth arithmetic status' and 'adds nothing to Axis 2', then uses it as a standalone label in the worked contrast, while also describing it as an inline companion to [ASSUMPTION]. A reader cannot tell whether '[INTERPRETATION]' alone is a complete label or must always accompany an Axis-2 status. The paragraph also states that 'the appendix uses "interpretation" as plain prose for an analytical read, never a sanctioned arithmetic status', which contradicts the bracketed use in the same section.
issue.evidence: Quoted text as printed; the standalone use appears in the 'One fact, three registers' worked contrast, where (a) is [DERIVED], (b) is [INTERPRETATION], (c) is [HYPOTHESIS] — three parallel labels, two of which are sanctioned statuses.
issue.root_cause: A reader-friendly layer was introduced over the three-axis taxonomy without a rule for how the two compose, and the prose describing the rule contradicts the examples that follow it.
issue.correction: State one rule: [INTERPRETATION] is a non-status qualifier that must always be paired with an Axis-2 status (e.g. [ASSUMPTION][INTERPRETATION]) and never stands alone; then fix the worked contrast to use the paired form and delete the sentence claiming it is never used as a label.
issue.acceptance_test: Every occurrence of [INTERPRETATION] in the book is either paired with an Axis-2 status or is explicitly declared a standalone marker; the worked contrast and the prose describe the same rule.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §2 (definition of [1P]) vs Appendix A 'Quantization implementation observations', 'Intel backend supplement', 'Video systems snapshot'
issue.quoted_clause: **[1P]** marks a first-party **source** — the original method paper authored by the method's creators, or a hardware-vendor specification (technical report, model card, or official documentation). ... [1P][FACT] ([NVFP4 CUTLASS](...)) ... At the pinned revision in the source ledger, `block_q4_K` occupies 144 bytes for 256 values ... The retrieved release APIs identify PyTorch v2.14.1 (September 30), vLLM v0.32.0 (October 18), SGLang v0.5.22 (October 19) ... Official release metadata: [A-S72]
issue.observed: The appendix labels source-code observations (vLLM and llama.cpp files at pinned commits), release-metadata observations (PyTorch / vLLM / SGLang / OpenVINO / Diffusers release dates), API documentation and blog posts as [1P]. Under Ch 26 §2's definition, [1P] covers only (a) an original method paper by the method's creators and (b) a hardware-vendor specification — none of which covers a vLLM source file or a PyTorch release timestamp. The definition and the usage disagree.
issue.evidence: Ch 26 §2: 'Keep the four categories distinct: (a) an original method paper by the method's creators, (b) a hardware-vendor specification, (c) a third-party evaluation ..., and (d) an own measured run ... Of these, [1P] covers (a) and (b) only'. Appendix A applies [1P] to code and release metadata as listed above.
issue.root_cause: Ch 26 §2's definition was written for hardware and method claims and was not generalised to software-artifact provenance, which the appendix's October notes require.
issue.correction: Broaden the Ch 26 §2 definition to 'a first-party artifact from the party that produces the thing — the method's own paper, the vendor's technical report / model card / datasheet, the project's own source code at a pinned revision, or its own release notes and documentation', and state that a code or release-metadata observation is a fact about the artifact, not about deployed performance. Alternatively introduce a distinct provenance token for source-code observations.
issue.acceptance_test: Every [1P] use in Appendix A falls under the Ch 26 §2 definition as amended; a reader can classify each appendix citation from the definition without ambiguity.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'This is a dated field guide' paragraph vs §8 'First-hand Sources'
issue.quoted_clause: **Reproduction status** is recorded per family in the First-hand Sources list (A.10): each entry carries its source URL/identifier, the version and release date where known, and the verification status (whether the claim is vendor-reported [1P] pending independent check, or independently verified). Where a number has not been independently validated, it is flagged — do not treat a model-card figure as an audited measurement.
issue.observed: The list as printed carries only URLs/identifiers plus one blanket note ('all parameters/claims are vendor-reported [1P]'). It carries no per-entry version, no release date, no verification status, and no per-claim flag for which numbers have been independently validated — although the same paragraph says such numbers 'is flagged'. The appendix's own register table lists 'Independent reproduction' as one of its three registers, so the reader expects per-claim status.
issue.evidence: §8 list as printed: '- DeepSeek-V4: technical report arXiv:2606.19348; model card https://...; org https://github.com/deepseek-ai' (and three analogous entries).
issue.root_cause: The list was simplified after the paragraph describing it was written; the description was not updated to match.
issue.correction: Either restore the per-entry fields (version/revision, release date, verification status per claim) in the list, or rewrite the paragraph to describe what the list actually provides and state plainly that no claim in the four-family comparison has been independently validated.
issue.acceptance_test: The paragraph's description of the list matches the list's actual columns; every claim in the four-family comparison is either flagged as independently validated or explicitly stated as vendor-reported only.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, Fig A.1 'Definition of "active"' and the caption paragraph
issue.quoted_clause: "active" (equivalently "activated") means the parameters that participate in the forward pass for a given token: the routed experts dispatched for that token, the shared/always-on experts, and the attention and embedding/head parameters that run for every token. ... the active fractions below are comparable only *after* this definition is fixed ... Qwen3.8-Flash-Next 125 B/6 B (~4.8% — *backbone-only ratio*: the denominator is the 125 B backbone; the separate 51 B n-gram embedding and 4 B MTP modules are excluded from both numerator and denominator
issue.observed: The stated definition counts embedding parameters that run for every token as active, but the Qwen figure excludes the 51 B N-gram embedding table from the denominator (and the 4 B MTP module from both). Under the stated definition, Qwen's active fraction would be 6 / (125 + 51 + 4) = 3.3%, not 4.8%. The claim that the four fractions are comparable 'only after this definition is fixed' therefore does not hold for the Qwen row.
issue.evidence: 6 / 125 = 4.8% (printed); 6 / (125 + 51 + 4) = 6 / 180 = 3.33%. The other three rows are unaffected (Kimi 104/2800 = 3.71%; DeepSeek-V4-Flash 13/284 = 4.58%; GLM-5.3-Flash 18/320 = 5.63%).
issue.root_cause: The definition was written for the general case; the Qwen row was computed on a narrower denominator without amending the definition or adding the second value.
issue.correction: Either amend the definition to state that the numerator and denominator are computed over the counted backbone (attention + experts + the embeddings that run per token within that backbone), or present both Qwen figures (4.8% backbone-only and 3.3% of the complete deployed inventory) and state explicitly that the four fractions are not on a single denominator.
issue.acceptance_test: Each of the four fractions can be recomputed from the definition as written, or the text states that the Qwen row uses a different denominator and gives both values.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A, 'The Signal in One Paragraph', lever 3; compare §6 lever table
issue.quoted_clause: Three **efficiency levers** every 2026 frontier family pulled: ... 3. **Efficiency is a first-class result, not an afterthought.** Training-stable optimizers (Muon) and post-training RL (GRPO, async RL) are now reported as core architecture, not tooling.
issue.observed: (a) Lever 3 is not a lever but a meta-claim, and it mixes a training-time optimizer (Muon) with post-training RL, which the appendix's own §6 lever table classifies as 'Capability (a major source in current frontier systems)'. The appendix therefore places post-training in the capability ledger in one section and counts it as an efficiency lever in another. (b) 'every 2026 frontier family pulled' is not supported by the appendix's own evidence: Muon is attributed only to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ('Muon + AdamW'); the DeepSeek-V4 and GLM-5.3-Flash entries do not mention Muon or GRPO.
issue.evidence: §6 lever table: '| Post-training / RL / reasoning | Capability (a major source in current frontier systems) |'. §3 (Qwen): 'Muon + AdamW'. §1 (DeepSeek) and §4 (GLM) decisive facts contain no mention of Muon or GRPO.
issue.root_cause: The three-item list was written as a summary of 'what changed' rather than as a list of efficiency levers, and the 'every family' quantifier was carried over from levers 1 and 2, which the four entries do support.
issue.correction: Split lever 3 out of the efficiency list and restate it as a capability / training-stack observation consistent with §6, or move it into the capability ledger; and replace 'every 2026 frontier family pulled' with a scoped statement naming the families for which each item is reported.
issue.acceptance_test: Every item in the 'efficiency levers' list is classified as efficiency in the §6 lever table, and each 'every family' claim is supported by all four family entries.

issue.page_hint: Appendix A §1 (DeepSeek-V4), 'What this means for the architect'
issue.quoted_clause: DeepSeek shows the *constant factor itself* can be cut ~10–14× across the V4 variants (the ~14× end is V4-Flash's ~7%-of-V3.2 single-token KV, §5) through attention re-architecture alone — the parameter count is unchanged, so the saving is architectural, not a smaller model.
issue.observed: As written, 'the parameter count is unchanged' is false or unresolvable. V4-Pro is 1.6 T total and V4-Flash is 284 B total, so the parameter count is not unchanged across the variants the sentence is about; and the appendix never states V3.2's parameter count, so the reader cannot check 'unchanged' against the reference model. The intended claim is that the KV/FLOP constant changed without the model being shrunk.
issue.evidence: §1: 'V4-Pro is 1.6 T total / 49 B activated, V4-Flash 284 B / 13 B activated'. No V3.2 parameter count appears anywhere in the chunk.
issue.root_cause: The sentence was written to make a point about the attention scheme and left ambiguous about which pair of models 'unchanged' refers to.
issue.correction: Rewrite: 'the saving comes from the attention scheme rather than from a smaller model — the parameter count is not what changed.' If the claim is meant relative to V3.2, state V3.2's parameter count and cite it.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence is true under every reading a reader can construct from the appendix's own numbers, or it names the reference model and its parameter count.

issue.quoted_clause: - **Mistake 1: Validating HYPOTHESIS claims without independent FACT anchors.** ... - **Mistake 4: Circular HYPOTHESIS validation.** Self-confirming predictions (e.g., a cache-hit threshold set by one load test and then "confirmed" by that same load test) bypass the FACT/DERIVED/HYPOTHESIS axis.
issue.observed: The four mistakes are generic process warnings. None addresses the specific, subtle trap the chapter's own capstone walks into: treating a modelled two-point latency distribution's quantile as if it were a measured p99, and comparing it against a service-time sum that has been labelled 'p99'. A reader who has followed the capstone's arithmetic is exposed to exactly this error and the chapter never names it.
issue.evidence: Step 2: 'a weighted average of component latency values is a mean, not a quantile, so the capstone separates the two' — the chapter teaches the mean/quantile distinction for the cached side but never teaches it for the baseline side, and never lists it as a mistake.
issue.root_cause: The Common Mistakes section was written as a generic checklist rather than as a list of the specific traps this chapter's own worked example sets.
issue.correction: Add a fifth mistake, e.g. '**Mistake 5: Reading a modelled quantile as a measured percentile.** A two-point latency model yields a p99 that is simply the slow point mass; it is a scenario value, not a percentile of a measured distribution, and it must not be compared against a service-time sum labelled "p99".' Explain why the error is plausible (the arithmetic is exact and the labels match).
issue.acceptance_test: The Common Mistakes section contains at least one entry naming a trap a reader of this chapter's own worked example could plausibly fall into, with the reason the incorrect reasoning looks right.

issue.quoted_clause: A growing AI startup moves from a single-node prototype to a fleet serving ~3,000 users. ... the capstone therefore states a concrete scaling assumption (the same ~2.0 rps sustained offered rate, ~5% concurrently active at peak, and a 35% cache-hit ratio held constant for illustration)
issue.observed: The mini-case is titled 'Capstone at Scale' but performs no scale computation: the offered rate is held at the single host's ~2 rps ceiling, so the fleet never grows, no host count is computed, and no topology or capacity consequence is drawn. The one step that would connect the pattern instance to the book's fleet-sizing arc (Ch 17/20) is skipped, even though the chapter has all the inputs (3,000 users, 5% concurrency, 8.6 s service time, 2.0 req/s per host, 35% hit ratio).
issue.evidence: Under the stated assumption: 3,000 × 5% = 150 concurrent users; at 8.6 s service time that is 150 / 8.6 ≈ 17.4 rps; at 2.0 req/s per host that is ~9 hosts; with the 35% cache hit ratio the engine sees 17.4 × 0.65 ≈ 11.3 rps, i.e. ~6 hosts. The chapter prints none of this.
issue.root_cause: The mini-case was scoped to validate the pattern instance (Step 3) and the scale step was reduced to a held-constant assumption, leaving the chapter's title unfulfilled and the fleet-level consequence undemonstrated.
issue.correction: Add the scale computation as an explicit sub-step: state the offered rate implied by the 3,000-user population under the declared assumption, convert it to engine rps after the cache, divide by the ~2.0 req/s per-host ceiling to get a host count, and state the resulting fleet (and note that the short-prompt workload's lower service time would reduce it). This also gives the 'Architecture Consequence' section a concrete instance.
issue.acceptance_test: The mini-case prints a host count derived from its own stated assumptions, and that count is consistent with the ~2.0 req/s per-host ceiling and the 35% hit ratio used elsewhere in the chapter.

issue.quoted_clause: answers the architect's question at multiple grainsizes: from the micro (which cache invalidation strategy?) to the macro (how does sharding affect fleet-wide latency?)
issue.observed: 'grainsizes' is not a word; the intended term is 'granularities' or 'scales of analysis'. Separately, the micro example given ('which cache invalidation strategy?') is never answered in the chapter: Pattern B lists invalidation triggers (permission change, deletion/withdrawal, index refresh, source update) but never compares invalidation strategies, so the promised micro-level guidance is not delivered.

issue.acceptance_test: Every micro/macro example named in §1 is answered somewhere in the chapter.

issue.page_hint: Ch 26 §2.1 matrix; Appendix A throughout; Ch 26 §8
issue.quoted_clause: the anchor for the Ch10 expert-parallelism serving calculus ... from a single model's tokens (Ch1–9) to parallelism (Ch10), serving (Ch11–16) ... Figure A.5 separates the parameter object from its invocations

issue.quoted_clause: Fig 26.2 — Pattern Application Diagram: the Pattern-Measurement-Feedback Loop applied to the capstone, closing on FACT → DERIVED → PATTERN. ... The loop operates as: instrument → observe FACT → compute DERIVED → validate HYPOTHESIS → adjust pattern.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode on the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The caption's stated prefill arithmetic intensity (~41 FLOP/byte) contradicts BOTH the plotted marker (~10^4 FLOP/byte) and the prose on the same page (~2K FLOP/byte). Three mutually inconsistent values are given for the single quantity the figure exists to convey. Worse, the caption's own number (41) is BELOW the ridge the figure labels (~295), so taken at face value the caption places prefill on the memory-bound side while simultaneously calling it 'the compute-bound side'.
issue.evidence: Caption (printed p.23): 'Low-batch decode (streaming weights per token) lands at ~1 FLOP/byte — the memory-bound side; long-prefix prefill lands at ~41 FLOP/byte — the compute-bound side.' Prose list item (1) on the same page: 'arithmetic intensity places the canonical prefill point ~2K FLOP/byte, well to the right of the ~295 ridge'. Figure: the blue 'prefill' triangle sits at the far right of the x-axis, at or beyond the 10000 tick (AI ~ 1e4), not at 41 and not at 2e3. Independent rederivation for the canonical 70B / 9,200-token prefill: FLOPs = 2 x 70e9 x 9200 = 1.29e15; bytes = 140 GB weights + 2.62 MB/token x 9200 = 24.1 GB KV writes = 1.64e11 B; AI = 1.29e15 / 1.64e11 ~ 7.8e3 FLOP/byte (plus ~17% from attention FLOPs -> ~9e3). None of 41, 2e3, or 1e4 is derivable from the canonical numbers as printed; 41 is also implausible on its face, since prefill AI is approximately the number of tokens processed (AI ~ T for large T), so 'long-prefix prefill' cannot be 41.
issue.root_cause: The figure, its caption, and the summary list were authored from three different (unstated) derivations of the same quantity; no single derivation is shown anywhere on the page, so no gate could catch the divergence.
issue.correction: Pick one canonical prefill AI, show its derivation (tokens, FLOPs, bytes, ratio) in the caption or in an adjacent worked example, and make the caption, the marker position, and the prose list item all state that same value. If the intended value is the derived ~8e3, move the marker to ~8e3 and rewrite the caption as '~8x10^3 FLOP/byte — the compute-bound side'. If a different scenario (e.g. a short prompt) is intended, label it as such and plot a second marker rather than silently changing the number.
issue.acceptance_test: One number appears for canonical prefill AI in the caption, in the marker x-position, and in prose item (1); the value exceeds 295 (so 'compute-bound side' is true of the stated number); and a reader can reproduce it from the canonical inputs printed in Ch. 4 / Table 2-1 without consulting another chapter.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode on the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The drawn roofline ridge is geometrically inconsistent with its own '~295' crossover label and with the H100 numbers the book uses elsewhere, and the decode marker is drawn ON the ridge, contradicting the figure's own annotation that markers lie below the roof.
issue.evidence: A roofline's bandwidth-limited segment is a straight line in log-log with slope = HBM bandwidth and NO intercept; it must pass through (AI=1, performance = bandwidth). For H100 SXM (FP16 dense 989 TFLOPS, HBM3 3.35 TB/s) the ridge is performance = 3.35e12 x AI, i.e. it crosses the 989 TFLOPS peak at AI = 295 and passes through (1, 3.35e12). The drawn line instead intercepts the y-axis at ~1e12 at AI = 1 and reaches 1e15 at AI ~ 295; those two constraints cannot be satisfied by one straight line (the drawn line implies a bandwidth of ~1.6 TB/s and a crossover at ~600, or, if the drawn slope is 1 decade/decade, a bandwidth of 1 TB/s and a crossover at 1000). The red 'decode' circle at (1, ~1.2e12) is drawn directly on the black ridge line, while the in-figure annotation states 'markers = regime, not measured MFU (real kernels run below the roof)'. The decode marker should sit clearly BELOW the ridge (roofline at AI=1 is 3.35e12; decode at batch 1 achieves ~3.35e12 only in the idealized bandwidth-bound limit, and real kernels sit below it).
issue.root_cause: The ridge was drawn by eye against the axis limits rather than computed from the peak/bandwidth pair, so the intercept, the crossover label, and the marker placement were never reconciled.
issue.correction: Redraw the ridge from the actual numbers: bandwidth-limited segment through (1, 3.35e12) and (295, 9.89e14), with the compute-bound plateau at 9.89e14 (label it 989 TFLOPS, not 1e15). Place the decode marker at (1, ~1e12) clearly below the ridge, and the prefill marker at its derived AI and at a plausible sub-peak performance (e.g. 3-5e14). If the intent was to show decode sitting exactly on the bandwidth roofline, say so in the caption and remove the 'run below the roof' annotation.
issue.acceptance_test: The drawn ridge satisfies performance = 3.35e12 x AI for AI <= 295 and performance = 9.89e14 for AI >= 295; the '~295' label coincides with the drawn crossover; no marker lies on the ridge line unless the caption explicitly says it is on the roofline; the y-axis plateau is labelled 989 TFLOPS.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.2 — Prefill and decode on the roofline ridge
issue.issue: The figure states no hardware, precision, or peak/bandwidth basis, so the ridge label '~295' and the y-axis ceiling '1e15' are uninterpretable in isolation; the surrounding prose then treats the 1e15 axis top as 'the regime peak' for an H100 whose FP16 dense peak is 989 TFLOPS.
issue.evidence: Figure contains only 'roofline ridge ~295' and a y-axis labelled 'attainable performance (FLOPS)' with a 1e15 top tick. Prose item (3) on the same page: 'The regime peak (1.0x10^15 FLOPS) — so one H100 is insufficient under that analytical deadline model.' 989 TFLOPS = 9.89e14, not 1.0e15; the axis ceiling is a plotting choice, not a hardware peak, and the caption does not say so.
issue.root_cause: The figure was designed as a conceptual schematic but is read (and cited in the prose) as a quantitative H100 roofline.
issue.correction: Add a subtitle inside the plot: 'H100 SXM, FP16 dense: 989 TFLOPS peak, 3.35 TB/s HBM3 -> ridge at 295 FLOP/byte'. Label the plateau '989 TFLOPS (FP16 dense)' rather than leaving 1e15 as an unlabeled ceiling, and either drop the '1.0x10^15' phrasing in prose item (3) or state that 1e15 is the axis limit.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who has never seen the book can state, from the figure alone, which GPU and precision the ridge represents and why the crossover is at 295.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline
issue.issue: The green 'initialize' arrow terminates at the RIGHT end of the DECODE band, directly above the 'next token' box, instead of at the 'previous token' box at the LEFT end. As drawn, the first sampled token appears to initialize the next-token output rather than to become the decode loop's input.
issue.evidence: In the render the green path leaves the right edge of 'first token' (x~450, y~175), runs right to x~467, drops to y~340, and turns left with an arrowhead at x~452 — inside the DECODE band, immediately above the 'next token' box (x 415-460, y 365-385). issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline
issue.issue: The caption identifies a path by color ('The green initialize path'), which is meaningless in grayscale and in color-vision-deficient printing; and the book's color semantics are inconsistent across the three figures in this batch (green = 'read for attention' in Fig. 1.1, green = tokenizer/embedding in Fig. 1.2, green = 'initialize' in Fig. 2.1; orange = 'append K/V' in Fig. 1.1 but 'Token IDs' in Fig. 1.2).

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline
issue.issue: The PREFILL band shows a single 'token + position' box for a pass the caption calls 'the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt', inviting the reading that prefill processes one token at a time — the exact misconception the prefill/decode distinction exists to prevent.
issue.evidence: PREFILL band: 'prompt -> token + position -> transformer -> logits + sampling -> first token' (one box). DECODE band: 'previous token -> token + position -> transformer -> logits + sampling -> next token' (one box, correctly, since decode is one token per step). Caption: 'PREFILL (top) is the one-shot parallel pass over the whole prompt.' The two bands are visually identical in token granularity, so the parallelism of prefill is carried only by prose.
issue.root_cause: The bands were drawn with a shared template that does not encode the one distinguishing property of prefill.
issue.correction: Label the prefill box 'tokens + positions (all in parallel)' and the decode box 'token + position (one per step)', and/or draw the prefill box as a stack/fan of tokens with a 'parallel' annotation. Consider adding a small 'N tokens at once' vs '1 token per step' cue.
issue.acceptance_test: A reader who sees only the figure (no caption) can state that prefill processes all prompt tokens in one parallel pass while decode processes one token per step.

issue.figure: FIGURE 2.1 — The canonical end-to-end inference pipeline
issue.issue: Layout inconsistencies: the italic note 'conceptual per-step, per-layer cache I/O' sits inside the DECODE band against its top border; the band labels are placed inconsistently ('PREFILL' above its band, 'DECODE' inside its band); the 'read' and 'append' arrows are only ~0.35 in apart with their labels offset to opposite sides, which is tight for a figure whose whole point is the read/write distinction.
issue.evidence: Rendered positions: 'PREFILL' at x~90-140, y~125-135 (above the band frame); 'DECODE' at x~165-200, y~335-345 (inside the band frame); the italic note at x~355-460, y~330-345 (inside the band, touching its top rule); 'read' label left of a downward arrow at x~285 and 'append' label right of an upward arrow at x~310.
issue.root_cause: Bands were drawn and labelled iteratively without a final alignment pass.
issue.correction: Place both band labels in the same position relative to their frames (e.g. above-left of each frame), move the italic note into clear space below the DECODE band or into the caption, and separate the read/append arrows (e.g. route 'read' down the left of the cache box and 'append' up the right) so each label sits directly above its own arrow.
issue.acceptance_test: Both band labels occupy identical relative positions; no annotation touches a frame rule; each of 'read' and 'append' sits directly above the arrow it names.

issue.issue: The figure depicts each token's K/V being appended on the SAME step the token is sampled, contradicting the figure's own caption and the book's prose. This is the single most consequential semantic detail in the chapter (it is what makes the KV cache a cache rather than a recomputation), and the drawing gets it backwards.
issue.evidence: Caption: 'every token adds one K/V per layer per head — written when that token is next processed as an input, one step after it is sampled.' Drawing: token1 ('sampled from prefill'), token2 ('first decode output'), token3 ('second decode output') each have a direct arrow into the 'append K/V per layer-head' box, i.e. the sampled token's own K/V is appended at the step it is sampled. Prose on printed p.14 (PDF p.34) states the opposite explicitly: 'the sampled next token is the output of this step and the input of the following step, whose forward pass then computes and appends its K/V. A token's K/V therefore enters the cache on the step in which it is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled.'
issue.root_cause: The figure was drawn as a token-to-cache accumulation story rather than as a step-indexed story, so the one-step lag that the caption and prose emphasize is not encoded.
issue.correction: Re-index the figure by step: show 'step t: input token_{i-1} -> compute K/V -> append K/V for token_{i-1}' and 'step t+1: input token_i -> ...', with the sampled token_i shown as the OUTPUT of step t and the INPUT of step t+1. At minimum, add a one-step offset between the token column and the append box (e.g. a bracket labelled 'appended on the NEXT step') and change the token sub-labels to 'sampled at step t' / 'appended at step t+1'.
issue.acceptance_test: Tracing only the arrows, a reader concludes that a token's K/V is written on the step in which that token is the input, not on the step in which it is sampled; the figure and the printed p.14 prose agree without needing the caption to arbitrate.

issue.issue: An unlabeled connector runs from the top of the token column across the top of the figure and drops into the top of the 'append K/V per layer-head' box. Its origin and meaning are not stated anywhere, and it duplicates the side connector from the same token column into the same box, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a feedback path, a second input, or a stray artifact.

The token column boxes sit at x~95-165 with their tops at y~185, so the line appears to originate just above token1. Separately, each token box has a short horizontal arrow into the left edge of the orange box.
issue.root_cause: A connector was added (probably intended as the 'read for attention -> next token' feedback) but was left unlabelled and unanchored.
issue.correction: Either delete the top connector, or give it a definite meaning and label it. If it is meant to express the loop (cache read -> next token -> next step), route it from the 'read for attention' box back to the token column and label it 'next step's input', which would also make the one-step lag of FIG-1.1-A visible.
issue.acceptance_test: Every connector in the figure has a label or an unambiguous source and destination; no two connectors connect the same pair of elements with different implied meanings.

issue.issue: The 'read K' connector is routed around the outside right edge of the 'stored V — values' box with only ~0.07 in of clearance, and it enters the 'read for attention' box from the right while 'read V' enters from the top.
