If it is not, either redraw proportionally (with a minimum-width floor stated in the subtitle) or amend the subtitle to 'payload widths are proportional to bytes; scale segments are drawn at a minimum legible width'.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.7 — Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host (640 GB pool)
issue.issue: The displayed substitution line under the figure reads "≈ 436 GB + 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests". The operator between the two quantities is a plus sign, but the arithmetic requires division (436 ÷ 24.9 = 17.51). As printed, the equation is false: 436 + 24.9 = 460.9, not 17.5. It also contradicts the line immediately above it, which correctly states "in-flight = KV budget ÷ KV per request".
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145, display block between the bar and the caption: line 1 "in-flight = KV budget ÷ KV per request"; line 2 "≈ 436 GB + 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests". Caption confirms the intended operation: "at 24.9 GB/request max-FP16 KV, C = 17.5 concurrent (floor 17, not 18…)". 436 ÷ 24.9 = 17.51 ✓; 436 + 24.9 = 460.9 ✗. The same figure's caption also uses the correct division for the FP8 case (436 ÷ 12.45 ≈ 35).
issue.acceptance_test: Open the source for the FIGURE 7.7 display and confirm the operator glyph is '÷' (or ' / '), not '+'. If the source is correct, re-render at 300 dpi and confirm the glyph is a division sign on the page; if the source is wrong, change '+' to '÷' and re-check that the display still reads "≈ 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB = 17.5 → ~17 requests". Also confirm no downstream text quotes the '+' form.

issue.issue: The caption sentence is grammatically broken and logically ambiguous: "and that KV budget is the per-request KV price sets concurrency". The intended relation (budget ÷ per-request price = concurrency) is not stated; as written the sentence has no main verb and could be read as claiming the budget *is* the price.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145, caption line 2–3: "…host's 640 GB pool, and that KV budget is the per-request KV price sets concurrency — at 24.9 GB/request max-FP16 KV, C = 17.5 concurrent…". The figure's own display (line 1) states the correct relation, so the caption is the only place the relation is stated in words.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as: "…and that KV budget, divided by the per-request KV price, sets concurrency — at 24.9 GB/request max-FP16 KV, C = 17.5 concurrent (floor 17, not 18…)". Confirm the rewritten sentence names both operands and the operation.

issue.issue: The "~64 GB runtime" segment and the "~436 GB KV budget" segment are drawn with the same green fill and the same white label treatment; only the weights segment is distinguished by a blue diagonal hatch. In grayscale the three-way decomposition of the 640 GB pool reduces to one green block plus one hatched block, and the runtime/KV boundary is carried only by a hairline and by the text inside a very narrow box. The runtime label is also set noticeably smaller than the weights label and is squeezed into a ~0.2 in box, wrapping onto two lines.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145: blue hatched "140 GB weights" (label ~9 pt) vs green "~64 GB runtime" (label ~7.5 pt, two lines, box ~30 px wide at 150 dpi) vs green "~436 GB KV budget". No legend or pattern key is present on the page.
issue.acceptance_test: Give the runtime segment a distinct fill (e.g. a different hatch or a lighter tint) so the three components are separable in grayscale, and set the runtime label at the same size as the other two segment labels (or move it above the bar with a leader line). Confirm by rendering the page to grayscale and checking that all three segments remain distinguishable without reading the labels.

issue.issue: "640 GB pool" is set as a free-floating label at the far right of the title line, horizontally aligned with the right end of the bar, where it can be misread as a label for the rightmost (KV) band rather than for the whole pool. The figure also never states that bar width is proportional to GB, so a reader cannot tell whether the three segments are drawn to scale (140 : 64 : 436).
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145: title row reads "Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host" with "640 GB pool" set at the far right, directly above the green KV band. Caption says "host's 640 GB pool" (the pool, not the KV band).
issue.acceptance_test: Move "640 GB pool" immediately after the title text (or into the title itself: "Concurrency budget — one 8×H100 host, 640 GB pool"), and add a one-line note such as "bar width ∝ GB" to the figure or caption. Confirm the drawn segment widths are proportional to 140 : 64 : 436 within a few percent.

issue.issue: The caption makes a specific, load-bearing claim about a graphic feature — "the faint vertical rules inside the KV band are those 24.9 GB request slots" — but the rules are drawn at very low contrast. At print size (and in the 150 dpi render) they are barely perceptible, so the reader cannot count the slots or see the 17.5-slot fractional remainder that the caption's "floor 17, not 18" argument depends on.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 145: the green KV band contains faint vertical rules that are visible only on close inspection; the caption's claim about them is not independently checkable at reading size.
issue.acceptance_test: Increase the rule contrast (or add a small tick/label at the 17th slot) so that the slot count is legible at 100% print size, and confirm the number of rules equals 17 full slots plus a visibly partial 18th, consistent with 436/24.9 = 17.5.

issue.figure: FIGURE 7.8 — Memory Tetris (scale note vs. drawing)
issue.issue: The figure's own note says "Bar heights are not to scale (GB)", yet the drawing is (or appears to be) to scale: the light horizontal rules are spaced at 80 GB intervals across the 640 GB pool, and the three bar tops land at roughly 36% / 45% / 84% of the 640 GB dashed line, i.e. 229 / 288 / 539 GB. One of the two statements is false. If the note is true, then the "640 GB = 8× 80 GB ranks" dashed line and the "light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries" are meaningless decoration and the reader will misread the 128K bar as nearly filling the host. If the note is false, the note is a factual error in the figure.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 146: note under the bars reads "The baseline (weights + runtime) is fixed; only the KV cache grows with context. Bar heights are not to scale (GB)." Against that: the red dashed 640 GB line sits above all three bars; the light rules are evenly spaced at ~1/8 of the plot height (consistent with 80 GB × 8); bar tops are at ≈229/288/539 GB, which are exactly the values printed under the bars ("= 229 GB used", "= 288 GB used", "= 539 GB used").
issue.acceptance_test: Decide which is intended and make them agree: (a) if to scale, delete "Bar heights are not to scale (GB)" and replace with "Bar heights are to scale (GB); light rules are 80 GB capacity gridlines"; (b) if not to scale, remove the 640 GB dashed line and the 80 GB rules and add the fill fractions numerically ("229/640 = 36%", "288/640 = 45%", "539/640 = 84%"). Verify by measuring the rendered bar tops against the 640 GB line.

issue.issue: The rules are labelled "light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries", but they are drawn as horizontal lines across the plot. A rank boundary is a division between GPUs (8 GPUs side by side), which can only be represented by vertical partitions; horizontal lines at 80 GB intervals are capacity gridlines, not rank boundaries. The caption repeats the mislabel ("the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide").
issue.evidence: Rendered page 146: subtitle "(light rules = 80 GB rank boundaries)" above a set of horizontal light rules; caption: "…the 80 GB rank-boundary lines are a visualization guide; sharding, KV partitioning, interconnect must be validated per rank." No vertical partition of the 640 GB pool into 8 × 80 GB is drawn anywhere.
issue.acceptance_test: Rename the rules to "80 GB capacity gridlines" in both the figure subtitle and the caption, or draw eight vertical partitions labelled R0…R7 to show the actual rank boundaries. Confirm the caption's caveat about per-rank validation still reads correctly against whichever treatment is chosen.

issue.issue: The concurrency consequence is stated only for two of the three bars, and the 128K figure is loose: "only ~1–2 at 128K". 436 / 335 = 1.30, i.e. one concurrent request (floor), not "~1–2". The 32K case (436 / 84 = 5.19 → 5 concurrent) is omitted entirely, even though the figure draws that bar.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 146 caption: "…consuming the fixed ~436 GB KV budget (17.5 concurrent at 9.5K, floor 17; only ~1–2 at 128K)". Figure labels: KV 24.9 GB (9.5K), KV 84 GB (32K), KV 335 GB (128K). 436/24.9 = 17.5 ✓; 436/84 = 5.19; 436/335 = 1.30.
issue.acceptance_test: State all three: "17.5 → 17 concurrent at 9.5K; 5.2 → 5 at 32K; 1.3 → 1 at 128K", using the same floor discipline already applied at 9.5K. Consider printing the concurrency figure under each bar in the figure itself so the reader can read capacity directly off the chart.

issue.issue: Typo in a figure label: the L2 cache box reads "L2 cache / on-dile". The intended word is "on-die" (or "on-chip").
issue.evidence: Rendered page 152, fourth box in the left column: "L2 cache" with sub-label "on-dile". The adjacent shared-memory box correctly reads "on-chip · close".
issue.acceptance_test: Correct the source string to "on-die" (or "on-chip") and re-render; confirm the corrected glyph in the L2 box.

issue.issue: The figure encodes three semantic classes by color alone — blue for on-chip compute levels, orange for HBM, green for interconnect/remote — with no key, no pattern differentiation, and no shape differentiation. In grayscale the compute/memory/interconnect grouping is lost entirely, and the reader is left with the caption's prose to supply the classification. The caption's own claim that "the same physical resource (e.g. HBM) can appear at different logical positions depending on the access pattern" is not illustrated anywhere, so the caveat has no anchor in the drawing.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 152: seven stacked boxes, four blue, one orange, two green; no legend. Caption: "…the same physical resource (e.g. HBM) can appear at different logical positions depending on the access pattern. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]" — no second HBM box or annotation exists in the figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Add a compact key (e.g. three swatches: compute / memory / interconnect) and give each class a distinct fill pattern as well as a distinct hue, so the grouping survives grayscale. Either illustrate the HBM-reappears caveat (e.g. a small callout showing HBM accessed as a weight stream vs. a KV stream) or delete that clause from the caption.

issue.issue: The red vertical arrow carries the figure's central gradient message but is ambiguous in two ways: it has a single arrowhead at the top (pointing toward "small · fast · close") while the adjacent red text describes the downward direction ("capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows"), and it spans only the middle portion of the stack (roughly L2 down to "other GPUs / remote") rather than the full ladder from registers to remote GPUs.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 152: red arrow runs from about the L2 level down to the "other GPUs / remote" level with the arrowhead at the top; the red three-line text "capacity grows / speed drops / distance grows" sits mid-arrow; the top of the stack (registers, tensor cores, shared mem) lies outside the arrow's span.
issue.acceptance_test: Make the arrow double-headed or relabel it explicitly ("↑ faster / smaller / closer"), and extend it to span the full stack from the registers box to the "other GPUs / remote" box so the gradient visibly covers every level.

issue.issue: The ladder is presented as a "speed↔capacity↔distance" ranking, but the ordering of HBM above GPU interconnect is a latency/distance statement, not a bandwidth statement: HBM bandwidth (3.35 TB/s on H100) is roughly 7× NVLink bandwidth (~450 GB/s). A reader who takes the ladder as a bandwidth ordering will mispredict which resource binds first in TP.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 152 caption: "The gradient of speed↔capacity↔distance is why compute, memory bandwidth, memory capacity and interconnect bandwidth are distinct architectural constraints…" The figure places "GPU interconnect" below "HBM (GPU memory)" on a single monotone ladder.
issue.acceptance_test: Add one clause to the caption, e.g. "the ladder ranks latency and distance, not bandwidth — HBM bandwidth exceeds interconnect bandwidth on the same device", so the ordering cannot be misread as a bandwidth ranking.

issue.issue: The caption states "the peak roofline is 989 TFLOPS (H100) / 1,979 TFLOPS (H200)". This is wrong and it contradicts the figure it captions: the drawing shows both curves plateauing at a single annotated "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS", and the figure's own ridge labels (295 for H100, 206 for H200) are only consistent with a 989 TFLOPS peak for both devices. H200 is the same compute die as H100: FP16 dense = 989 TFLOPS (1,979 TFLOPS is the *sparsity* figure, and 1,979 is also H100/H200 FP8 dense). A reader who adopts the caption's 1,979 for H200 will compute an H200 ridge of 1,979/4.8 = 412 FLOP/byte instead of 206, and will misplace the compute-bound boundary.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159 caption: "Convention: a multiply-add counts as 2 FLOPs, so the peak roofline is 989 TFLOPS (H100) / 1,979 TFLOPS (H200)." Figure: one shared plateau annotated "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS"; ridge labels "ridge = 295" (H100) and "ridge = 206" (H200). Check: 989/3.35 = 295 ✓ and 989/4.8 = 206 ✓; 1,979/4.8 = 412 ✗ (matches no label in the figure).
issue.acceptance_test: Correct the caption to "the peak roofline is 989 TFLOPS dense FP16 for both H100 and H200 (1,979 TFLOPS is the sparsity figure, and the FP8 dense figure)", and confirm the figure's plateau annotation and both ridge labels remain consistent with 989 TFLOPS. Add a regression check that no H200 dense-FP16 peak of 1,979 appears anywhere in the book.

issue.issue: The caption contains a direct self-contradiction about the same operating point: "decode (batch=1) sits to the left, on the compute-bound side; decode (batch=1) sits to the left, on the memory-bound slope". Decode at batch=1 cannot be on both sides. The correct statement (per the facing page) is that decode at batch=1 sits at ≈1 FLOP/byte, far left, on the memory-bound slope, and that batching moves it rightward up that slope. Two further clauses are garbled: "the ridge point is the memory-bound slope (per-GPU)" (the ridge is where the memory-bound slope meets the compute-bound plateau) and "host-level attainable performance adds additional depends on scheduling and communication".
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159 caption, sentences 3–5: "…Prefill (9.2K input) sits to the right of the compute-bound ridge (batch=1) — it is not a measured latency; decode (batch=1) sits to the left, on the compute-bound side; decode (batch=1) sits to the left, on the memory-bound slope and continues batching climbs the slope as batch grows." Facing page (printed 140): "decode intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte at batch=1 and ≈ 32 FLOP/byte at batch=32".
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite the caption so each operating point is described exactly once and consistently: prefill (9.2K) right of the ridge; decode batch=1 left of the ridge on the memory-bound slope; decode batched climbing that slope toward the ridge. Replace "the ridge point is the memory-bound slope" with "the ridge point is where the memory-bound slope meets the compute-bound plateau", and fix "adds additional depends on" to "additionally depends on". Confirm no clause remains that places decode batch=1 on the compute-bound side.

issue.issue: The three vertical guides must span 1.65 decades on the log x-axis: H200 ridge 206 (just above 10²), H100 ridge 295 (mid-way between 10² and 10³), prefill 9.2K (immediately left of 10⁴). In the rendered page the orange prefill guide and the blue ridge guide appear separated by only a small fraction of a decade, and the orange guide appears to sit to the LEFT of the blue one — which would place the prefill operating point left of the ridge, the exact opposite of the caption's claim ("Prefill (9.2K input) sits to the right of the compute-bound ridge"). The separation between the decode ridge and the prefill operating point is the single most important thing this figure exists to show, so it cannot be left to a fraction of a decade.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159: x-axis ticks 10⁻¹…10⁴; the orange dotted guide descends from the "prefill 9.2K intensity = 9.2K FLOP/byte" label and the blue dotted guide is drawn close beside it, both in the region between the 10³ and 10⁴ ticks rather than at 10²·³, 10²·⁵ and 10³·⁹⁶. Expected x-positions (55 px/decade, 10⁻¹ at x≈127): 206 → x≈307; 295 → x≈316; 9,200 → x≈396.
issue.acceptance_test: Measure the three guide lines in the vector source and confirm they land at 206, 295 and 9,200 FLOP/byte on the log axis (i.e. 10²·³¹, 10²·⁴⁷, 10³·⁹⁶), with the orange prefill guide to the RIGHT of both ridge guides. If the guides are drawn at the wrong positions, reposition them and re-check that the caption's "prefill sits to the right of the ridge" is visually true. Escalate to P1 if the orange guide is confirmed left of the ridge guides.

issue.issue: The two leader arrows labelled "decode batch=1" and "decode batched" appear to converge on essentially the same point on the H100 curve. Per the book's own arithmetic these must be 1.5 decades apart on the x-axis: decode at batch=1 sits at ≈1 FLOP/byte (≈3.35 TFLOPS, i.e. just above 10⁰ on the y-axis) and decode at batch=32 sits at ≈32 FLOP/byte (≈107 TFLOPS, i.e. just above 10²). If both markers are drawn in the same place, the figure cannot show the effect the caption claims ("as batching continues, decode climbs the slope").
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159: the "decode batch=1" and "decode batched" leader lines both terminate in the region of a single blue marker near AI ≈ 10¹, performance ≈ 10¹·⁵. Facing page (printed 140): "decode intensity ≈ 1 FLOP/byte at batch=1 and ≈ 32 FLOP/byte at batch=32"; "the effective intensity is ≈ 32 FLOP/byte, still ≪ below the 295 ridge".
issue.acceptance_test: Confirm in the source that the batch=1 marker is placed at (1 FLOP/byte, 3.35 TFLOPS) and the batched marker at (32 FLOP/byte, 107 TFLOPS) on the H100 curve, with visibly separate leader lines and labels. Verify the batched marker lies left of the H100 ridge guide at 295.

issue.issue: The legend lists only the bandwidths ("H100 FP16 (3.35 TB/s)", "H200 FP16 (4.8 TB/s)") and the plateau is annotated once, outside the curve pair. Nothing in the figure states that both curves share the same 989 TFLOPS dense-FP16 compute ceiling — which is exactly the fact the caption gets wrong (see FIG-8.2-01) and exactly the fact a reader needs in order to understand why the H200 curve is steeper but reaches the same ceiling. A reader who assumes the H200 curve plateaus higher will misread the whole chart.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159: legend bottom-right lists only bandwidth; the annotation "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS" sits to the right of the plot area, detached from either curve, with no leader line to the shared plateau.
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the legend entries to "H100 FP16 (3.35 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS peak)" and "H200 FP16 (4.8 TB/s, 989 TFLOPS peak)", or add a leader line from the "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS" annotation to the point where both curves meet the plateau, so the shared ceiling is unambiguous.

issue.issue: The "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS" annotation and the legend box appear to sit at or beyond the right edge of the plotting frame rather than inside the axes, so the annotation floats in the margin with no visual tie to the curves it describes. The y-axis label also reads "Achievable performance (TFLOPS)", whereas the roofline's upper bound is a peak/ceiling, not an achieved value.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 159: the plot frame's right border runs down the page at roughly the 10⁴ tick, while the "compute plateau = 989 TFLOPS" text and the legend extend to the right of that border.
issue.acceptance_test: Move the plateau annotation inside the axes with a leader line to the plateau, keep the legend inside the frame, and relabel the y-axis "Peak achievable performance (TFLOPS) — per GPU" (or "Roofline ceiling (TFLOPS) — per GPU"). Confirm nothing overlaps the frame or the page margin at 100% print size.

issue.issue: The caption's frame-count identity is written incorrectly: "For aligned F = 4k+1, F = 1+4(T_j−1) = 31 latent time positions correspond to 121 frames." As written, 1 + 4(T_j−1) with T_j = 31 equals 121, not 31, and the symbol F (frames) is used for the latent-time-position count. The figure's own box states the correct identity ("Aligned endpoint: 1 × 4 × (31 − 1) = 121 frames"), so the caption contradicts the figure and states a false arithmetic equality.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 164 caption: "The fetched implementation uses T_j = (F−1)/4 + 1, H_j = H/16 and W_j = W/16. For aligned F = 4k+1, F = 1+4(T_j−1) = 31 latent time positions correspond to 121 frames." Figure box: "VAE stride (T, H, W) = (4, 16, 16) / Aligned endpoint: 1 × 4 × (31 − 1) = 121 frames". Check: T_j = (121−1)/4 + 1 = 31 ✓; F = 1 + 4(31−1) = 121 ✓; the caption's "= 31" is wrong.
issue.acceptance_test: Rewrite as: "For aligned F = 4k+1, T_j = (F−1)/4 + 1 = 31 latent time positions and F = 1 + 4(T_j−1) = 121 frames." Confirm the caption's two identities match the figure's "Aligned endpoint" box and that no symbol is used for two different quantities.

issue.issue: FIGURE 8.2 carries an in-figure evidence badge ("PER GPU | ANALYTICAL | DERIVED") while FIGURE 8.3 carries none, even though its caption mixes a [1P][FACT] geometry/loop claim with arithmetic derivations from that geometry. The reader cannot tell, from the figure alone, which parts of the drawn pipeline are first-party facts and which are derived arithmetic.

issue.acceptance_test: Add a badge to FIGURE 8.3 in the same house style, e.g. "[1P][FACT] geometry + [DERIVED] token/frame counts", and confirm the badge vocabulary matches the taxonomy used in Ch. 4 / Appendix A.

issue.issue: The figure's only key explains line style ("Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning.") but not fill/border color, which is the figure's other semantic channel: blue-bordered boxes carry data/state (inputs, latent, and the final output) while orange-bordered boxes carry computation (the denoiser+scheduler and the VAE decode). Because the final output box is styled identically to the input boxes, a reader scanning the figure cannot tell the result from the inputs without reading the text.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 164: "Prompt", "Optional reference image", "Initial noise (FP32)", "UMT5-XXL", "VAE encode", "Latent" and the output box "121 frames · 1280 × 704 · 24 fps" all share the same blue border; the two compute boxes share an orange border. The note under the figure mentions only solid/dashed.
issue.acceptance_test: Extend the note to "Solid: data/state flow. Dashed: denoiser conditioning. Blue: data/state. Orange: compute." and/or give the output box a distinct treatment (e.g. a filled or double border) so the result is visually distinct from the inputs. Confirm the scheme survives grayscale (border weight or fill, not hue alone).

issue.issue: The latent is labelled "T × H × W × C / 31 × 44 × 80 × 48" (H before W), but the output is labelled "121 frames · 1280 × 704", i.e. W before H (80×16 = 1280 = W, 44×16 = 704 = H). The two boxes use opposite dimension orders, so a reader checking the VAE stride against the output has to reverse the axes mentally.
issue.evidence: Rendered page 164: latent box "Latent: T × H × W × C / 31 × 44 × 80 × 48"; output box "121 frames · 1280 × 704 · 24 fps"; VAE decode box "VAE stride (T, H, W) = (4, 16, 16)". Check: H = 44×16 = 704, W = 80×16 = 1280 ✓.
issue.acceptance_test: Write the output as "121 frames · 704 (H) × 1280 (W) · 24 fps" (or state the order explicitly) so it matches the T×H×W convention used in the latent box and the caption's "31×44×80×48".

issue.issue: The text-encoder box reads "UMT5-XXL / s512 prompt tokens". The token "s512" is not defined anywhere on the page and is not a standard abbreviation; it is presumably "512 prompt tokens" (or "≤512"), but as printed it reads as a typo or an undefined symbol.

issue.figure: FIGURE 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue.issue: The HDR series is labelled with a bandwidth basis that contradicts the figure's own title and the ring model's byte count. The figure title promises 'directional bandwidth' and the ring model divides one-directional per-rank sent bytes (245 GB) by a bandwidth, but the legend entry reads 'Two-way HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s' and the caption repeats 'an assumed effective two-way HDR path'. 'Two-way' in interconnect usage means bidirectional aggregate. If it is read that way, the denominator is a bidirectional figure applied to a unidirectional byte count and the HDR ring time is understated by 2x (245 GB / 20 GB/s per direction = 12.25 s, not 6.125 s). The book's own definition on printed 157 is different again: 'a realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node)'. So the number is right but the label names the wrong quantity, and the caption reinforces the wrong term.
issue.evidence: Figure legend: 'Two-way HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s'; figure header: 'HDR 6,125 ms'; caption: '40 GB/s for an assumed effective two-way HDR path'. Title: 'Ring traffic and directional bandwidth'. Printed 157: 'A realistic effective throughput is roughly 40 GB/s (aggregated across 2 HDR rails/ports per node — the multi-rail effective throughput referenced in §9.2 and Fig 9.1)'. Printed 157 also states HDR payload is '25 GB/s in both link coding', i.e. 25 GB/s per direction, 50 GB/s bidirectional, so 40 GB/s 'two-way' would be 20 GB/s per direction.
issue.acceptance_test: The legend entry, the figure header, and the caption all state the same basis in words that cannot be read two ways, e.g. 'HDR, 2 rails, per-direction effective 40 GB/s'. A reader who computes 245 GB / 40 GB/s = 6.1 s from the figure alone reproduces the printed 6,125 ms, and a reader who reads the label as bidirectional can no longer derive 12.25 s from it. The figure title's word 'directional' is then true of all three series.

issue.figure: FIGURE 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue.issue: The three curves are not like-for-like: one is a hardware peak and two are assumed effective (attainable) throughputs, and the figure does not say so. The legend distinguishes them by wording only ('directional peak 450 GB/s' vs 'assumed effective 40 GB/s' / 'assumed effective 2.5 GB/s'), so the NVLink curve is systematically optimistic relative to the other two by roughly the same margin that the others are pessimistic. The caption's blanket 'No curve is measured performance' does not disclose that the three curves sit at different points between peak and sustained.
issue.evidence: Legend: 'H100 NVLink: directional peak 450 GB/s' / 'Two-way HDR: assumed effective 40 GB/s' / '25GbE RoCE: assumed effective 2.5 GB/s'. Caption: 'Curves use 450 GB/s for H100 NVLink (one direction of the 900 GB/s bidirectional peak), 40 GB/s for an assumed effective two-way HDR path, and 2.5 GB/s for an assumed effective 25GbE RoCE path.' Figure annotation: 'Analytical model; no offload, latency or overlap; not measured'.
issue.acceptance_test: Either (a) all three series are stated on the same basis (e.g. all 'assumed effective per-direction', with the NVLink effective value derived from the same efficiency assumption used for HDR and RoCE), or (b) the figure carries an explicit note that the NVLink curve is a peak and therefore an upper bound while the other two are effective-throughput estimates, so the vertical gaps between curves are not a like-for-like comparison. The caption must state which basis each curve uses.

issue.figure: Pull-quote callout (unnumbered), lower third of page
issue.issue: The pull-quote's own numbers contradict the linear law it states. It claims '2·70B · L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 1K → ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K'. Under 2·70B·L, L=1,000 gives 1.4e14 FLOP = 0.14 PFLOP, not 0.28; and 0.28 PFLOP scaled linearly to 32K would be 8.96 PFLOP, not 4.5. The 32K value (4.59 PFLOP) and the canonical 9.2K value (1.29 PFLOP) are both correct under 2·70B·L, so the '1K' figure is the sole outlier and is 2x too high. A reader who trusts the callout will mis-estimate prefill cost at short context by a factor of two.
issue.evidence: Pull-quote: 'Prefill FLOP also grows with context: 2·70B · L tokens scales linearly — ~0.28 PFLOP at 1K → ~4.5 PFLOP at 32K for a 70B model ... the canonical 9.2K point the prefill is ~1.29 PFLOP (Table 8-1).' Recomputation: 2 x 70e9 x 1000 = 1.4e14 FLOP = 0.14 PFLOP; 2 x 70e9 x 32768 = 4.59e15 = 4.59 PFLOP; 2 x 70e9 x 9200 = 1.288e15 = 1.29 PFLOP (matches the printed 1.29). Ratio check: 4.5 / 0.28 = 16.1, but 32K / 1K = 32.
issue.acceptance_test: The callout's 1K value equals 2 x 70e9 x 1000 / 1e15 = 0.14 PFLOP, and the printed pair (0.14 PFLOP at 1K, 4.5 PFLOP at 32K) satisfies the stated 32x linear ratio. The 9.2K value remains 1.29 PFLOP and agrees with Table 8-1.

issue.issue: A link-rate unit slip: 'HDR InfiniBand delivers 200 GB/s per link (25 GB/s in both link coding; NDR doubles this to 400 GB/s)'. The parenthetical gives the correct payload figure (25 GB/s per direction after line coding), which corresponds to a 200 Gb/s raw link, not 200 GB/s. As printed, the sentence asserts a 200 GB/s link and then, in the same breath, a 25 GB/s payload — an 8x internal contradiction that a reader sizing links or NICs will trip over. The same slip repeats for NDR ('400 GB/s' for a 400 Gb/s link).
issue.evidence: Printed 177: 'HDR InfiniBand delivers 200 GB/s per link (25 GB/s in both link coding; NDR doubles this to 400 GB/s).' 200 Gb/s x 64/66 = 193.9 Gb/s = 24.2 GB/s per direction, i.e. ~25 GB/s payload; bidirectional = ~50 GB/s. NDR 400 Gb/s -> ~50 GB/s per direction.
issue.acceptance_test: The sentence reads 'HDR InfiniBand delivers 200 Gb/s per link (~25 GB/s per direction after line coding; NDR doubles this to 400 Gb/s, ~50 GB/s per direction)', and the per-direction and bidirectional figures are both stated so that the 40 GB/s multi-rail effective figure used in Fig 9.1 and in the worked example can be derived from it without ambiguity.

issue.figure: FIGURE 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue.issue: The header annotation '140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75x)' does not say whether 140 GB is per rank or the whole ring, while the x-axis label ('Logical input tensor per rank (GB)') and the caption ('At 140 GB the ideal times are about 0.54 s, 6.1 s and 98 s') do. A reader scanning the header alone can read '140 GB tensor' as the total across eight ranks, in which case the sent bytes would be 1.75 x 140/8 = 30.6 GB and every printed time would be off by 8x.
issue.evidence: Figure header: '140 GB tensor (245 GB sent at 1.75x); NVLink 544 ms | HDR 6,125 ms | RoCE 98,000 ms'. X-axis: 'Logical input tensor per rank (GB)'. Caption: 'Each rank sends 1.75 times the logical tensor size and receives the same amount.' 245 = 1.75 x 140 confirms the per-rank reading.
issue.acceptance_test: The header reads '140 GB per rank (245 GB sent per rank at 1.75x)', matching the x-axis label and the caption, so that the header, axis, and caption cannot be read on different denominators.

issue.figure: FIGURE 9.1 — Ring traffic and directional bandwidth
issue.issue: The endpoint markers sit on the plot frame and are visually clipped: the RoCE series ends at 98,000 ms against a top tick of 100,000 ms (log10 4.991, i.e. effectively on the top spine), and all three series end exactly at the rightmost x tick (140 GB), so the final markers touch the right spine. issue.figure: FIGURE 11.3 (P/D disaggregation: two cases, two different KV links)
issue.issue: The caption's KV-transfer time contradicts the figure's own numbers by a factor of ~10. Caption: 'it moves the per-request KV state (~35 GB, 0.8 s) across the joining link'. issue.issue: The discrete panel contradicts its own annotation: all four rows show an identical blue 'sequence in flight' block of the same width, so no sequence finishes before the others, yet the note states 'GPU slots idle (pink) when a sequence finishes early'. The pink region therefore has no depicted cause and the reader cannot see the phenomenon the figure exists to illustrate.

Figure note: 'GPU slots idle (pink) when a sequence finishes early'. Caption: 'a batch is locked until its slowest member finishes, so short outputs idle in the ... slots'.

issue.issue: Sequence-vs-slot conflation. The caption says 'each row is one sequence (slot) evolving over time', the legend calls pink an 'idle slot (bubble)', and the note says 'GPU slots idle (pink)'. If rows are sequences, the pink is per-sequence dead time, not slot occupancy; the bubble in discrete batching is a slot-level (column) property — the slot is occupied by the batch but under-filled. A reader can plausibly conclude the wrong thing about what is wasted.
issue.evidence: Rendered p.200: legend 'idle slot (bubble)'; caption 'each row is one sequence (slot) evolving over time'; note 'GPU slots idle (pink) when a sequence finishes early'. The horizontal axis is labelled 'time (decode steps / iterations)', so rows cannot simultaneously be slots.
issue.acceptance_test: State the semantics unambiguously in one sentence, e.g. 'rows are sequences; pink marks slot time during which this sequence has already finished but the batch has not', and change the legend entry to 'slot time with this sequence finished (bubble)'. Alternatively redraw the bubble as a column-wise gap so slot occupancy is visible.

issue.figure: n/a — prose page (no figure on this page); reviewed because it supplies the arithmetic that Figure 15.1 (PDF 248) rests on
issue.issue: The attention-FLOP substitution is arithmetically false by two orders of magnitude, and the error inverts the book's own conclusion about which term dominates prefill. The text states: "the per-layer cost is ~ 4 · L² · d_model, where d_model = 8,192. That is 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.2 × 10¹⁶ FLOPs — the quadratic attention term that grows dominant at long context." The left-hand side of that substitution evaluates to 4 × 84,640,000 × 8,192 = 2.77 × 10¹² FLOPs per layer, not 2.2 × 10¹⁶. Multiplying by the 80 layers named in the preceding clause ("Across 80 layers that is ...") gives 2.22 × 10¹⁴ FLOPs — i.e. the printed exponent should be 10¹⁴, not 10¹⁶. The printed 2.2 × 10¹⁶ is exactly what one obtains with L = 92,000 rather than 9,200, which suggests a dropped factor of ten in L.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 4 × 9,200² × 8,192 = 2.773e12 (per layer); × 80 layers = 2.218e14. Cross-check against the book's own dense-matmul estimate on the same page: 2P/token with P = 70e9 gives 1.4e11 FLOP/token; over the canonical 9,200-token prompt that is 1.29e15 FLOP. So at the canonical context, attention (2.2e14, or 1.1e14 if the causal half is taken) is roughly 8–17% of the prefill cost, NOT the dominant term. The printed 2.2e16 would make attention ~17× the dense-matmul term and would be the only thing that makes the clause "grows dominant at long context" true at 9,200 tokens. The error therefore propagates into the reader's mental model of the prefill/decode cost split and into the roofline reasoning that Figure 15.1 illustrates.
issue.acceptance_test: The printed substitution must evaluate to the printed result. Correct to "4 × 9,200² × 8,192 ≈ 2.8 × 10¹² FLOPs per layer; across 80 layers ≈ 2.2 × 10¹⁴ FLOPs", and the sentence must then say that attention is a minority term at the canonical 9,200-token context and becomes dominant only at substantially longer contexts (state the crossover, e.g. the L at which 4·L²·d·80 exceeds 1.4e11·L). Separately, state explicitly whether the 4·L²·d convention is causal or dense: causal attention is 2·L²·d per layer, so the factor of two must be declared and used consistently wherever attention FLOPs are compared with the 2P/token dense term.

issue.issue: The verdict cell prints a numerically false relation and the wrong required throughput: "conditional final — ✗ throughput at a single prefill host (~19.8K ≈ 9.2K); prefill pool must itself scale to ~5 hosts (92K × 19.8K ≈ 4.65), plus a decode pool: 2× capes plus fabric." As printed, "19.8K ≈ 9.2K" asserts that two numbers differing by a factor of 2.15 are approximately equal, and it names 9.2K as the relevant requirement — while the very next clause in the same cell uses 92K as the requirement. The intended statement is almost certainly "~19.8K ≪ 92K" (a single prefill host delivers 19.8K tok/s against a 92K tok/s requirement).
issue.evidence: Internal inconsistency within one cell: the requirement appears as 9.2K in the first clause and 92K in the second. The second clause's own arithmetic (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → ~5 hosts) confirms 92K as the requirement. A reader who takes the printed '≈' at face value cannot reconstruct the ~5-host conclusion, and a reader who takes 9.2K as the requirement would conclude a single prefill host already exceeds it by 2×, which contradicts the '✗' verdict in the same cell.
issue.acceptance_test: The cell must read, verbatim in substance: "✗ throughput at a single prefill host (~19.8K ≪ 92K required); prefill pool must scale to ~5 hosts (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65), plus a decode pool: ...". The requirement figure (92K) must appear exactly once and identically in both clauses, and the relation operator must be the one the author intends (≪, not ≈).

issue.issue: The host-count derivation uses multiplication where division is required: "(92K × 19.8K ≈ 4.65)". 92,000 × 19,800 = 1.82 × 10⁹, which is not 4.65; the intended operation is 92K ÷ 19.8K = 4.65 hosts.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 92,000 / 19,800 = 4.646 → ~5 hosts, matching the stated conclusion. The printed operator makes the expression self-evidently wrong to any reader, and it is the only derivation in the cell that justifies the host count.
issue.acceptance_test: Replace '×' with '÷' and add the unit to the result: "92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 hosts". A reader must be able to reproduce 4.65 from the two printed operands with the printed operator.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (a) 'Caching removes prefill work' — y-axis
issue.issue: The y-axis is labelled "Prefill FLOPs / req (GFLOP)" with the no-cache series drawn flat at 100, but the caption describes the same quantity as "a percent of no-cache prefill work". The axis unit and the caption unit are different quantities, and the absolute reading (100 GFLOP per request of prefill) contradicts the book's own canonical arithmetic by roughly five orders of magnitude.
issue.evidence: The book's canonical prefill cost at 70B and 9,200 prompt tokens is 2P/token × 9,200 = 1.4e11 × 9,200 = 1.29e15 FLOP ≈ 1.3 × 10⁶ GFLOP per request — not 100 GFLOP. The same page's prose (printed 227) uses 10¹⁴–10¹⁶ FLOP magnitudes for prefill. A reader who trusts the axis label will believe prefill costs ~100 GFLOP/request and will mis-scale every roofline or capacity calculation built on it; a reader who trusts the caption will read the axis as a percentage. The figure cannot be both.
issue.acceptance_test: Choose one unit and make axis, caption, and any prose agree. Preferred: relabel the y-axis "Prefill FLOPs per request (% of no-cache)" with the no-cache series at 100, and state the absolute no-cache value in the caption (e.g. 'no-cache prefill ≈ 1.3 × 10¹⁵ FLOP at the canonical 70B/9,200-token prompt'). If the absolute GFLOP axis is retained instead, the plotted values must be rescaled to the canonical absolute figures and the caption must drop the 'percent' wording.

issue.figure: FIGURE 12.1 'Candidate architecture synthesis', stage 4 OUTCOME box
issue.issue: The outcome box asserts "CLEARS CAPACITY GATE (a)·(b)" with no qualification, which contradicts Table 12-2 on the facing page: row (b) P/D-disaggregated is judged "conditional final — ✗ throughput at a single prefill host", i.e. the 2 × 8×H100 baseline does NOT clear the capacity gate until the prefill pool is scaled to ~5 hosts. The figure also omits the decode pool that the same table requires for (b), and it omits the open validation gates for (a) and (b) that the caption itself asserts ("each with its own open validation gate (not a settled verdict)"). Only (c) is drawn as gated, so the visual grammar of the figure says 'a and b are approved, c is not'.
issue.evidence: Table 12-2 (printed 202) row (b): verdict 'conditional final — ✗ throughput at a single prefill host (~19.8K ≪ 92K); prefill pool must itself scale to ~5 hosts ... plus a decode pool'. Figure 12.1 (printed 203) stage 4: 'CLEARS CAPACITY GATE (a)·(b) / each needs ~5 hosts of prefill capacity'. The caption's own hedge ('each with its own open validation gate (not a settled verdict)') is contradicted by the figure's green, unqualified outcome box. A reader who reads only the figure will conclude that the 2-pool baseline is capacity-feasible as drawn.
issue.acceptance_test: The OUTCOME box must carry the condition, e.g. 'CLEARS CAPACITY GATE ONLY AFTER SCALING (a)·(b): (b) needs ~5 prefill hosts + a decode pool', and must show that (a) and (b) still carry an open throughput-validation gate (e.g. a small 'throughput gate open' tag), so that the figure's visual state matches the caption's 'not a settled verdict'. The figure must not imply the 2 × 8×H100 baseline passes as drawn.

issue.issue: The drawn 'with prefix cache' curve is concave-decreasing (roughly 100 → 96 → 92 → 88 → 83 → 76 → 65 at reuse 1, 2, 3, 5.6, 10.6, 30, 100), i.e. the saving per decade of reuse grows with reuse. That is the opposite of the amortization law the caption describes. If a prefix of P tokens is shared by r requests and each request also carries an uncached suffix S, per-request prefill falls from (S + P) to (S + P/r), so the ratio f(r) = (S + P/r)/(S + P) is convex-decreasing: the largest saving occurs between r = 1 and r = 10 and the curve then flattens toward S/(S + P).
issue.evidence: Fitting the drawn curve to f(r) is impossible for any S/P: the drawn curve drops 15 points over r = 1→10 but a further 18 points over r = 10→100, whereas f(r) drops monotonically less per decade. For example, with S = 1.475P (which fits the drawn endpoint of 65 at r = 100), f(10) = 64 — the drawn value at r ≈ 10 is ≈ 83. The figure therefore teaches 'prefix caching's per-request saving accelerates with reuse', which is a false model of the mechanism and would mislead a reader sizing prefill headroom.
issue.acceptance_test: Re-plot panel (a) from the stated model: choose and print a prefix/suffix split (e.g. P = 40% of the prompt), plot f(r) = (S + P/r)/(S + P) on the log-r axis, and label the curve with that formula or its parameters. The curve must be monotone and convex-decreasing, with the r = 1 point equal to the no-cache series. If a synthetic curve is retained for illustration, it must still satisfy the amortization shape.

issue.figure: FIGURE 13.1 'The reference-architecture escalation ladder' — de-escalation arrow
issue.issue: The caption twice assigns the de-escalation arrow the colour green ("de-escalation (green) fires on privacy, data sovereignty, and cost"; "de-escalation (green: data sovereignty, cost) moving a workload between tiers"), but the figure draws the de-escalation arrow as a BLUE dashed arrow. In the same figure, green is used for the tier boxes and for the '▼ constraints → STOP' labels, so the caption's colour key is wrong in both directions. If the intended trigger is latency, the caption must say latency; if privacy, the arrow label must say privacy. The caption's colour key must be checked against the rendered figure for every colour it names.

issue.figure: FIGURE 13.1 — placement of the three red escalation-trigger labels
issue.issue: Each red trigger label is drawn in the vertical gap immediately BELOW its own tier box, adjacent to that box's connector into the red escalation arrow: 'demand > ceiling → forces scale-up' sits below the Cluster/fleet box, 'goodput < demand → forces scale-up' below Multi-host, and 'KV residency > cap → forces scale-up' below Single host. Read that way, the Cluster/fleet tier is told to escalate because 'demand > ceiling', which has no destination — the ladder is already at the top. The caption's semantics are the opposite: "Escalation (red) fires when demand, KV residency, or goodput outcomes exceed a tier", i.e. the trigger fires AT a tier and pushes the workload to the next tier up. Under that reading 'demand > ceiling' belongs to the Multi-host tier, not to Cluster/fleet.
issue.evidence: Rendered geometry: label baselines sit below the corresponding box centres and above the next box's top edge, so the nearest antecedent for each label is the box above it. The caption's wording ('exceed a tier') supports the other reading. The figure is therefore readable in two ways, and one of them is incoherent.
issue.acceptance_test: Place each trigger label immediately below the tier at which it fires and add an explicit upward arrow to the next tier (e.g. 'Single host: KV residency > cap → escalate to Multi-host'), or relabel the labels as arrival reasons ('why we moved here'). A reader must be able to state, for each tier, which trigger fires there and which tier it leads to, without consulting the caption.

issue.figure: FIGURE 13.1 — the four green '▼ constraints → STOP' labels
issue.issue: Every tier carries a green '▼ constraints → STOP' annotation that the caption never explains. The caption discusses escalation triggers and de-escalation criteria but says nothing about a per-tier stop condition, so the reader is left to guess whether 'constraints → STOP' means 'this tier's constraints are binding, stop here', 'this tier cannot be scaled further', or 'stop escalating at this tier'. The annotation is also the only green element besides the tier boxes, which is what makes the caption's 'de-escalation (green)' mis-key so damaging.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: four identical green '▼ constraints → STOP' lines, one under each tier box; the caption's two paragraphs mention only escalation triggers, de-escalation criteria, and the measurable-threshold example. No text in the caption or the figure defines the STOP annotation.
issue.acceptance_test: Either define the STOP annotation in the caption in one sentence (state what constraint stops escalation at that tier and give one example, e.g. 'Single GPU: KV residency > cap → STOP, escalate to Single host'), or remove it. It must not remain an unexplained visual element, and its colour must not collide with the de-escalation colour key.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.1 'FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic', AFTER panel
issue.issue: The AFTER panel draws exactly two arrows between the on-chip box and the HBM box (one up, one down), which reads as 'read K/V once, write once' — i.e. a single global K/V pass. The caption explicitly disclaims that reading: "the tile-level on-chip reuse is per-tile: it is not a guarantee that every K/V element is read exactly once globally across all query blocks (the exact number of K/V re-reads depends on the tile scheduling, sequence length, and SRAM size)". The in-panel note ('KV reused per tile — no single global K/V pass') mitigates but does not resolve the conflict, because the drawn arrow count is the strongest visual signal and it encodes exactly the claim the caption retracts.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: BEFORE panel shows a fan of ~7 red arrows; AFTER panel shows 2 green arrows. The caption's scope note is the only textual guard against reading the 2 arrows as 'one global read'. A reader scanning the figure will take the arrow count as the traffic story.
issue.acceptance_test: Label the AFTER arrows with what they represent (e.g. 'read K/V block per tile' and 'write O only') and add an in-panel note that the number of K/V re-reads equals the number of query tiles, or replace the arrow count with a per-tile loop glyph so the figure cannot be read as a single global pass. The figure must not, by arrow count alone, assert a global single-read.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.2, panel (b) title 'Decode bottleneck unaffected by caching'
issue.issue: The panel title asserts a claim the panel does not show. Panel (b) plots 'Relative decode goodput (a.u.)' against 'Decode batch size' with a single blue curve; there is no caching axis, no cached/uncached pair, and no reference to prefix caching anywhere in the panel. The title is therefore an assertion about the absence of an effect that the data cannot demonstrate. The caption's own framing ('They are not competing on the same axis') is the defensible statement; the panel title is not.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: panel (b) contains one series, one x-axis (decode batch size), one y-axis (relative decode goodput), one red dashed marker at batch ≈ 10, and a red annotation. Nothing in the panel encodes caching, so the title's claim is untested by the figure.
issue.acceptance_test: Retitle panel (b) to what the axes show, e.g. 'Decode goodput scales with batch size (caching-independent axis)', and move the 'unaffected by caching' statement into the caption where it can be argued rather than asserted. If the claim is to be shown, the panel must include a cached and an uncached series.

issue.figure: FIGURE 11.4 'Device visibility is not a validated serving path'
issue.issue: The dashed arrows that carry the three paths to the red qualification gate are drawn from the HARDWARE boxes only, not from the complete column. The figure's own subtitle says 'Dashed: qualify the complete path' and the caption says 'dashed arrows bring the complete path to the qualification gate', but the geometry shows three dashed connectors rising from the Hardware row into the gate. A reader who reads the diagram literally concludes that hardware visibility is what is qualified — the exact inverse of the figure's thesis, and the exact misconception the gate box's last line ('A visible device or a loaded model does not pass this gate') exists to prevent.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: within each column, solid arrows run Serving stack → Backend entry → Kernels/runtime → Hardware; the only dashed segments are the three short connectors from the Hardware boxes down to the red gate box. The gate box text lists weights + KV + workspace, operators + attention/cache path, correctness + isolation, collectives, measured SLO — none of which is a hardware-only property.
issue.acceptance_test: Draw the dashed connector from the whole column (e.g. a bracket or a dashed outline enclosing the four boxes per column) into the gate, or replace the three dashed arrows with a single dashed arrow from a 'complete path' node. The drawn geometry must not permit the inference that the hardware row alone is qualified.

issue.issue: The cell prints "−576 GB at the full KV budget (140 + 436)". A negative memory footprint is not meaningful, and the parenthetical arithmetic gives +576 GB (140 + 436 = 576). The leading glyph is either a mistyped minus sign or a mangled approximation sign; as rendered it asserts a negative quantity.
issue.evidence: Recomputed: 140 + 436 = 576 GB. The same row's other cell prints '164 GB single-request (140 + 24)', which is correct and shows the intended '+' convention. The reader cannot tell whether the sign is a typo or a deliberate delta (e.g. '−576 GB' as a reduction), and in the latter case the units and baseline are unstated.
issue.acceptance_test: Print '576 GB at the full KV budget (140 + 436)' (or '≈576 GB'), matching the '+' convention used in the adjacent cell. If a delta was intended, state the baseline explicitly ('+436 GB KV over the 140 GB weights').

issue.issue: The two host-count figures are quoted on different operating points without saying so. Row (b) says the prefill pool 'must itself scale to ~5 hosts' (which is the peak requirement, since 92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 is derived from the peak load), while row (c) says '~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate'. The reader is invited to compare '~5' with '~4' as if they were the same quantity; they are not (peak vs average), and the table's own note that host counts are 'an illustrative capacity screen from the fixed per-host prefill rates' does not resolve it.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: row (b) verdict '...prefill pool must itself scale to ~5 hosts (92K × 19.8K ≈ 4.65)...'; row (c) verdict '...~4 avg / ~15 peak hosts at the single-H100 rate (Table 12-2)'. The 4.65 derivation uses the 92K peak figure, so '~5' is a peak number; row (c) explicitly labels its two numbers as avg and peak.
issue.acceptance_test: Label the operating point on every host count in the table (e.g. '~5 hosts at peak'), and use the same avg/peak pairing for rows (a) and (b) so the three candidates are comparable on one basis. A reader must be able to compare (a), (b), and (c) host counts without guessing which basis each uses.

issue.figure: FIGURE 14.1 'Select models: screen on capability, then benchmark on the workload'
issue.issue: The figure's reading order does not match the process it depicts. The top row is laid out left-to-right as 'Candidate models → Survivors → Selection', and the bottom row as 'Capability MMLU/GSM8K → Deploy bench (prodput) → TCO + SLO gate → deployed', with the actual process encoded as vertical green arrows ('screen', 'benchmark', 'gate'). The true sequence is therefore down-right-down-right-right, but the eye enters at the top-left and naturally reads the top row straight across, which yields the wrong order (Candidate models → Survivors → Selection as a linear pipeline). The caption's own summary is a clean two-stage sequence ('capability screen → deployment benchmark'), which the layout does not reproduce.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: three blue boxes in a top row with black horizontal arrows, three orange boxes in a bottom row with black horizontal arrows, and green vertical arrows labelled screen / benchmark / gate. The 'deployed' node hangs off the bottom-right box, so the diagram's terminal state is in the bottom row while the top row ends at 'Selection' — the reader must reconstruct the serpentine path.
issue.acceptance_test: Re-lay the figure as a single left-to-right flow (Candidate models → Capability screen → Survivors → Deployment benchmark → Selection → TCO + SLO gate → deployed), or number the stages 1–5 in the order they execute. The figure must be readable in one pass without the reader having to infer the serpentine order.

issue.issue: The headline claims 'far less HBM traffic' (a byte quantity) while the figure's own bottom line and the caption both claim 'fewer HBM round-trips' (a count). The book is explicit elsewhere that these are different units — the facing page warns 'be precise about the units: one often sees a FlashAttention-class kernel reported at a different achieved HBM bandwidth ... That is a rate, not a byte count.' The headline therefore uses the weaker claim's units for the stronger claim's benefit.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: headline 'FlashAttention: the same math, far less HBM traffic'; in-panel green line 'the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not cheaper attention'; caption 'the gain is fewer HBM round-trips, not a change to the attention mathematics'.
issue.acceptance_test: Change the headline to 'far fewer HBM round-trips' (or state the traffic reduction explicitly, e.g. 'O(L²) → O(L) HBM traffic for the intermediate'), so that the headline, the in-panel line, and the caption use one unit.

issue.figure: FIGURE 15.1, BEFORE panel, HBM box label
issue.issue: Both panels label the HBM box 'Q/K/V', but the BEFORE panel's defining feature — the materialized O(L²) intermediate attention matrix written to and re-read from HBM — is not drawn or labelled in the box; it appears only in the small note below the panel. The visual therefore shows the naive path as 'Q/K/V in HBM, many round-trips' without the artifact that actually causes the traffic, which weakens the before/after contrast the figure exists to make.
issue.evidence: Rendered page: BEFORE panel HBM box reads 'Q/K/V'; the note below reads 'O(L²) HBM traffic: L×L intermediate written + every query re-reads the KV rows'. The AFTER panel's HBM box also reads 'Q/K/V'.

issue.issue: The figure's headline object — the frozen self-host line at $155,816.93/mo — is not visibly drawn in the plot area, and the legend's single pink swatch is keyed to two different encodings ('price band $15–25/K' and 'self-host $155,816.93/mo (21 hosts)'). issue.issue: The price unit 'K' is never disambiguated anywhere in the figure: legend 'managed $20.80/K' and 'price band $15–25/K'; note 'a $15–25/1K price band'; y-axis 'Cost/month (USD, log)' against x-axis 'Requests/month (log)'. The book's own arithmetic requires $0.0208 per request, i.e. $20.80 per 1,000 REQUESTS: 155,816.93 / 0.0208 = 7,491,198.56 req/mo, and 6.24M × 0.0208 = $129,792/mo. Under the universal API-pricing reading ($/1K tokens) with the book's canonical 9,200-token request, managed cost per request would be 9.2 × $20.80 = $191.36 and the break-even would be 155,816.93 / 191.36 = 814 req/mo — a factor of ~9,200 away from the plotted 7.5M. A reader who reads '$/K' as '$/1K tokens' will invert the chapter's conclusion. (Escalates to P0 if Ch 16 does not define the unit explicitly elsewhere.)

issue.acceptance_test: Label the price unit explicitly in the legend and note (e.g. 'managed $20.80 per 1,000 requests'), and add one line to the note giving the per-request price ($0.0208) and the tokens-per-request assumption behind it. issue.page: PDF 278 / printed 258 (figure note) vs PDF 274 / printed 254 (prose)
issue.issue: The figure's note states 'Feasible max = 40 rps × 624,000 active s/mo = 24.96M req/mo' (40 × 624,000 = 24,960,000 — correct), but the prose on printed p. 254 states 'the canonical active window of 62,000 active seconds/month (6.24M requests = 10 rps × 8 h), so the most it can serve is 40 rps × 62,000 s = 2,480,000 active s/month = 24.96M requests/month'. 40 × 62,000 = 2,480,000 REQUESTS, not 'active s/month'; 2,480,000 × 10 rps = 24.8M, not 24.96M; and 10 rps × 8 h = 288,000 s = 2.88M requests, not 6.24M. The figure's note is the arithmetically correct form, so the prose must be corrected to match it — but as printed, the figure and the prose that explains it disagree on the single number that sets the plot's right edge.

issue.acceptance_test: Correct printed p. 254 to '624,000 active seconds/month' and '40 rps × 624,000 s = 24.96M requests/month', and either drop '(6.24M requests = 10 rps × 8 h)' or replace it with the correct decomposition (6.24M / 10 rps = 624,000 s = 173.3 h). Confirm the figure note and the prose then agree exactly.

issue.issue: The x-axis is 'Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak', but the two anchors on that axis use different rates: the canonical point 6.24M req/mo is 10 rps over the active window (printed p. 254), while the feasible max 24.96M req/mo is 40 rps over the same window (figure note). So 'requests/month' is not a single-valued function of the varied quantity (duration), and a reader cannot tell which rate maps a given x-position to a duration. The natural reading (x = 40 rps × duration) puts the canonical point at 156,000 s, contradicting the 624,000 s window.
issue.evidence: X-axis label 'Requests/month (log) — duration varied at FIXED 40 rps peak, FIXED 21-host fleet'; note 'Feasible max = 40 rps × 624,000 active s/mo = 24.96M req/mo'; printed p. 254 '6.24M requests = 10 rps × 8 h'.
issue.acceptance_test: State the rate basis on the axis or in the note (e.g. 'x = requests/month at 10 rps average; peak 40 rps; feasible max = 40 rps × 624,000 s'), and confirm the canonical point and the feasible max are derived from one stated rate basis.

issue.figure: FIGURE 17.1 — Sizing a fleet of one model
issue.issue: The caption's failover caveat contains a self-contradictory arithmetic statement: 'the N = 1 residual (~6 req/s) clears the burst only at ρ = 1 — at ρ = 0.85 it is 3 × 2.0 = 6.0 rps, below the ~5.5 burst (ρ = 0.917 is needed to clear it)'. 6.0 rps is ABOVE the 5.5 burst, not below it; the ρ = 0.85 value is 0.85 × 6.0 = 5.1 rps. As printed, the sentence asserts the residual fails at ρ = 1 while the figure draws it at 6.0 rps above the 5.5 burst — a reader can conclude the failover case is infeasible even at ideal utilization, which is the opposite of the drawn geometry.

issue.issue: The grey shaded band across the top of the plot (roughly y = 8 to 12) carries the label 'ideal ρ = 1 analytical ceiling — no SLO claim', which describes a LINE, not a band. issue.issue: The x-axis carries six tick labels ('(single-shot) 0 1 2 3 4') against five drawn bars, so the reader cannot determine which bar is the single-shot case and which is turn 0.

The caption says 'from 24.9 GB single-shot to 34.0 GB at four turns', which implies six distinct states (single-shot plus turns 0–4), while only five bars are drawn. Turn 0 and single-shot are numerically identical (9,200 + 300 = 9,500 tokens), so the ambiguity is benign arithmetically but not visually.
issue.acceptance_test: Relabel the axis so the first bar reads 'single-shot' and the remaining four read 'turns 1–4' (or draw six bars and label them 'single-shot, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4'), and confirm the caption's 'from 24.9 GB single-shot to 34.0 GB at four turns' maps one-to-one onto the drawn bars.

issue.evidence: All five red value labels in panel (b) are set vertically above their bars; the same figure's panel (a) uses horizontal text throughout, so the two panels are typographically inconsistent.
issue.acceptance_test: Set all five value labels horizontally above their bars, centred, with >= 2 pt clearance from the bar top and from the panel title; confirm the labels remain legible in grayscale (red on white is fine; verify the value is not lost against the bar's dot hatch).

issue.issue: The four-entry legend is set as a single wide row that spans both panels and is squeezed into the same vertical band as the colliding note text, with no visual separation from the plot.
issue.evidence: Legend row reads 'initial context (L0) | retrieved (S=800) | generated (Y=65) | output (O=300)' and sits directly beneath the overlapping note lines, with the swatches and labels rendered at the smallest type in the figure.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.3 (Turn 4: three state-management policies) — formula note; and the L_T equation in section 19.5
issue.issue: The formula printed under Figure 19.3 for the append-only total omits the initial-context term, so as printed it does not evaluate to the plotted 34.0 GB; the same formula is written a second, differently-broken way in the prose on printed p. 306.
issue.evidence: Figure 19.3 note: 'append-only total = L4 = T*S + T*Y + O_final @ 2.62 MB/token'. With T=4, S=800, Y=65, O_final=300 this gives 3,760 tokens = 9.9 GB, not the 12,960 tokens / 34.0 GB plotted and labelled. The correct form is L_T = L0 + T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300 (T=4 -> 12,960 -> 33.96 GB ~ 34.0 GB). The prose on printed p. 306 prints 'L_T = T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800*T + 65*T = 300', which (i) equates a sum that omits 9,200 with a sum that includes it, and (ii) ends in '= 300' where '+ 300' is required. Figure 19.2's legend already uses the correct symbol for the initial context ('initial context (L0)'), so the book's own notation is available.
issue.acceptance_test: Print the formula in both places as L_T = L0 + T*S + T*Y + O_final = 9,200 + 800T + 65T + 300, and verify by substitution that T=0 -> 9,500 tokens -> 24.9 GB and T=4 -> 12,960 tokens -> 34.0 GB, matching the labels in Figures 19.2 and 19.3 exactly.

issue.issue: The compaction bar is drawn terminating exactly on the 'single-shot 24.9 GB' reference line and labelled with an equals sign, which asserts an exact equality that the caption's own wording ('holds the footprint roughly flat') and the ILLUSTRATIVE status do not support.
issue.evidence: The green bar's right edge coincides with the dashed 'single-shot 24.9 GB' line and carries the label '= 24.9 GB'. The caption states 'compaction (summarize or truncate accumulated history each turn) holds the footprint roughly flat', and the figure's own annotation labels the bar '[ILLUSTRATIVE] summarize/truncate each turn — moves the footprint'. A compaction policy that summarizes each turn still retains the current turn's context plus a summary, so exact equality with the single-shot footprint is not implied.
issue.acceptance_test: Either draw the compaction bar slightly below the 24.9 GB reference line and label it '~ 24.9 GB (illustrative)', or keep the coincidence and change the label to '~ 24.9 GB' with the caption changed to 'returns the footprint to approximately the single-shot level'. The label and the caption must agree on exact vs approximate.

issue.issue: The three value labels are set on top of, or hard against, the right ends of their bars, and the compaction label is green text over a green hatched bar.
issue.evidence: '34.0 GB' (red) sits over the right end of the red dotted bar; '= 24.9 GB' (green) sits over the right end of the green diagonally-hatched bar; '34.0 GB unchanged' (blue) abuts the right end of the blue cross-hatched bar. In grayscale the green-on-green-hatch case loses the glyph edges entirely.
issue.acceptance_test: Place all three value labels outside the bar ends with >= 3 pt clearance from the bar boundary, or place them inside the bars in white with a solid (non-hatched) backing. Verify each label remains readable when the page is converted to grayscale.

issue.issue: The parenthetical '(L4 = 9.2K input, S = 800 retrieved, Y = 65 generated, O_final = 300 output) (once)' mislabels the initial context as L4, which the figure itself defines as the four-turn total.
issue.evidence: The note reads 'L4 = 9.2K input' while the line above defines 'append-only total = L4'. The 9.2K figure is the initial context, which Figure 19.2's legend calls L0.
issue.acceptance_test: Change to '(L0 = 9.2K input, S = 800 retrieved, Y = 65 generated, O_final = 300 output) (once)' and confirm the symbol L0 is used consistently with Figure 19.2's legend.

issue.figure: FIGURE 19.1 (The agent loop: a four-state machine)
issue.issue: The figure is rendered at roughly 55–60% of the text-block width, which forces its role annotations and edge labels to be the smallest type in the book; the state machine is the chapter's central mental model and is currently under-sized for the page it occupies.
issue.evidence: The four state boxes plus the two terminal boxes occupy about half the measure, leaving large empty margins left and right. The italic role words ('model', 'action', 'state', 'check'), the sub-labels ('read, plan', 'tool call', 'append result', 'resolved?') and the edge labels ('loop (iterate) — not resolved', 'resolved', 'limit hit') are all visibly smaller than the caption's type.

Confirm the enlarged figure does not push the caption to the next page.

issue.issue: The 'resolved' label is positioned in the junction where the dashed loop-back line, the Decide-to-Final-answer arrow and the Decide-to-Stopped arrow meet, so it is ambiguous which edge it annotates.
issue.evidence: The word 'resolved' sits immediately below the dashed 'loop (iterate) — not resolved' line and above the 'Final answer' box, on the vertical segment that also carries the 'limit hit' branch. A reader can plausibly read 'resolved' as labelling the dashed loop-back edge (whose own label already says 'not resolved'), which would invert the meaning.
issue.acceptance_test: Move 'resolved' onto the Decide -> Final answer edge (offset to the left of that segment, clear of the dashed line) and 'limit hit' onto the Decide -> Stopped edge, with each label >= 3 pt from any other line or label. Verify at 300 dpi that no label can be read as belonging to a different edge.

issue.issue: Six different fill colours are used with no legend and no stated semantics, so colour appears to encode something that it does not.
issue.evidence: Plan is blue, Execute and Observe are green, Decide is pink, Final answer is purple, Stopped is orange; the italic role words are coloured to match. Nothing in the figure or caption says what the colours mean, and the only meaningful distinction (continuing states vs terminal states) is already carried by position and by the dashed vs solid loop line.

issue.figure: FIGURE 18.1 (Routing every request to the right specialised model)

issue.issue: The note is a run-on: the parenthetical '(early exit on a match)' is followed immediately by 'policy:' with no separator, so the sentence reads as if 'policy' were inside the parenthesis.

issue.figure: FIGURE 18.1, edge labels and leaf colours
issue.issue: The 'no' edge labels are the smallest type in the figure and are set in a colour that is not explained, while the three specialist leaves use two different fills (blue for Embedding/Vision, dark red for Math/reason) with no stated meaning — inviting the reader to infer a distinction that does not exist.
